News.title: UK wildfires: Flames rage near Shrewsbury as major incident also declared in Wales
News.content:
Firefighters are battling wildfires in Shropshire and South Wales, with crews declaring a major incident as they tackle the blaze in the Rhondda Valley

Firefighters in Shropshire are tackling a large blaze near a historic site, while crews in South Wales have declared a major incident as they battle a wildfire close to homes.

The blaze at Battlefield Heritage Park, a country park north of Shrewsbury, broke out on Monday afternoon. It is understood to be just a few fields away from the site associated with the 1403 Battle of Shrewsbury, fought between King Henry IV and a rebel army led by Henry "Harry Hotspur" Percy.

Meanwhile, crews from South Wales Fire and Rescue Service are battling a wildfire in the Llanwonno area of Rhondda Cynon Taf. The blaze, which began on Saturday afternoon, has already spread across around 150 hectares - roughly the size of 210 football pitches.

No homes have been evacuated, but Rhondda Cynon Taf Council said a rest centre has been set up at a local sports centre for residents affected by smoke and poor air quality from the fire.

News.title: Astonishing moment ram-raiding thieves drag cash machine away in a matter of seconds
News.content:
Astonishing moment ram-raiding thieves drag cash machine away in a matter of seconds

The Metropolitan Police is investigating the footage, which shows brazen thieves tow the cash machine away after attaching it to a car in Teddington, southwest London

Ram-raiding thieves try to break into cash machine with hammer - before towing ATM out of the ground

Shocking new footage shows the moment a band of ram-raiding thieves tow away a cash machine after trying to smash through it with a hammer.

‌



The brazen theft in Teddington, southwest London, was captured by a young woman on her mobile phone early on Wednesday morning, with police now hunting four men after seizing an abandoned vehicle.

‌



In CCTV footage, one man dressed in a black top, jeans, and a beanie hat, appears to use a hammer to try to smash the back of the machine.

‌



A few seconds later, a man is seen reversing from the busy road onto the pavement close to the standalone ATM, which was on the pavement outside a Londis.

View 2 Images One of the men attempted to smash into the cash machine with a hammer before it was taken by thieves (Image: / SWNS)

Man accused of killing Brit woman and stuffing body in suitcase is professional boxer READ MORE :

The same man then works with an accomplice to attach leads to the machine, after taking them from the boot of the car.

‌



A few seconds later, the car pulls away at speed, tearing the entire cash machine from its mounting on the pavement and onto the tarmac, sending sparks flying in its wake.

One of the men remains at the scene, standing over the empty space with a hammer in his hands.

View 2 Images Police said they are looking for four men in connection with the incident (Image: / SWNS)

‌



A local resident said: “I couldn’t really understand what had happened because I saw the machine lying on its side on the pavement on Tuesday morning and I assumed someone had crashed into it, not tried to take it away.”

No one has been arrested, though police have seized an abandoned vehicle believed to be connected with the incident.

A spokesperson from the Metropolitan Police said: “Police are investigating the theft of a cash machine from the outside a shop in Kingston Road, Teddington at 00:53hrs on Wednesday, 29 July.

Article continues below

“Although no arrests have been made at this stage, an abandoned vehicle has been seized in connection with the incident, and officers continue to work at pace to identify the four men believed to be involved.

“Anyone with information is asked to contact police on 101, quoting 302/29JUL.

“Anonymous reports can be shared via Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111 using the same reference number.”

News.title: Children at nursery where man drove off with wrong child 'put at significant risk of harm'
News.content:
Children at nursery where man drove off with wrong child 'put at significant risk of harm'

Jody Riley, from Merseyside, will now take care of her daughter Rosie full-time after the toddler was handed to the wrong grandad by staff at Kids Planet Crosby

View 2 Images Kids Planet Crosby (Image: Google Maps)

Staff at a Merseyside nursery where a grandad was given the wrong child and drove away are not consistently keeping children safe, Ofsted have found.

‌



An inspection from the education watchdog, found that safeguarding standards are not met at Kids Planet Crosby. The nursery referred itself to the watchdog after a two-year-old was handed to the wrong grandad on June 10.

‌



Jody Riley, 37 and from Formby, Merseyside, previously told the Liverpool ECHO that she received a call from the nursery saying her daughter Rosie was picked up by another child's grandfather. Two-year-old Rosie was driven away for at least 10 minutes before the man noticed the mistake and returned her to the nursery.

‌



The mother explained she was not going to take her daughter to Kids Planet Crosby again, adding she would be looking after her child full-time. An Ofsted inspection followed as a result with the findings published today, Liverpool ECHO reports.

View 2 Images Jody Riley pictured with her daughter, Rosie (Image: Liverpool Echo)

Two areas that require improvement are "children's welfare and wellbeing" and "leadership and governance", inspectors found. The report states: "Leaders have not ensured that safeguarding procedures are implemented consistently to keep children safe.

‌



"Weaknesses in staff deployment, supervision and collection procedures place children at significant risk of harm. As a result, children do not consistently benefit from the robust systems needed to protect their safety.

"During the inspection, children's privacy was not consistently considered during toileting and intimate care. The provider took immediate action to address this. However, children do not consistently experience the safe and well-organised environment they deserve."

Despite the "weaknesses", Ofsted stated that children develop warm and secure relationships with staff members, who know the kids' care routines, including sleeping, feeding and emotional needs, well. The report reads: "These positive aspects do not outweigh the significant weaknesses in the promotion of children's welfare and wellbeing."

‌



Regarding safeguarding, inspectors explained that leaders have not ensured that there is "an open and positive culture" around this. The report states: "This puts children at significant risk of harm.

"Weaknesses in the implementation of safeguarding policies and procedures mean children are not consistently kept safe. Staffing arrangements do not always assure children's safety and risk assessment arrangements are not sufficiently effective in identifying, managing and reducing known risks.

"As a result, children are exposed to unnecessary risk and their safety and welfare are not consistently promoted." It added: "Following a significant safeguarding incident, leaders took prompt action to strengthen safeguarding arrangements.

‌



"They improved collection procedures and restricted access to nursery rooms to reduce the risk of a similar incident occurring again. Furthermore, during the inspection, leaders took immediate action to ensure children's privacy is consistently maintained during toileting and intimate care.

"However, leaders cannot demonstrate that safeguarding arrangements consistently protect children from harm." The nursery failed to meet safeguarding standards and the requirements of the compulsory or voluntary part of the Childcare Register.

Due to this, the watchdog now plans to take enforcement action. The report said a Welfare Requirements Notice requiring the provider to undertake a four-point action plan had an assigned completion date of July 20, 2026.

‌



Across the four other areas inspected by Ofsted, which included achievement, behaviour, curriculum and inclusion, the nursery achieved expected standard. A spokesperson for Kids Planet said: "We remain deeply sorry for the serious safeguarding incident at Kids Planet Crosby. This was an isolated and unprecedented incident, caused by human error when relevant and well established procedures were not followed.

"We cooperated fully with the relevant authorities and police, all of whom have concluded their independent investigations and are satisfied the matter was handled appropriately. We also immediately reviewed collection procedures and security arrangements and carried out an extensive internal investigation.

"We take Ofsted’s findings extremely seriously and have implemented a comprehensive action plan covering safeguarding, training, supervision, staffing and risk assessments. Ofsted returned on 22 July to review this work, with its outcome summary to follow.

Article continues below

"Ofsted’s report recognises our prompt response to the incident while also highlighting the setting’s strengths, including children’s progress, warm relationships with staff, inclusive practice and strong partnerships with parents and professionals.

"Children’s safety and wellbeing remain, and will always remain, our absolute priority. We are committed to learning fully from this incident and ensuring that the improvements made are rigorously and consistently upheld."

News.title: DARREN LEWIS: 'Stop and search bias is leaving kids with lasting pain'
News.content:
Scrolling through the news on my break last week, I came across some footage that has stayed on my mind. It was of a bewildered young Black boy, who looked no older than 10 or 11, forced to lie face down by a Metropolitan Police officer who’d handcuffed him ­unnecessarily in East London.

The child was found to be entirely innocent but not before a trauma all too often dismissed by the advocates of stop and search targeting Black young men.

“What have I done? Why am I being arrested?” he pleaded with a voice yet to break, his hands locked behind his back and an officer crouched over him.

Witnesses claim the youngster had been among a group of white and Black kids play-fighting who’d dispersed at the sight of the officers approaching. The kind of harmless thing lots of mischievous young boys have done over the years.

‌



View 2 Images Darren says: "The data shows clearly that even as youngsters, Black people are seen by police as more of a threat." (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

“You’re not being arrested, you’re being detained,” said the officer who was handcuffing him.

So why shackle him? If the kid was simply being given “words of advice about his behaviour” as the Met Police claim, why embarrass and dehumanise him in order to do so?

Here’s where the term adultification bias comes into play. It describes the practice of harshly treating young boys and girls as though they are adults. A breach of child safeguarding and equalities legislation and guidance.

‌



In policing, adultification disproportionately affects Black ­children who are perceived as less vulnerable, and more culpable, than their white peers.

It resurfaced a few years ago with the horrendous case of Child Q, the 15-year-old Black schoolgirl ­wrongfully and traumatically ­strip-searched while menstruating by Metropolitan Police officers at her school in East London.

Statistics reveal Black children are up to eight times more likely to be strip-searched, face higher rates of stop-and-search and experience inflated risk assessments in the justice system – where their chance of ­reoffending is weighed up. In other words, the data shows clearly that even as youngsters, Black people are seen by police as more of a threat.

Mercifully last week, a white man passing by stopped to intervene. Widely praised for his role in ­de-escalating the incident, which went viral on social media, the man warned the officer repeatedly: “Be gentle with him, he’s a child.”

‌



Yet to be identified, the man calmed the distressed youngster down, comforted him and remained on the scene to, in effect, act in loco parentis.

A Met Police statement later claimed the officers on patrol had spotted “a group fighting” and that “from a distance it was not possible to tell how old they were”. The statement continued: “On noticing the police officers, the group ran from the area and dispersed, discarding items – including a balaclava – as they did so.

“Officers pursued two of the group on foot and detained one boy…[and] a stop and search was carried out.” Now, again. Why handcuff him? Why not just question him with the man who’d ­advocated for him as a witness?

“That decision [to stop and search] wasn’t based on race, [one] other boy just got away from a second officer,” said the statement. “The stop and search was done respectfully and officers fully explained why they had chased and stopped the boy.”

‌



So, “we humiliated and dehumanised him unnecessarily – but we did it respectfully”. As the Met admit themselves: “No offences were identified and all involved were given words of advice around their behaviour.”

We obviously support the police position of not wanting the public intimidated. But there has to be a better way.

Because proponents of the ­handcuff-first-ask-questions-later approach couldn’t care less about the lasting effects on those Black boys and girls, more often than not, found ­innocent. And those children matter. Their self-esteem matters. Their mental health matters. Their dignity matters.

News.title: UK travel company plunges into liquidation as customers issued vital update
News.content:
UK travel company plunges into liquidation as customers issued vital update

Ski Yodl, based in Norwich, has entered voluntary liquidation, according to The Gazette, after operating for eight years

View Image A UK travel firm has entered voluntary liquidation (Image: Getty Images)

A UK travel company is set to close after voluntarily entering liquidation.

‌



Ski Yodl Ltd, founded in March 2018, offered ski holiday packages to destinations including the French Alps.

‌



But after its eight years in operation, the company is now set to close. The company's Facebook profile says it offers holidaymakers the chance to "book an amazing, flexible, ski trip" and adds "We have the best locations".

‌



One customer praised the firm for "easy booking with cracking deals" and added "Wouldn't go anywhere else". Another said "Amazing. Great locations, self catered and great customer service."

A voluntary winding-up order was agreed on July 22, according to The Gazette, with Richard Cacho from RCM Advisory Limited appointed liquidator.

‌



UK travel firm that's been running for 24 years goes bust with holidays cancelled READ MORE :

All holidays cancelled with no refunds as major UK travel company goes bust READ MORE :

ABTA, one of the UK's largest travel trade associations, said: "We do not believe that there were any current customer bookings for package holidays at the time of liquidation.

"However, any customers who believe they may be affected should contact ABTA by emailing claimsrequest@abta.co.uk with details of their booking."

The company also arranged accommodation-only bookings, which were not covered by ABTA protection.

Article continues below

ABTA advised: "Customers that paid by credit or debit card and had accommodation-only bookings will need to contact their card issuer for assistance with obtaining a refund.

"Any customers that paid by other means such as bank transfer will need to register their claim with the liquidator, RCM Advisory Limited, on 01603 331960 or info@rcmadvisory.co.uk."

News.title: Father in his 30s shot dead as tributes pour in - 'I'll never forget you daddy'
News.content:
Father in his 30s shot dead as tributes pour in - 'I'll never forget you daddy'

Jimmy Ward, who died after a fatal shooting in Calcutt, near Cricklade in Wiltshire, has been described as a 'proud' father and grandfather

View Image Jimmy Ward (Image: Jimmy Ward/Facebook)

Tributes are pouring in for a "lovely" father who has been identified as the victim of a fatal shooting.

‌



Jimmy Ward, aged in his 30s, suffered a fatal gunshot wound as emergency services were called to the scene of the incident at around 8am yesterday. A murder investigation is now ongoing following the shooting at a traveller site in Calcutt, near Cricklade in Wiltshire.

‌



Two people who were arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and possession of a firearm remain in police custody. One suspect remains outstanding as they are believed to have "interacted" with the victim on Saturday evening.

‌



A police cordon is still in place at the scene and Wiltshire Police said this will likely remain so in the coming days. Tributes have now started pouring in for Mr Ward, who has been praised as a "legend" father and grandfather.

Six dead and dozens injured as tourist bus in horror head-on crash in Italy READ MORE :

One tribute written on social media read: "My lovely legend of a daddy, I'll never forget you daddy. I'll make sure you're done proud.

‌



"You were a proud daddy and grandad and carried my child around like he was a trophy. I love you forever my lovely beautiful daddy. I can't believe you're gone."

Another message read: "Rest in peace my cousin, Jimmy Ward. Lord watch over his family." Another message stated: "Rest in peace to my daughter-in-law's dad, Jimmy Ward. Please everyone pray for all the family. My heart goes out to them all."

One more tribute read: "Rest in peace Jimmy. I can't believe it. May you get the best bed in heaven my cousin."

Article continues below

Detective Chief Inspector Phil Walker, of Wiltshire Police, explained that officers are working at pace to locate the outstanding suspect. He said: "First and foremost, my thoughts remain with the victim’s friends and family at this sad time.

"Our investigation has been continuing at pace since the incident was first reported and it is a Force priority to locate the outstanding suspect, who is thought to have left the Wiltshire area. I understand the concern that this incident will have caused for our local communities.

"Our officers are currently at the scene and the Mobile Police Station is in Cricklade today – if you have any concerns or questions then please don’t hesitate to speak with us."

News.title: Man accused of killing Brit woman and stuffing body in suitcase is professional boxer
News.content:
Man accused of killing Brit woman and stuffing body in suitcase is professional boxer

Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, is accused of killing 38-year-old British charity worker Elisabeth Jane Ross, from Edinburgh, after her body was found inside a suitcase in an abandoned building in Greece

View 3 Images Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, is suspected of killing 38-year-old British charity worker Elisabeth Jane Ross (Image: INSTAGRAM)

A boxer accused of killing a British woman in Athens and stuffing her body in a suitcase has been pictured for the first time.

Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, is at the centre of a police investigation after the remains of Elisabeth Jane Ross, 38, from Edinburgh, were discovered in an abandoned building in the Kypseli district of Greece's capital last week.

Ahmadzai is accused of using Elisabeth's bank card to withdraw thousands of pounds from her account in the hours after the killing on July 16, and sending text messages from her phone in a bid to convince relatives she was alive.

Ms Ross's body was found by a homeless man inside a suitcase in a derelict building on July 18.

View 3 Images Elisabeth Jane Ross was found dead inside an abandoned building in Athens (Image: Facebook)

In one newly-released photograph, father-of-one Ahmadzai is seen brandishing a belt from the Professional Boxing Federation of Greece, having won a super lightweight boxing title in March.

The Afghani national arrived in the Greek island of Lesvos in 2016, and married American Alaina Hall in 2023.

The couple reportedly met Ms Ross, a Christian volunteer, through their charity Love Every Nation Athens, which they set up to help homeless people and refugees in the city.

Ms Hall raised concerns to the police about his behaviour in the days following Elisabeth's death, according to the Daily Mail and the Times.

She allegedly told detectives that he went missing on the evening of July 15, and that a location tracking app allegedly showed him at Elisabeth’s flat, which the couple had a key to access.

View 3 Images Ahmadzai pictured with his American wife Alaina Hall (Image: FACEBOOK)

Ahmadzai reportedly tried to give his wife €2,550 (£2,200) in cash along with a new Apple iPhone 17 Pro, but she later handed the items over to the police, suspecting they had been bought using her money.

When officers raided his home on August 1, they discovered a black metal replica pistol and a black military-style knife, local media said.

During questioning, Ahmadzai reportedly told detectives that Elisabeth was already dead when he found her, claiming he only put her in a suitcase so he could steal her money without drawing any suspicion.

Ahmadzai has since been arrested and charged in connection with Ms Ross's death. He faces charges of intentional homicide, robbery and weapons offences.

Article continues below

A statement from Hellenic Police said: "A 26-year-old foreigner was identified in the case and arrested for violating the weapons law. Cooperation was carried out with police authorities of the United States of America, the United Kingdom, and Scotland."

News.title: Toddler dies of heatstroke after being 'left in car' in scorching Canary Islands
News.content:
Toddler dies of heatstroke after being 'left in car' in scorching Canary Islands

The 20-month-old boy died at the Materno Infantil University Hospital in Gran Canaria's capital, Las Palmas

View 2 Images Las Palmas, Gran Canaria, Spain (Image: Getty Images)

A toddler has died of heatstroke after he was reportedly left in a car in scorching temperatures on a Spanish holiday island.

‌



The child, who was 20 months old, was in a serious condition when he was taken ill on Fuerteventura and then rushed to the island's general hospital on Saturday. He was then taken to a public hospital on Gran Canaria by air ambulance.

‌



The boy died in the early hours of Sunday at the Materno Infantil University Hospital in Gran Canaria's capital, Las Palmas. While local reports state the boy was left inside the vehicle, no other details have yet been released.

‌



It is unclear where the boy was from. Temperatures in the Canary Islands reached 45C at the weekend, with the current heatwave affecting the popular holiday destination for several few days.

View 2 Images Hospital Universitario Materno Infantil where the child was treated (Image: Google)

UK wildfires live: Flames rage near Shrewsbury as major incident also declared in Wales READ MORE :

Seven killed as drone hits packed Russian beach and tourists run for their lives READ MORE :

Gran Canaria was on red alert today and parts of the neighbouring island of Tenerife on orange alert because of the high temperatures.

‌



An 18-month-old called Sofia died last month after she was left inside a licensed nursery transport vehicle close to a famous tourist viewpoint near Lisbon for seven hours.

The girl is said to have been "forgotten" inside the vehicle in Almada on the southern bank of the Tagus River directly opposite the Portuguese capital. It was parked by the access to the giant religious Cristo Rei shrine featuring a tall statue of Jesus Christ with open arms facing the Portuguese capital.

Hundreds of tourists are said to have passed by the spot where the youngster was slowly dying in temperatures which reached 30C without seeing her behind the darkened and closed windows of the seven-seater SUV. The child's mum went to collect her in the afternoon on July 23 but was told the girl never arrived at the nursery.

Article continues below

Emergency services were then alerted just before 4pm but the girl was found in "critical condition" inside a Peugeot 5008 outside the main nursery campus. Despite resuscitation attempts, the girl was pronounced dead at the scene.

The creche which was supposed to take care of the toddler has been named as Colegio Mestre Cuco. A police investigation was launched.

In June, two children aged two and four were found dead in their family’s car in the town of Carpentras in southeastern France during a heatwave.

News.title: France hits out at Reform UK plan to return migrants using Navy
News.content:
France has hit out at a Reform UK plan to return migrant boats using the Navy, saying the proposals would violate its sovereignty and breach international law.

Nigel Farage's party announced that if it was in power it would intercept boats crossing the English Channel and return migrants to French ports, even if France disagreed.

Opposition parties branded the plan unworkable, while a Labour minister said it would lead to "a lot of time arguing with France" instead of "actually getting to grips with the problem".

Responding to the French government, a Reform spokesperson said: "We will always stand up for British interests and protect our people, whether Emmanuel Macron likes it or not."

The spokesperson added: "Humanitarian missions do not violate maritime or international law."

Under the plans, which Reform said it would bring in if it entered government after the next election, military-crewed inflatable boats deployed from 10 Navy patrol vessels would be used to "come alongside" migrant boats crossing the English Channel.

Border Force officers and police stationed onboard would be tasked with arresting people in the boats, and they would then be returned to France or Belgium by Navy personnel or Marines.

The party said returns operations would be conducted by military personnel with Border Force officers on hand in case of "non-compliance", with a Bay Class landing ship providing "detention capacity at sea" for up to 700 people.

Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Reform's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the party would aim to get agreement to disembark arrested migrants at French ports.

He added: "If the Elysee Palace refuses, make no mistake - His Majesty's Royal Marines will disembark them safely on the very shore they left that morning".

Speaking alongside him, Farage played down the prospect of a diplomatic confrontation with the French, claiming that attitudes in France towards the idea were "softening".

But in a statement issued later on Monday, the French interior ministry said: "This would constitute a violation of French sovereignty, as well as a violation of the law of the sea and international law."

A spokesperson for the department added that measures agreed with the UK, as well as "operations deployed at the local level", had already led to a reduction in crossings so far this year compared to the same period in 2025.

News.title: West Ham co-owner David Sullivan advised to stay away from home matches
News.content:
The recommendation from London Stadium comes after a joint investigation by BBC Panorama and The Times revealed that seven women have accused Sullivan of sexually exploitative and predatory behaviour. He has categorically denied the allegations.

He stood down as joint chairman of the club shortly before the investigation was broadcast, saying he wanted to focus on fighting what he called "factually incorrect and entirely false, decades-old allegations concerning my personal life". He remains the club's largest shareholder.

The investigation also revealed that Sullivan has been banned from contact with West Ham's women's and youth teams for three years due to safeguarding concerns. London Stadium were unaware of the restrictions until the BBC's report.

Sullivan was banned after a historic allegation about his conduct was raised with the Football Association in 2023. He has previously said the allegation was false and that because he had never met any academy or women's team players "1-2-1" during his 16 years at the club, he accepted what he saw as a "meaningless restrictionâ¦for a quiet life".

West Ham were relegated from the Premier League in May and are due to play their first home game of the new season, a Carabao Cup match against Portsmouth, on Saturday.

Sullivan was a regular attendee at the London Stadium last season, where he was photographed watching games from the directors' box.

A spokesperson for London Stadium, the operator of the publicly owned venue, said that "following media reports at the end of the season regarding a safeguarding matter being managed by the club, London Stadium sought further information to ensure it could fulfil its own safeguarding responsibilities".

It said that West Ham had told it that the "matter was investigated and that the club does not consider there to be an ongoing safeguarding risk associated with Mr Sullivan attending the stadium".

However it said that, despite this, it had recommended the businessman stay away from games because of the "potential for demonstrations and anti-social behaviour by some spectators".

Sullivan has previously faced criticism from fans over his running of the club, with thousands joining a protest in September last year calling for his departure.

West Ham declined to comment. It is understood that the club intends to work with the stadium operators to facilitate Sullivan's attendance at games.

Sullivan has not responded to a request for comment.

Meanwhile, presenter Tony Livesey left BBC Radio 5 Live on Monday after 16 years at the station, the corporation announced.

Livesey stepped back from his weekday late night talk show in June, following allegations made against Sullivan. He had previously worked as editor-in-chief of Sullivan's Daily and Sunday Sport publications.

One alleged victim said that Livesey had arranged a meeting between her and Sullivan in 1999.

Livesey said he had "no recollection" of introducing the young woman to Sullivan and that it was "not part" of his job to do so.

He added that he had "great sympathy for a woman who may have become a victim", but rejected any suggestion that he had played "any role whatsoever in that scenario" and said he found the allegation "abhorrent".

News.title: Inside city gripped by deadly protests in Pakistan-administered Kashmir
News.content:
Dozens of people have been killed in clashes between security officials and protesters across Pakistan-administered Kashmir over the last two months, following a crackdown that left the city of Rawalakot mostly sealed off from the world.

Leading the demonstrations is the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), which says it is protesting for rights including healthcare and electricity.

Authorities say the JAAC is trying to disrupt the current regional elections, that the group is armed, and will not be allowed to leave Rawalakot.

The JAAC was banned in June; they have been labelled foreign-funded terrorists by the government. They reject this characterisation, saying they are peaceful and - though funded from the Pakistan-administered Kashmir community abroad - not sponsored by India.

The BBC is the first media to gain access to the city and speak to people on the ground about what is going on at the heart of the protests. Pakistan correspondent Caroline Davies reports from Islamabad.

News.title: Son who kept mum's body in freezer for years collected £78k of her benefits
News.content:
The court heard Phillips moved downstairs to sleep next to his mother's body. At times he would open the freezer and hold her hand.

Sylvia Phillips had 26 appointments with her local GP practice in 2021, and six in 2022, after which there was no further contact.

The court heard she was last seen in A&E on 24 September 2022 and her local GP made a house call on 26 September but her son continued to pick up her prescriptions.

Sylvia Phillips was invited to a review by the practice, but her son said she would not come to the surgery and she did not need the blood tests.

Christopher Phillips received a total of Â£78,190.92 in state pension, pensions credit, attendance allowance, winter fuel payments, cost-of-living payments and housing benefit payments, which would have ceased had the death been reported.

He had been her primary carer since 2008, and the court heard he had resigned from his job in late 2022 when her health declined further. The pair were described as "somewhat isolated".

Ruth Smith, defending, said Phillips had told police: "I basically didn't want to let her go."

She added: "He described talking to her as if she was still aliveâ¦ Sitting next to her, talking to her about television programmes, Coronation Street, the horse racing, just as they always did," she said, adding that he was a "vulnerable individual".

Phillips sobbed in the dock as Smith said her client was "extremely close to his mother" and was in "extreme grief" following her death.

She said he showed a "lack of acceptance" about her passing and "had almost created a false narrative that she was still alive".

Sentencing Phillips to two years and four months - of which he will spend 40% in custody and the rest on licence - Judge Lloyd-Clarke said he had "deliberately concealed" his mother's death and "took steps to give the impression that she was still alive".

"You continued to collect her prescription and lied to medical professionals and eventually the police," Lloyd-Clarke added.

"Rather than notify the authorities and make arrangements for her lawful burial, you purchased a chest freezer on March 10th and concealed her body within it," she said.

Lloyd-Clarke added that a timescale for confiscation proceedings would follow.

News.title: X Factor finalist denies murdering influencer by running her over with car
News.content:
A former X Factor finalist has denied murdering a social media influencer by running her over with a car in central London.

Gabrielle Carrington of Manchester, allegedly struck Klaudia Zakrzewska outside Inca nightclub in Argyll Street, Soho, at 04:30 BST on 19 April.

The 29-year-old appeared at the Old Bailey by video link from Bronzefield prison to deny the charge. She had been initially charged with attempted murder but that was changed to murder after Zakrzewska died from her injuries six days later.

Carrington, who was not represented in court by a barrister, also denied a second charge of causing grievous bodily harm with intent to security guard Anoush Chyche.

The defendant was not asked to enter a plea to a third charge of driving with excess alcohol.

Family members of the victims shook their heads as the accused read out her pleas.

Judge Sarah Whitehouse KC confirmed the trial would be held at the same court from 5 January.

Carrington appeared emotional on the video link, wiping tears from her face throughout the hearing and was placed into custody afterwards.

News.title: Newspaper columnist and broadcaster Rod Liddle dies aged 66
News.content:
Newspaper columnist and broadcaster Rod Liddle has died aged 66 after a short illness.

Liddle's children paid tribute to their father, who they described as their guide "on how to live an extraordinary life", while CEO of News UK, Rebekah Brooks, called him "an inimitable journalistic force."

Brooks added that "he challenged conventional thinking and left an indelible mark on British journalism."

Liddle, a columnist for the Sun and the Sunday Times, died at The James Cook University Hospital in Middlesbrough on Sunday evening.

A former editor of BBC Radio 4's flagship Today programme, he also had a weekly column in the Spectator, as well as a show on Times Radio.

His children, Wilder, Tyler and Emmy, said: "We're all very saddened and shocked at the sudden passing of our wonderful father.

"He raised us much as you might imagine, to be inquisitive, brave and always humorous.

"Even in hospital in the last few weeks, he consistently held the room and never let the awful situation show.

"He has left a legacy that we are all incredibly proud of, he will always be our guide on how to live an extraordinary life."

News.title: Farage says he discussed return to politics months before general election
News.content:
Nigel Farage has told the BBC he discussed the "potential liabilities" of returning to politics before the 2024 general election.

It comes after The Sunday Times, external reported Farage had negotiated a deal in March and April 2024 with then-Reform leader Richard Tice to return to lead the party.

Farage confirmed he spoke with Tice in spring 2024 to scope out what would happen to Reform's finances if he returned but said it "wasn't a deal, it wasn't an agreement", adding that talks came "quite some time after" he received a Â£5m gift from a billionaire donor.

Labour said Farage's remarks had "blown a gaping hole" in his argument for not declaring the gift after becoming an MP in July 2024.

Farage has repeatedly argued the Â£5m from British cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne was an "unconditional gift", was intended for his personal security, "wasn't political in any sense at all" and he was not an MP when he received it.

Reform's opponents have said he should have declared it in the MPs' register of interests when he was elected to Parliament.

The Parliamentary Standards Commissioner was investigating whether Farage broke the rules, but the process was suspended when he stood down as Clacton MP last month to force a by-election.

Farage said he took this decision as the "people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions". The investigation will be resumed if Farage wins the by-election, which is taking place on 13 August.

Farage left frontline politics in 2021 and embarked on a broadcasting career.

In May 2024, Farage was serving as Reform's honorary president but announced he would not be standing as a candidate in the general election in July of that year.

He reversed this position at the beginning of June and took over the leadership of the party.

Appearing at a press conference on Monday, Farage was asked if he had negotiated a deal on what would happen to Reform's finances if he came back as leader - in light of the report in The Sunday Times.

He replied: "I had no intention of returning to politics or as leader of Reform, but in the spring of that year I did talk to Richard Tice about what the liabilities would be if I was to come back to that position.

"And you'd be a bit of a mug, wouldn't you, to walk into a job and not find out what the potential liabilities were, and they were substantial.

"But without Richard, the party wouldn't have even survived, so that was useful for me to know. But it wasn't a deal, it wasn't an agreement, it was subject to if I came back."

He added: "If you want clarification on this, that came quite some time after the gift, which is perhaps the important point."

Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, said: "Nigel Farage has blown a gaping hole in his excuse for why his secret Â£5m 'gift' from a crypto billionaire did not need to be declared."

The Commons code of conduct states that new MPs "must register all their current financial interests, and any registrable benefits (other than earnings) received in the 12 months before their election within one month of their election".

The rules say "purely personal gifts or benefits" from family or commercial loans would not normally have to be registered.

The rules also say "both the possible motive of the giver and the use to which the gift is to be put should be considered", adding "if there is any doubt, the benefit should be registered".

News.title: Xbox Series X price hiked by £170 due to rising memory chip costs
News.content:
Microsoft has increased the price of Xbox consoles worldwide, citing rising memory and storage chip costs.

Its premium Series X console with a disc drive will now cost Â£670, when it previously retailed for Â£500.

Meanwhile a baseline Xbox Series S console now costs Â£430 - a roughly 43% increase on its previous Â£300 price tag.

It is among a host of tech firms to have told consumers that spiralling component costs mean they must charge more, with rival Sony hiking PlayStation 5 prices by Â£90 in March.

Microsoft said in June it had "hoped another price increase would not be necessary", but blamed the rising cost of console storage and memory for needing to raise prices on consumers.

In the US, its basic consoles rose by $100 to $499, and the cost of a console with more memory increased by $150 to $749.

Similar increases have been revealed in the EU as well - where a Series S console with more storage will cost roughly â¬200 more than it did before.

As well as Sony increasing PlayStation prices, Steam Machine maker Valve launched its PC-console hybrid at a much higher cost than expected.

Both likewise pointed to mounting costs for the hardware and storage components needed to power their devices.

News.title: Woman has pioneering womb surgery to fix 'miracle' baby with intestines outside its body
News.content:
Doctors have used ground-breaking surgery on an unborn baby to successfully correct a birth defect while he was still inside the womb.

His mother, Maisie Savage, from London, was operated on by doctors in the US while she was 26 weeks pregnant.

Baby Theo, who is now five months old and thriving, had gastroschisis, where the belly button does not develop properly, causing the intestines to grow externally.

Doctors partially exposed his mother's womb and then gently pushed his organs back inside his abdomen using keyhole surgery.

He was the third baby in the world to benefit from the first-of-its-kind clinical trial.

Maisie, 29, and Theo's father, Josh French, 36, both teachers, say they are incredibly relieved by the success of the pioneering surgery.

"He's a little miracle, isn't he?" Maisie told BBC News.

But they both know things could have been very different.

The serious birth defect affects one in 3,000 UK babies each year. In the best-case scenarios, babies can require weeks in intensive care and nutritional feeding through a tube or IV and corrective surgery.

For the most complex cases, like Theo's, outcomes are far more serious with up to six months in neonatal intensive care, multiple surgeries, IV nutritional feeding for up to two years, and a possible intestinal transplant.

Even with the highest level of medical care, one in 10 babies will die.

News.title: Author La Plante banned from driving for six months
News.content:
The court heard she already had nine points on her licence, from three speeding offences in June 2023 and then June and July 2025.

She told the court she believed she would have to have the dog rehomed if she was unable to drive him to his daily walks, saying: "I think the emotional turmoil of that would truly damn my career as a writer.

"It's very, very solitary and I work exceptionally hard and I would just stop."

La Plante, who is best known for creating Prime Suspect's no-nonsense Det Ch Insp Jane Tennison, admitted driving at 24mph twice, 25mph, 26mph and 27mph in the latest offences, which all happened as she was on her way to take her dog for his daily walk.

Giving evidence, La Plante said she got her dog Theo after suffering the devastation of the untimely death of another dog, Hugo.

Fighting back tears, she said she "lost it" when Hugo died and she "didn't know what to do with [her] life".

She added her new dog had helped her through the grieving process.

News.title: Driest July on record for England and Wales
News.content:
July 2026 was the driest for England and Wales since records began 190 years ago, according to the Met Office, external.

England recorded just 6.5mm of rainfall and Wales had 9.3mm, both less than half of the previous records for the nations.

The dry conditions have been accompanied by exceptional warmth across much of the UK. It was the second warmest July for the UK as a whole and Wales' warmest ever.

The month was also the UK's sunniest July on record. For England and Wales, it was the sunniest calendar month ever observed.

So far this year, six months of 2026 have seen above average sunshine hours for the UK, with just February seeing below the monthly average.

News.title: Man sniffed out by police dog while hiding behind fake wall on 300-plant cannabis farm
News.content:
A man has been jailed for six months after being found by a sniffer dog behind a fake wall on a cannabis farm.

Albert Hysaj, 42, pleaded guilty to producing cannabis and was sentenced at Cardiff Crown Court on Friday.

Hysaj was caught after a police dog named Asko located him in the commercial property on the Bowen Industrial Estate, in Aberbargoed, Caerphilly county, in May.

Gwent Police found 313 cannabis plants inside two linked units over three rooms, which included a living area with kitchen and bathroom.

News.title: Presenter Tony Livesey leaves BBC Radio 5 Live after 16 years
News.content:
Presenter Tony Livesey has left BBC Radio 5 Live after 16 years at the station, the corporation has announced.

Livesey stepped back from his weekday late night talk show in June, following allegations made against his former newspaper boss David Sullivan.

He had previously worked as editor-in-chief of Sullivan's Daily and Sunday Sport publications.

Several women have accused Sullivan, a billionaire businessman and West Ham co-owner, of abusing his power and preying on them for sex, in some cases when they were teenagers. Sullivan has strongly denied the allegations.

The claims against Sullivan were made in a joint investigation by the Times and BBC Panorama.

The BBC previously said Livesey had asked to take a break from presenting his programme while the issues raised by the investigation were being examined.

One alleged victim said that Livesey had arranged a meeting between her and Sullivan in 1999.

Livesey said he had "no recollection" of introducing the young woman to Sullivan and that it was "not part" of his job to do so.

He added that he had "great sympathy for a woman who may have become a victim", but rejected any suggestion that he had played "any role whatsoever in that scenario" and said he found the allegation "abhorrent".

In an email sent to 5 Live staff on Monday morning, the station's controller Heidi Dawson said he had now decided to leave.

"Tony has asked me to pass on his heartfelt thanks to the brilliant colleagues at 5 Live who he has had the pleasure of working with over the years," she wrote.

"I know many of you have also really enjoyed working with Tony, and we wish him well for all his future endeavours."

The award-winning presenter worked for the BBC from 2006 - the same year he left the newspapers - appearing on 5 Live from 2010 onwards, including a successful stint hosting its drivetime show.

He won radio awards - ARIA and APAs - for his reporting on how it feels to lose your mother as a child, and an ARIAS gold award after he was asked by the late Dame Deborah James to conduct her final interview.

His topical three-hour programme was broadcast on 5 Live from Monday to Thursday, featuring interviews and phone calls from listeners.

News.title: Comedian Jimmy Cricket dies aged 80
News.content:
Comedian Jimmy Cricket has died aged 80 after a short illness, his family said.

In a statement posted to social media they said Cricket spent his last few days surrounded by his family, love, laughter and songs.

"Forever our clown, he was cracking jokes to the wonderful NHS staff and to us all, right until the end. His courage, dignity and positivity through all he endured was inspirational," they added.

The comedian, from Northern Ireland, became a household name in the 1970s.

James Joseph Mulgrew was born in Cookstown, County Tyrone in 1945, Cricket left school at 16 and started the summer season of 1966 as a Redcoat for Butlins.

He worked the comedy club scene in the 1970s and 1980s, going on to win LWT's Search for a Star talent contest and eventually getting his own TV show on ITV and a radio series on BBC Radio 2.

Cricket's family said he had been a "force for joy" and the world was a "far less sillier place today".

"We were going to end by using his famous catchphrase and say: 'There's no More'.

"But Jimmy was a man of great faith and a Papal Knight of the Catholic Church.

"He believed that death is not the end and was looking forward to eternity, so reallyâ¦ And there's more."

News.title: I didn't know I'd been hosting a parasite for years - until the most intense pain of my life
News.content:
Jones remembers the May 2016 night when he went into hospital â he was supposed to go out to a dinner with his wife Eileen, but he stayed at home as he felt unwell.

"I hadn't been able to control the pain, and it was more intense than anything I had before.

"Then about midnight, we had to call the ambulance, and they took me to Nevill Hall. Whatever they gave me there cured the pain. I haven't experienced pain like that before."

Jones was in hospital for 10 days, and says the doctors there suspected he had hydatid cysts immediately.

He said: "There was a lot of it around this area at the time, and I remember the Ministry of Agriculture giving worming treatment to the dogs on the local farms.

"Whether they could see that I was an old sheep farmer or not, that might have had a bearing on it. We had plenty of experience in this area â Breconshire as a whole â of hydatid cysts, people that have suffered through it, numerous examples."

Jones was then referred to "the main expert on hydatid cysts" in London where he had two operations in 2018 and 2019 to remove them, one from each lung.

"I swapped two cysts for two scars on the ribs," he said, adding that he still has a cyst on his liver, which surgeons decided not to remove.

News.title: Grooming gang found guilty of exploiting teenage girls for sex
News.content:
Four men and a woman have been found guilty of being part of a grooming gang that exploited teenage girls for sex.

Mustafa Iqbal, Mohamed Arshad, Ziaullah Badshah, Jaswinder Singh were convicted of conspiracy to traffic their victims, who were aged 14,15 and 16.

At Caernarfon Crown Court on Monday, Iqbal, Arshad and Badshah were also found guilty of rape while another member of the gang, Sarah Gray, was found guilty of perverting the course of justice and assisting an offender.

The men were remanded in custody ahead of sentencing on 25 September, while Gray was released on bail.

Prosecutor Owen Edwards KC said the men had used the three girls - named only as Child A, B and C - like "sexual commodities".

"They took full sexual advantage of Girl B in particular," he said.

The jury was told Child A had been treated as a "sexual plaything", who finally had gone to the police after having been handcuffed by Iqbal and had been raped.

The court heard the teenagers were given drugs and sexually abused in cars, homes and businesses in Rhyl, Denbighshire and the surrounding area between April 2022 and March 2024.

The first two victims, Child B who was 15 and Child C who was 14, were approached by Iqbal, 43, near a petrol station in the town, and he persuaded them to come back to his home.

They were later joined by local coffee shop owner Arshad, 36, and his friend Badshah, 25.

During the trial the jury had been told how the two girls stated they were 17, had smoked cannabis with the men and had played a game of spin the bottle.

Badshah, who came to Rhyl as a refugee from Pakistan when he was 15, admitted kissing Child B and Child C, and on later occasions having sex with Child B at his home.

Badshah, of Brighton Road, Rhyl, was found guilty of two counts of rape, two counts of conspiracy to traffic, two counts of conspiracy to require a person to perform compulsory labour, supplying cannabis to another.

Arshad, 36, of Clifton Grove, Rhyl, was found guilty of three counts of rape, two counts of conspiracy to traffic, two counts of conspiracy to require a person to perform compulsory labour, and supplying cannabis to another.

The court heard one of the counts of rape happened in an alleyway outside his former business, Zayn's Coffee House.

Iqbal, of Trellewelyn Road, Rhyl, was found guilty of raping Child B and also sexually assaulting Child C. He was also found guilty of raping another teenager, Child A, who was 16 and lived in a care home.

Described as a drug dealer during the trial, he supplied Child A with crack cocaine and cannabis in return for sex.

Iqbal was convicted of 21 offences, including four of rape and three of sexual assault. He was also found guilty of conspiracy to traffic and conspiracy to supply cannabis and cocaine, breaching a trafficking risk order, and he pleaded guilty to possessing a prohibited weapon.

The gang was unmasked after another friend of the men took Child B to London.

Former builder Singh, 61, claimed the girl was looking after his dog and there was no sexual motive in taking her on the trip to see his family in the capital, but a concerned adult was alarmed by Singh's intentions and reported him to the police.

Singh, of River Street, Rhyl, was found guilty of two counts of conspiracy to traffic and one count of supplying cannabis to another.

Gray, 53, of Llanasa Road, Gronant, was also found guilty of conspiracy to supply cocaine to another and conspiracy to supply cannabis to another.

After the guilty verdicts Det Ch Insp Richard Sidney said his thoughts were the three young victims.

"They were children, aged just 14 to 16, when they were subjected to exploitation and abuse by adults who took advantage of their vulnerabilities and sought to manipulate and control them for their own gain," he said.

"No child should have to experience what these young women endured."

He said that the five defendants had denied almost every allegation against them from the outset.

"I hope today's outcome sends a clear message that those who seek to groom and exploit vulnerable children will be relentlessly pursued," he said.

A spokesperson for Denbighshire council said its thoughts were with the young women at the centre of the case, adding that it wanted to "recognise the courage and bravery they have shown".

The spokesperson said the council would work with the North Wales Safeguarding Board on a review, separate to the criminal process, that would "examine agencies' involvement with the young people and to identify what lessons can be learnt for the future".

"We understand that this case has been challenging and has brought up strong feelings. We ask that everyone respects the legal process and each other as we process this outcome," they added.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line

A major incident has been declared in south Wales as firefighters battle a vast wildfire that has ravaged 150 hectares of land in the Rhondda valley.

Crews have been at the scene in Llanwonno, near Ferndale, since Saturday afternoon, grappling with the blaze across forest, scrubland, and vegetation.

South Wales Fire and Rescue Service (SWFRS) confirmed the significant scale of the fire, noting that the steep terrain has made efforts to bring it under control particularly challenging.

Drone footage has captured stark images of blackened ground and thick smoke billowing high above the valley, illustrating the intensity of the inferno.

Crews have been at the scene in Llanwonno, near Ferndale, since Saturday afternoon ( South Wales Fire and Rescue Service )

While residents of Blaenllechau and Ferndale have not been ordered to evacuate, a rest centre has been established at Rhondda Fach Leisure Centre in Tylorstown.

This facility is available for those who choose not to remain in their homes due to concerns over poor air quality caused by the smoke.

Those who wish to remain at home have been told to keep their windows and doors closed if they are affected by the smoke.

People have also been urged to avoid the area where possible and to follow advice from emergency services.

A no-fly zone has been put in place for the next week at the site of the wildfire.

The fire service anticipates that the incident will persist for several more days, with crews expected to remain on site overnight on Monday to conduct controlled burns as part of their strategy to manage the extensive wildfire.

A spokesperson for SWFRS said: “We have declared it a major incident as it requires a greater demand on our resource and as such more co-ordination.

“There are currently 20 fire engines at the scene, supported by two specialist wildfire teams, senior officers, a high-volume pumping unit and drone capability.”

The wildfire comes as provisional statistics from the Met Office showed Wales had its driest July in records dating back to 1836, amid a summer of extreme weather that has seen the whole country plunged into drought.

It comes amid a summer of extreme heat and dry weather across the country, which has seen four back-to-back heatwaves and left all of Wales and half of England plunged into drought.

The Democratic National Committee didn’t release a critical draft chapter as part of its report on the state of the party after the failures of the 2024 election, according to the report’s author.

Democratic strategist Paul Rivera told The New York Times that he hand-delivered a binder containing the chapter, entitled “What Happened in 2024,” to DNC Chair Ken Martin during a meeting in January.

The chapter, which Rivera shared in full with the paper, questions Joe Biden’s decision to seek reelection, scrutinizes how the party lost support among voters of color and takes aim at the influence of allegedly out-of-touch political consultants that got “generationally wealthy off politics.”

“In every other aspect of professional life, when you fail, you look back to understand what went wrong — not in politics and certainly not in this party,” Rivera told the paper. “The inability to accept responsibility gets in the way of change, reform, growth and progress, and that’s a huge missed opportunity for the party.”

The DNC strongly denied ever receiving the chapter.

open image in gallery The author of an infamous draft post-2024 ‘autopsy’ report about the Democrats claims the party didn’t release a key chapter ( AFP/Getty )

“As we said at the time, in May we released all of the draft report as we’d received it from the author,” DNC Chair Ken Martin told The Independent in a statement. “If we had this in May, we would have released it with the rest of the report.”

“To the best of our knowledge, this alleged report section was never shared with nor reviewed by the DNC — and we did not locate it in an extensive search of our files,” he added.

The drama over the autopsy is the latest twist in an increasingly public fight over the state of the party.

In December, Martin said the postmortem would not be released, calling it a “distraction.”

Under pressure from activists and political commentators, the DNC released a highly annotated draft version in May, though Martin disavowed its contents.

open image in gallery Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer. The Democratic Party is expected to make major gains during the 2026 midterms, though the DNC is well behind the Republicans on fundraising ( Reuters )

“When I received the report late last year, it wasn’t ready for primetime. Not even close,” Martin said in a statement at the time, adding that neither he nor the DNC endorsed its conclusions.

Critics claimed the released draft report left out other key details.

The postmortem report on the 2024 election did not mention questions regarding whether the Biden administration’s stance on Gaza hurt its campaign chances, nor did it detail the impact of concerns over Biden’s mental fitness.

The party, and Martin’s leadership, are under heavy scrutiny, with the DNC reportedly $2 million in debt and facing a pause from major donors.

Martin allegedly feels his time is up and has presided over a tense atmosphere inside the DNC. He is accused of throwing a phone onto a staffer’s desk, prompting a conversation with human resources, The New York Times previously reported.

The DNC declined to comment on the alleged incident.

Democrats are forecast to retake the House and potentially the Senate in the 2026 midterms this fall, but the party remains deeply divided over issues ranging from support for Israel to democratic socialist candidates.

News.title: West End star opens up on ‘impossible’ relationship with member of royal family
News.content:
Ruthie Henshall has opened up on her romance with Prince Edward, revealing that it was “never going to work”.

The West End icon had an on-off five-year relationship with the royal, after first meeting in 1988 when she was starring in Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Cats.

Appearing on Sunday Brunch on Sunday (2 August), the 59-year-old discussed her new memoir, The Showgirl and the Prince, which details the pair’s romance.

Host Tim Lovejoy described it as “the impossible relationship”. He explained: “He’s a prince and you’ve got a great career, it could never really work, could it?”

“No. It was never going to work,” she agreed, as she spoke about the complexities that come with being involved with the royal family.

Taylor Sheridan’s thriller series Lioness centers on an all-female undercover CIA operation that is loosely based on a real-life U.S. Marine unit.

Lioness, which returned with its third season August 2 on Paramount+, follows Zoe Saldaña’s character Joe McNamara, a CIA operative who leads a top-secret group of female special operatives recruited from various branches of the military and tasked with infiltrating terrorist organizations by befriending their wives and daughters.

In real life, Task Force Lioness operated out of Iraq and Afghanistan to identify women who might have been used to carry out terrorist activities. The concept inspired Lioness executive producer Jill Wagner, who also acts in the show, and her husband David Lemanowicz to approach Sheridan to write a series about it.

“I feared that someone would get a hold of this idea and just create Barbies with guns or try to make the women feel too superhero-like,” Wagner told Decider. “People have to understand that there are many female heroes in the world, and they’re not necessarily in Marvel movies. They’re out there sacrificing for our country, and they have really interesting stories to tell. Because of Taylor’s voice and his mind, I knew he was the one person who could do them justice. So that’s why I went to him.”

Read on for the true story of the all-female Lioness team.

open image in gallery Zoe Saldaña and Nicole Kidman star in ‘Lioness,’ which is loosely based on a real military group used in the Iraq War ( Paramount+ )

open image in gallery ‘Lioness’ is created by Taylor Sheridan, the mastermind behind ‘Yellowstone’ and its many spin-offs ( Paramount+ )

Who were the real-life Lionesses?

During the Iraq War in 2003, the American military ran into a problem as male soldiers stationed in Iraq were not allowed to search female civilians due to strict Muslim beliefs that prohibited any man from touching an unrelated woman.

Rebels quickly caught on to the issue and began to use women to smuggle weapons and explosives for terrorist attacks.

Soon, the Marine Corps and the Army formed the Lionesses to conduct more thorough surveillance on hijabi women. Team Lioness consisted of boots-on-the-ground female soldiers — often mechanics, clerks and engineers — who were deployed to combat units in Iraq and Afghanistan.

The women accompanied male troops on patrols and house-to-house operations, conducted searches on women and children at checkpoints and established rapport with women in the community for the sake of disseminating information and identifying people who might be involved in terrorist activity.

open image in gallery Team Lioness led to the establishment of the Female Engagement Team that was sent to Afghanistan in 2010 ( Getty )

The teams typically consisted of two to three female soldiers who joined combat and infantry units.

Eventually, the Lionesses trained local women on how to properly search other women and children so that they could take on the security responsibility after the troops left Iraq and Afghanistan.

Although women were prohibited from fighting in ground combat at the time due to the combat exclusion rule, many Team Lioness soldiers were caught up in conflicts like firefights and IED attacks that they were unequipped to handle as they were sent out to diffuse tensions between Iraqi citizens.

A 2008 PBS documentary called Lioness, directed by Meg McLagan and Daria Sommers, examined five women who were unexpectedly drawn into battle while volunteering for the unit.

“This may come as a shock to America, but we went on lots of missions,” said Shannon Morgan, a Team Lioness soldier who served in the U.S. Army’s 1st Engineer Battalion, in the documentary, according to USA Today.

“But if our government is going to allow us to play infantry, they should start training us for it. We pretty much wing it.”

What happened to the Lioness program?

Although Team Lioness was successful, the initiative was eventually phased out because of its short-term tactics. However, the program led to the Marine Corps officially establishing Female Engagement Teams in 2009, which focused more on gaining access to the community rather than being attached to combat units.

In 2013, the Department of Defense also lifted the combat exclusion rule, which allowed female members of the military to join combat units and further eliminated the need for a separate female team.

Although hundreds of women cycled through the all-female unit Team Lioness, the characters in Sheridan’s show — which stars Saldaña, Nicole Kidman and Morgan Freeman — are fictionalized and not based on any specific person.

New episodes of Lioness air Sundays at 3 a.m. ET / 12 a.m. PT on Paramount+.

Boeing has finally gotten FAA approval for the smallest variant of its Max jetliner, the 737 Max 7.

The plane can now enter commercial service, a decision that comes nearly a decade after the aircraft's initial unveiling.

The certification marks a significant turning point for Boeing, which has grappled with extensive safety, quality, and production issues for years. The 737 Max 7, a long-awaited addition to Boeing's best-selling 737 family, offers 135 to 160 seats.

The FAA confirmed that its clearance followed years of rigorous testing, design modifications, and a comprehensive evaluation of the aircraft's systems.

The approval process faced considerable delays as Boeing contended with technical problems and intensified regulatory oversight in the wake of two fatal crashes involving the larger Max 8 which claimed 346 lives in 2018 and 2019.

open image in gallery The first Boeing 737 MAX 7 aircraft sits on the tarmac outside of the Boeing factory on February 5, 2018 in Renton, Washington ( Getty Images )

These tragedies, occurring off the coast of Indonesia and in Ethiopia, prompted the FAA to completely revise its aircraft certification procedures for Boeing.

The agency stated that its scrutiny of the company would persist even after the Max 7's approval. Prior to granting its final endorsement, the FAA mandated several critical safety enhancements from Boeing. These included updates to flight-control software, improved cockpit alerts for pilots, and a redesign of the engine anti-ice system to mitigate overheating risks.

Stephanie Pope, president and CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, acknowledged the arduous journey, stating: "Our team of dedicated engineers and test experts worked through challenges, an extended pandemic, and the transition to new certification processes."

The agency further indicated that safety inspectors would maintain a presence at Boeing's production facilities to oversee manufacturing processes, including the company’s Safety Management System and its broader safety culture.

Boeing has built about 30 Max 7s and nine Max 10s, which are awaiting delivery, ‌according ⁠to aviation analytics firm Cirium.

The Max 7 is anticipated to serve primarily short- and medium-haul routes, with several airlines, notably Southwest Airlines, holding outstanding orders for the aircraft.

Southwest Airlines celebrated the approval and said it looks forward to the plane entering service in the coming months, though it does not have the Max 7 on its current schedule, which is through March 2027.

A company co-founded by the son of Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell plans to build and install tens of thousands of batteries in residential backyards — as the expansion of artificial intelligence data centers puts increased demand on power grids.

Energy startup Base Power, co-founded by Zach Dell and Justin Lopas, is installing batteries at homes in Texas and parts of Chicago that can be used when electricity demand spikes. The company acts as a retail power provider — it can feed energy to the grid during periods of high demand or provide backup power during outages.

Base, which launched three years ago, secured $1 billion in funding, boosting its valuation to $13 billion. The company has raised over $2.5 billion in all, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The financing round was led by Ribbit, Addition, Valor ​Equity Partners and JPMorganChase’s Strategic Investment Group. The co-founder’s father, Michael Dell, who recently made headlines for donating $6 billion to President Donald Trump’s “Trump Accounts,” is not a backer.

U.S. electricity demand hit record levels in 2025 — and is expected to continue to rise due to increased AI use, which requires even more energy storage.

open image in gallery Energy startup Base Power plans to install tens of thousands of batteries in backyards to help increased energy demand ( Getty Images )

The company has experienced rapid growth, installing more than 23,000 batteries across Texas and Chicago, but has plans to enter more states and eventually international markets, Zach Dell told the Journal.

Electrical grids in Texas, where Base mainly operates, have long experienced troubles under increased demand, including in 2021, when a powerful winter storm left millions of homes without power in freezing conditions, leading to over 200 deaths.

Base notes on its website that its tech is meant to withstand conditions spanning from Texas summers to Chicago winters, and has completed testing for “-22 to 122 Fahrenheit, flash flooding and submersion-rated to 3 feet.”

Base does about 100 installations each day, but anticipates being able to double that pace by the end of the year. Its systems sit near a home’s electric meter and are about the size of an air conditioning compressor unit, according to the report.

The batteries are also built to withstand extreme weather conditions and provide extended outage protection, Reuters reported.

open image in gallery Zach Dell’s father, Michael (left), recently donated $6 billion to President Trump’s ‘Trump Accounts’ ( AFP/Getty )

In deregulated markets, Base owns and operates the batteries while serving as the customer’s electricity provider, offering a more cost-effective electricity rate.

Meanwhile, in regulated markets, Base works with utilities and electric cooperatives to use the batteries to relieve local grid bottlenecks.

The company leases a space once occupied by the newspaper, the Austin American-Stateman, but is also planning to build a factory.

The company’s quick growth comes as battery demand in the U.S. is skyrocketing, as the systems are now viewed as a key way to strengthen power grids.

Base also said that it has entered partnerships with utilities including El Paso Electric, Austin Energy and CoServ.

You’ve probably heard that hitting 10,000 steps a day is the key to health and longevity. This magic number feels like a medical rule, handed down by doctors across the globe.

But where did it come from? And is it even true?

open image in gallery You’ve probably heard that hitting 10,000 steps a day is the key to health and longevity ( Getty/iStock )

Let’s step back to Japan in 1964

Believe it or not, but the infamous 10,000 steps a day recommendation didn’t come from a research laboratory. In fact, it is not scientific at all. It came from a Japanese pedometer called the manpo-kei which translates to “10,000-step meter”.

This pedometer went on sale just after the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, at a time when there was a growing worry people in Japan weren’t moving enough.

The number was mainly chosen was because it was catchy and easy to remember. The Japanese kanji character for 10,000 – 万 – even looks a little like a walking person, which may have played a role in deciding on the number.

So 10,000 was a slogan to sell a step-counter, not an evidence-based recommendation.

So many ideas about what makes us sick, or keeps us well, sound plausible. Early studies might sound promising. But then something gets twisted. In this series, we investigate how a grain of truth ends up as a common health myth. And we untangle what went wrong along the way.

So what does the research say?

Getting 10,000 steps a day can be a useful goal, and it will have a positive impact on your health. But you can reap health benefits from even less.

A recently published systematic review combined the results of 57 studies and more than 160,000 adults to examine the relationship between daily steps and health. Interestingly, they found 7,000 steps a day was where health benefits were maximised.

Reaching 7,000 steps a day was linked to a 47% lower risk of dying early, a 25% lower risk of cardiovascular disease (heart disease and stroke), a 14% lower risk of type 2 diabetes, a 38% lower risk of dementia, a 22% lower some of depression and a 28% lower risk of falls.

Some health benefits started well before 7,000 steps.

The researchers found going from about 2,000 to 4,000 steps a day makes a real difference. These health benefits then increase again slightly from 4,000 to 7,000 steps a day, after which the benefits start to plateau.

These results align closely with other research looking at all types of physical activity, where going from being inactive to moderately active yields the largest health improvements. Moving from a moderate to high level of activity does provide additional benefits, but these are much smaller in magnitude.

Why walking is good for you

Walking is a form of “aerobic” exercise. It raises your heart rate and places stress on your respiratory, muscular and cardiovascular systems.

If you do it regularly, it can improve your heart and metabolic health, and reduce your bodyweight.

Walking can also reduce stress and improve mental health, possibly due improvements in feelings of self-esteem and self-efficacy that comes with regular movement.

Steps versus minutes

There is some additional nuance that needs to be considered when discussing how far you walk each day: how hard you walk.

Most people choose a walking pace that pushes them into the realm of “moderate intensity” exercise. However, the health benefits of exercise scale up with exercise intensity: you get more bang for your buck from more intense exercise.

So, if you pick up the pace and move towards a vigorous exercise intensity (where it’s hard to maintain a conversation), you will get larger health benefits in less time. This is why official exercise guidelines treat 75 minutes of vigorous activity as roughly equal to 150 minutes of moderate activity.

With this in mind, rather than focusing on steps, you might be better off focusing on the number of minutes you accumulate each week.

About the author Hunter Bennett is a Lecturer in Exercise Science, Adelaide University. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

Recent research even suggests short bursts of high-intensity exercise spread across the day can have surprising health benefits.

So, if you’re short on time, walking faster is one of the simplest ways to get more out of that same walk.

But walking alone isn’t enough

Walking covers the “aerobic” side of fitness well. However, it doesn’t really address the “anaerobic” side.

Anaerobic fitness refers to your muscle mass, muscle strength, and power. Having higher anaerobic fitness is linked to having a better quality of life and lower risk of mortality as you get older.

This is why most health authorities recommend muscle-strengthening activities (such as lifting weights) at least two days a week.

This will also help reduce your risk of type 2 diabetes, while also helping you avoid falls and stay independent for longer as you get older.

If you can aim to hit 7,000 steps each day, and add in weight training twice per week, you’re going to have most of your bases covered from a health perspective.

News.title: Bestselling author Lynda La Plante says six-month driving ban could end her career
News.content:
