World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ð½ðððð¢ ððððððð (@nancysinatra)

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.

World.title: Full Moon in June 2025: Date, Meaning, and What’s Ahead in the Night Sky
World.content:
The full moon in June 2025 will occur on Wednesday, June 11, and will be visible in most regions depending on local moonrise and moonset times. Known as the Strawberry Moon, this lunar event is tied to Native American traditions marking the ripening of wild strawberries and the approach of summer in the Northern Hemisphere.

In Argentina, for example, the moon will rise around 5:52 p.m. and set at 9:19 a.m. on June 12. This full moon, like others throughout the year, has long held cultural, astrological, and even emotional significance. World.title: Japan Tops Global Waste Index 2025; U.S., Israel, and Chile Rank as Worst Polluters
World.content:
Japan has emerged as the world leader in waste management, while Israel, Chile, and the United States rank among the worst-performing countries, according to the Global Waste Index 2025 released by Slovak-based waste technology company Sensoneo.

The report, which ranks all 38 OECD member states based on their waste generation and disposal practices, highlights significant disparities in global waste management. Sensoneoâs index evaluates countries on per capita waste generation, recycling, incineration, and landfill use.

Israel and Chile ranked last and second-to-last, respectively, primarily due to their heavy reliance on environmentally damaging landfilling practices. Israel sends 524 of the 650 kilograms of waste it generates per person each year directly to landfills. Chile recycles just 1% of its waste and sends more than 95% to landfill.

The United States, which increased its per capita waste generation from 811 to 951 kilograms since 2022, remains the highest generator of municipal solid waste globally. The U.S. disposes of nearly half of that â 447 kilograms â in landfills annually. Neighboring Canada also performed poorly, landfilling 67% of its annual 694 kg per capita waste.

At the other end of the spectrum, Japan ranked No. 1, followed by South Korea and Estonia, all of which combine relatively low waste generation with efficient disposal methods. Japan sends only 3 kilograms per capita to landfill, relying heavily on incineration (245 kg) and maintaining a controlled recycling rate.

European countries dominated the top 10 rankings, with Austria, Germany, Finland, Belgium, Sweden, Norway, and Switzerland all demonstrating strong waste management systems. Austria topped the recycling chart with 334 kilograms of municipal waste recycled per person annually â accounting for 42% of its total waste.

Meanwhile, Spain fell four places to 27th despite minor improvements. The country reduced its landfill and incineration rates slightly while increasing recycling by 10 kilograms per capita. However, its overall waste generation rose by 10 kg compared to the 2022 index.

The index revealed that in 12 of the 38 countries, over half of all waste is still landfilled â including in developed nations like Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. By contrast, Switzerland was the only country to report zero landfill disposal, while Belgium, Finland, Estonia, and Japan landfilled less than 3 kg per person.

Other key findings include:

New Zealand , Finland , and Iceland posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita.

, , and posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita. From an environmental standpoint, incineration is considered preferable to landfilling, but excessive reliance on either suggests a need for stronger waste reduction and recycling strategies.

About the Index and Sensoneo

First launched in 2019, the Global Waste Index is published every three years by Sensoneo, a company specializing in digital transformation for waste management systems. The 2025 edition is based on the latest available national data.

Sensoneo operates in 87 countries and provides waste monitoring solutions to cities, industries, and governments. It is the only company to have successfully implemented deposit return systems (DRS) IT infrastructure in nine countries, achieving recycling rates above 90%.

In Madrid, Sensoneo is deploying 11,100 smart sensors, marking the worldâs largest smart waste monitoring installation to date.

World.title: South Korean Model and Actor Kim Jong Suk Dies at 29, Family Urges Respect Amid Speculation
World.content:
South Korean model and television personality Kim Jong Suk has died at the age of 29, his family confirmed on June 6. The news has shocked fans and colleagues across the countryâs entertainment industry, where Kim rose to prominence following his appearance on tvNâs 2022 reality dating show Skip Dating.

Kim, who began his career in modeling before transitioning to television, had been steadily gaining popularity in recent years. His sudden death has prompted an outpouring of grief and speculation online.

While the exact cause of death remains unconfirmed, some media reports have linked Kimâs passing to an incident in Hanam involving a violent altercation between a young man and his girlfriend. According to the reports, law enforcement responded to the scene, after which the man allegedly died by suicide after jumping from a high-rise building.

Amid widespread online discussion and conjecture, Kimâs family issued a public plea for restraint, asking the public and media to refrain from spreading misinformation or making disrespectful assumptions.

Kimâs older sister posted on social media, expressing the family’s devastation and emotional exhaustion. âWe ask for privacy and understanding during this difficult time,â she wrote, emphasizing the familyâs wish to grieve in peace.

Details regarding funeral arrangements have not been made public.

World.title: Infantino opponents threaten non-cooperation with FIFA unless he resigns
World.content:
Infantino opponents threaten non-cooperation with FIFA unless he resigns

3rd Monday, August 2026 - 20:24 UTC Full article

The scope of that non-cooperation has not been defined. One senior figure told the broadcaster a refusal to take part in FIFA meetings could be expected

Officials opposed to FIFA president Gianni Infantino are considering withdrawing cooperation with the governing body for as long as he remains in office, according to UEFA sources cited by the BBC, as the fallout deepens over the plan to open a commercial subsidiary handling the rights to its tournaments to private investors.

The scope of that non-cooperation has not been defined. One senior figure told the broadcaster a refusal to take part in FIFA meetings could be expected. Others involved say there is no going back while Infantino remains in place.

FIFA withdrew the project, known as FIFA Forward Enterprise, on Saturday, August 1, hours after Conmebol issued a statement seeking clarification without taking a position. The South American body was the last of the six confederations to respond, following rejections from UEFA, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation. Infantino said all views had been heard and that the initiative would not proceed.

The withdrawal did not end the dispute. UEFA sent a letter warning that it is weighing legal action, arbitration or regulatory complaints, and demanding the preservation of all documentation linked to the project, including emails, instant messaging and meeting notes, regardless of internal deletion policies. UEFA vice-president Laura McAllister described the governance process behind the initiative as deficient and said she hoped for a change of leadership next year.

Two statutory routes exist to force a departure. An emergency meeting of the FIFA Council requires a request from 19 of its 37 members and must be held within two weeks; UEFA holds nine seats, the AFC seven, Africa six, Concacaf five, Conmebol five and Oceania three, alongside Infantino and Secretary General Mattias Grafström. Separately, and according to The Telegraph, UEFA is prepared to pursue a no-confidence motion, which would need the backing of 43 associations.

Wales was the first country to publicly withdraw support for Infantino's bid for a fourth term; Serbia, Sweden and Finland followed, and the English Football Association is expected to do the same. Morocco, Qatar, Lebanon, Kuwait and Sri Lanka have pledged support for his continuation. The election takes place in March 2027 and requires 106 of the 211 votes: UEFA holds 55, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10.

Figures on the project vary by source. The BBC reports that Infantino offered associations 40 million dollars, with an initial 20 million if they accepted before September 19; other coverage puts at 4.2 billion dollars the capital being sought. The investor group was reportedly to be led by the New York firm founded by Joshua Kushner, brother of the US president's son-in-law. Infantino's senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned on July 31.

World.title: Milei: the alliance with Washington is the "key" to sovereignty over the Falklands
World.content:
Milei: the alliance with Washington is the “key” to sovereignty over the Falklands

3rd Monday, August 2026 - 19:14 UTC Full article

Milei described the claim as non-negotiable and said his government has achieved the greatest diplomatic progress since 1983 toward placing the archipelago under Argentine administration

Argentine President Javier Milei said on Monday that his government's alignment with the United States will advance Argentina's sovereignty claim over the Falklands, in remarks to Radio Mitre.

The United States has changed its strategic view of the world, he said, and needs a reliable ally on the passage from the Atlantic to the Pacific; Argentina meets those conditions, and that is the key that will allow it to recover the islands. No public statement from Washington supports that reading: the US position on the sovereignty dispute has historically been one of neutrality.

Milei described the claim as non-negotiable and said his government has achieved the greatest diplomatic progress since 1983 toward placing the archipelago, along with South Georgia, the South Sandwich Islands and surrounding maritime areas, under Argentine administration. That is the president's own assessment.

He also said that for the first time the UN is obliging the United Kingdom to sit down for talks. The claim is inaccurate. Resolutions by the Decolonization Committee urging Argentina and the United Kingdom to resume discussions are non-binding and have been adopted for decades, without sovereignty negotiations taking place. Britain's consistent position is that sovereignty is not up for discussion and that any change would depend on the islanders' wishes.

The Falklands are a British Overseas Territory. In a 2013 referendum, residents voted overwhelmingly to retain that status. Argentina maintains a claim over the archipelago, which the United Kingdom has administered since 1833.

Asked about the Sea Lion oil project, developed by British and Israeli companies in waters near the islands that Argentina claims, Milei said his government had lodged the corresponding diplomatic protests but defended the venture's private character. Argentina is an ally of the United States and Israel, he said, but the company is private, and a serious country does not interfere in the private sector. The project's first phase envisages investment of around 1.8 billion dollars and estimated output above 170 million barrels.

The president also addressed the banner reading “Las Malvinas son argentinas” displayed by Argentine players after the World Cup semifinal against England, saying the episode had not affected dialogue with London. Sporting matters are one thing and matters of national identity another, he said. On July 29, FIFA opened disciplinary proceedings against the Argentine Football Association that include messages with political content.

The strategy is not new: Milei had already set it out at the April 2 commemoration, when he linked the claim to alignment with Washington and to rearmament.

World.title: Traditional right-wing technocrats and Christian voices will share Colombia's new cabinet
World.content:
Traditional right-wing technocrats and Christian voices will share Colombia's new cabinet

3rd Monday, August 2026 - 18:48 UTC Full article

The inauguration will take place on Friday, August 7, at the Arena USC of the Santiago de Cali University, outside the capital, for the 2026-2030 term

Colombia's president-elect, Abelardo de la Espriella, has completed all eighteen posts in his cabinet four days before taking office, with a team that will combine technical profiles drawn from the traditional right with figures close to Christian movements and to positions aligned with Trumpism.

The inauguration will take place on Friday, August 7, at the Arena USC of the Santiago de Cali University, outside the capital, for the 2026-2030 term. The government program is called “Patria Milagro.” Vice President-elect José Manuel Restrepo, an economist who served as trade and finance minister under Iván Duque, heads the transition team working with Gustavo Petro's outgoing government.

Several appointments come from the right with institutional track records. The Interior Ministry will go to Rodrigo Lara, a former Cambio Radical senator; Finance to Miguel Gómez; and Justice to criminal lawyer Iván Cancino. Transport will be headed by Elsa Noguera, former mayor of Barranquilla and former governor of Atlántico, who served as housing minister under Juan Manuel Santos and built her career within Cambio Radical. Defense will be led by retired Major General Jorge Eduardo Mora López, who should not be confused with General Jorge Enrique Mora Rangel, a negotiator in the Havana peace talks.

The Health Ministry will fall to Ana María Vesga, a lawyer with fifteen years in the sector who until now headed Acemi, the association representing the eleven private insurers of the contributory health regime, entities the ministry regulates. The president-elect has tasked her with an emergency plan for the system's crisis. Culture will go to Paola Holguín, a Centro Democrático senator between 2014 and 2026.

Other appointments reflect a different profile. The foreign ministry will be headed by diplomat Omar Bula, who according to El País criticizes the United Nations, warns of what he calls an anti-Western globalist agenda and holds that climate change is an ideological construct. Those positions have not been independently verified. Housing will go to pastor and former Bucaramanga mayor Jaime Andrés Beltrán, and Education to former senator and former attorney general Viviane Morales, who has publicly opposed same-sex marriage, adoption by same-sex couples, euthanasia and abortion. Her appointment, to a portfolio outside her field, has raised concern among LGBTI organizations.

De la Espriella, a criminal defense lawyer with no previous experience in public office, won the June 21 election on a campaign built around a break with the political establishment. He has announced measures with strong symbolic weight, including moving national agencies out of Bogotá, designating Barranquilla as an alternate seat of government and turning the current presidential palace into a museum, alongside ultimatums to illegal armed groups, tougher sentencing and tax cuts.

World.title: Rhine barges run at 20% of capacity as freight rates surge
World.content:
Rhine barges run at 20% of capacity as freight rates surge

3rd Monday, August 2026 - 18:47 UTC Full article

At levels of 40 to 50 centimeters, vessels can carry around 20% of their normal volume

Falling water levels on the Rhine are forcing barges to operate with a fraction of their usual load and have sharply raised the cost of river transport, as drought and extreme temperatures affect Europe's main inland waterways.

At levels of 40 to 50 centimeters, vessels can carry around 20% of their normal volume, according to Germany's federal waterways administration; industry estimates put current operations at between 20% and 30%. Freight rates from Rotterdam have more than tripled in two months, according to figures reported by the Dutch press, which puts them at around 45 euros per ton in June and close to 150 in July.

The gauge at Kaub, near Koblenz, is the benchmark indicator because it determines how heavily vessels can be loaded. On Friday it fell to 25 centimeters, matching the 2018 low, before recovering slightly on Monday. A drop to 24 centimeters, forecast for this week, would mark the lowest level since records began in 1880, according to German federal data compiled by ETH Zurich.

Records have been broken elsewhere. At Cologne and at Lobith, where the river enters the Netherlands, levels were the lowest in the historical series: at Lobith, 6.47 meters above the Dutch reference datum, below the August 2022 low. Inflow is running at around 692 cubic meters per second, against roughly 1,900 typical for this time of year. Germany's low-water information system recorded extremely low levels at the end of July at 44% of Rhine measuring stations and 78% of those on the Danube.

An official from the Rhine waterways and shipping authority told broadcaster WDR that a full halt to traffic is unlikely, but that cargo will have to be spread across more vessels, which over time raises costs and creates bottlenecks.

The effects extend to electricity supply. Hungary shut down its only nuclear plant entirely on Sunday, for the first time in 44 years of operation, removing around 40% of its generating capacity and forcing higher imports. Serbia cut output at its coal-fired plants because of cooling problems, and Romania carried out a controlled blast on the Danube to redirect water toward the Cernavodă plant. Two Romanian car plants agreed to halt production for more than a fortnight to reduce electricity consumption.

In Italy, the Po reached a historic low near Cremona in late July and the drought alert was raised to high across the entire valley. Reduced discharge has allowed saltwater to push in from the sea, damaging irrigated crops.

David Hannah, professor of hydrology at the University of Birmingham, said warming raises baseline temperatures and reduces river flows, and pointed to diminished snow and glacier runoff from the Alps. Dominik Schumacher, of ETH Zurich, said human-induced warming has already made this drought more severe.

World.title: Milei on Lula: released over a procedural flaw, not for being innocent
World.content:
Milei on Lula: released over a procedural flaw, not for being innocent

3rd Monday, August 2026 - 16:08 UTC Full article

Lula is a “thief and corrupt,” Milei said; he was “convicted and imprisoned, and was released over an administrative flaw rather than for being innocent.”

Argentine President Javier Milei repeated his accusations against Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday, arguing that the corruption convictions once against him were annulled on formal grounds, in remarks that came just as Brazil's ambassador to Buenos Aires was preparing to return after being recalled for consultations.

Lula is a “thief and corrupt,” Milei said; he was “convicted and imprisoned, and was released over an administrative flaw rather than for being innocent.” He spoke in an interview recorded at the presidential palace and broadcast by LN+. Asked whether his tone was aggressive, he replied that calling a thief a thief is milder than the act of theft itself. These are the Argentine president's accusations, not judicial findings.

The legal sequence is more complex than described. Lula was convicted in 2017 and 2019 in the Lava Jato investigation and spent 580 days in detention. He left prison in November 2019 after a Supreme Federal Court ruling holding that no one may be jailed before appeals are exhausted, a decision grounded in the presumption of innocence. In March 2021, Justice Edson Fachin annulled the convictions on the grounds that the Curitiba court lacked jurisdiction, a finding the full court upheld eight votes to three. That June, the court's Second Panel further ruled that Judge Sergio Moro, who had issued the first conviction and later served as Jair Bolsonaro's justice minister, had been biased — a ruling on due process rather than a technicality. In 2023, the court also annulled the evidence gathered by the Lava Jato team.

Lula holds no valid convictions, regained his political rights and was elected president in 2022. No court ruled on the merits of the accusations.

Milei described his remarks as spontaneous and framed them within a regional ideological dispute. He said he is criticized for what he says while the insults he claims to have received from figures such as Gustavo Petro, Evo Morales, Rafael Correa and Pedro Sánchez go unmentioned.

The crisis began on Saturday, July 25, when Milei addressed the Liberal Party convention in São Paulo, backing Flávio Bolsonaro's candidacy. There he called Lula a thief, corrupt and a convict, and directed an insult about the physical appearance of Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes. Itamaraty summoned Argentine Ambassador Daniel Raimondi, called the episode unprecedented and recalled Julio Bitelli. Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira ruled out tougher measures for now, such as withdrawing diplomatic representation; the embassy is being run by Minister-Counsellor Eduardo Uziel.

On Thursday, Brasília authorized Bitelli's return without setting a date. According to Infobae, Lula sharpened his tone over the weekend at an event in Ceará, saying that as long as he lives the far right will not govern Brazil again.

World.title: Milei says he has chosen a 2027 running mate amid rupture with his vice president
World.content:
Milei says he has chosen a 2027 running mate amid rupture with his vice president

3rd Monday, August 2026 - 07:24 UTC Full article

He said he has settled on his running mate for next year but prefers to keep the name to himself for now, in an interview published on Sunday by Diario Río Negro

Argentine President Javier Milei said he has already decided who will run alongside him as vice-presidential candidate in the October 2027 elections, while withholding the name, in remarks that come amid an open confrontation with his current vice president, Victoria Villarruel.

He said he has settled on his running mate for next year but prefers to keep the name to himself for now, in an interview published on Sunday by Diario Río Negro. The wording implies he will not repeat the 2023 ticket. Milei and Villarruel are not on speaking terms and criticize each other publicly; Cabinet Chief Diego Santilli called for her resignation after remarks she made about the president. Argentina's constitution permits one consecutive re-election.

Milei had already confirmed weeks earlier, at an event at the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange, that he would seek a second term. The new element is the choice of a vice-presidential candidate.

In the same interview he renewed his call to abolish the open, simultaneous and mandatory primaries, putting their cost to the state at 250 million dollars a year, and argued parties should settle internal contests without public funding. The primaries were suspended for the 2025 elections and their status for 2027 has not been settled.

The president also confirmed that the overhaul of the central bank's charter will be the government's main legislative initiative this semester. The bill, submitted to the Chamber of Deputies on Friday, establishes preserving the value of the currency as the institution's sole mission and bars all channels of financing to the Treasury. Central bank presidents need to be shielded from removal by whoever holds power, he said.

On the economy, Milei said results are exceeding expectations and credited his administration with maintaining a fiscal surplus, slowing inflation, lifting currency controls and rebuilding reserves. He projected the country will post three consecutive years of growth for the first time in fifteen years and said economic activity had surpassed its historical peak. These are the president's own assertions, without independent verification.

He acknowledged that part of the population has yet to feel the improvement, saying it is normal that some Argentines do not yet see the trend in their pockets, that fixing in two years what took a century to break requires time, and that he will not offer shortcuts.

Milei also highlighted the incentive regime for large investments, citing more than 46 billion dollars in approved projects and over 100 billion under evaluation, with particular weight in the Patagonian provinces. At the Stock Exchange he had pledged that, if growth holds, his government would by 2031 have returned 500 billion dollars to Argentines through tax cuts.

World.title: Conflicting accounts over whether Spanish intelligence warned of mass entry into Ceuta
World.content:
Conflicting accounts over whether Spanish intelligence warned of mass entry into Ceuta

3rd Monday, August 2026 - 07:20 UTC Full article

The newspaper The Objective reported that intelligence assessments had flagged a possible mass entry into Ceuta and Melilla coinciding with Morocco's Throne Day

Spanish intelligence services concluded that Morocco did not plan last Thursday's mass entry of people into Ceuta, although it allowed the crossings and drew political benefit from the international attention, according to sources cited by El País. Other reporting contradicts that account on a key point: whether the government was warned in advance.

The newspaper The Objective reported that intelligence assessments had flagged a possible mass entry into Ceuta and Melilla coinciding with Morocco's Throne Day. Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said in Ceuta on Saturday, by contrast, that the intelligence services gave no warning of what was building on the other side of the border. Both versions rest on unidentified sources, and the Defense Ministry has neither confirmed nor denied them, citing the classified status of National Intelligence Center reports.

Morocco commented publicly for the first time on Monday, attributing the events to human trafficking networks, disinformation and misreadings of a Spanish Supreme Court ruling. Spain's Interior Ministry and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez hold the same view of the trigger.

That ruling, issued by the administrative chamber, established that people reaching Ceuta and Melilla by swimming cannot be summarily returned without a formal procedure. It does not declare border returns illegal nor amend immigration law: it sets binding interpretation of an existing provision. A distorted reading circulated on social media and messaging groups spread the notion that Spain would not repatriate those who entered.

Maritime arrivals had been rising through July, with Civil Guard unions warning of inadequate resources. On Thursday, coinciding with the Moroccan holiday, border surveillance was scaled back and then withdrawn. The provisional toll on Monday stood at at least 72 dead, most of them drowned. A comparable episode occurred in 2021, involving between 8,000 and 10,000 people, amid a diplomatic crisis over Spain's hosting of the Polisario Front leader.

Sánchez sent a letter to European institutions criticizing the response of some member states, describing as selfish, polarizing and unlawful measures such as Italy's reintroduction of border checks and proposals from Finland and Denmark to exclude Spain from the Schengen area. A group of 22 countries favoring tighter migration controls requested a meeting of EU interior ministers, scheduled for Tuesday.

On Friday, Sánchez described the events as an attack and a violation of Spain's territorial integrity, though the government has not named Morocco as responsible and has not convened the National Security Council. The Defense Ministry placed some 1,600 troops at the Interior Ministry's disposal for surveillance duties. Ceuta and Melilla are Spanish territory; Morocco maintains a claim over both cities.

World.title: Why Europe still buys Siberian larch? Properties, supply overview
World.content:
Why Europe still buys Siberian larch? Properties, supply overview

3rd Monday, August 2026 - 00:30 UTC Full article

Photo: Unsplash

Russia holds roughly a fifth of the world's forest area, and for two decades one species from that vast resource dominated Europe's timber facades: Siberian larch. Dense, cheap for what it offered, and shipped west in enormous volumes, it became the default cladding board from Norway to the Netherlands. Then, in 2022, the trade stopped almost overnight — and the European market has been improvising ever since.

What makes the timber different

Larix sibirica grows across a huge belt of continental Russia where summers are short and winters brutal. Trees put on growth so slowly that the annual rings pack tightly together, producing kiln-dried timber commonly quoted at around 590 kilograms per cubic metre — markedly denser than Scots pine at roughly 510 or spruce at around 430.

That slow growth translates into practical advantages outdoors. Under the European EN 350 durability standard the heartwood is generally rated class three, moderately durable, which in practice means decades of service in vertical cladding without any chemical treatment. Left uncoated, the boards weather from warm honey tones to an even silver-grey that many architects deliberately design for.

- High density gives good resistance to knocks and abrasion, which suits ground-floor facades, gates and exposed corners.

- Natural resins make the heartwood unappealing to fungi and insects without preservative treatment.

- The same hardness means installers pre-drill near board ends to avoid splitting, a routine step with this species.

A supply chain redrawn by sanctions

The European Union's fifth sanctions package, adopted in April 2022, banned imports of Russian wood, with existing contracts wound down by that July; the United Kingdom introduced its own restrictions in parallel. The major forest certification schemes had moved even earlier, suspending Russian and Belarusian certificates in March 2022 and classifying the material as conflict timber, which shut it out of most professionally procured projects regardless of law.

Stock already inside Europe was worked through quickly, and buyers turned to substitutes. European and Japanese larch, much of it grown in Britain and the Alps, took a large share of the demand, while thermally modified softwoods absorbed the specifiers who cared most about stability. Genuine new-harvest Siberian material offered on the open market today deserves careful questions about provenance.

The adjustment showed up in prices and lead times before it showed up in catalogues. Merchants reported larch quotations moving sharply through 2022 as remaining certified stock was allocated, and grading became a talking point, since British-grown larch tends to carry more knots than the slow-grown Siberian boards architects had been used to specifying.

What buyers choose instead

For most projects the realistic decision is now between European-grown larch, modified timber and coated softwood, judged on budget and the look the designer wants. Suppliers have also broadened their finishes: factory-coated and charred boards deliver the dark, dramatic facades that clients ask for while using timber from uncontroversial sources.

UK suppliers such as TimberSol have adapted their ranges accordingly, pairing larch's density with modern dark coatings so that the sanctioned trade route is no longer something a British self-builder needs to think about.

None of this has dented the appetite for the look itself. Dense, slow-grown larch remains the reference point buyers compare everything else against; the difference is that boards now arrive with paperwork purchasers actually read, and provenance questions have become a standard part of ordering timber rather than an afterthought.

World.title: Tulum, known for its beaches and Maya ruins, is named the happiest travel destination in the world
World.content:
A detailed analysis of more than a million travel reviews has led an Irish travel insurance company to conclude that Tulum — one of the more laid-back beach resorts on Mexico’s Caribbean coast — is the happiest travel destination on earth.

The company, JustCover, pored through written comments on all kinds of tourist attractions — national parks, entertainment venues, scenic places and urban areas, as well as resorts — looking for vocabulary such as “happy” and “joy.”

Based on their research, they assigned a “Happy Place Score” to each destination on a scale of 0 to 100. Tulum ended up with a perfect 100 out of 100 score.

Tulum has indeed become extremely popular in recent years as a more tranquil option to bustling Cancún in Quintana Roo state. JustCover mentioned Tulum’s preserved Maya ruins, perched on a cliff overlooking the Caribbean Sea, its nature reserves and picturesque view.

“Tulum also draws visitors with its thriving food, nightlife and wellness scene,” the company pointed out.

Tulum boasts several smaller resorts and boutique hotels, which many tourists are opting for over Cancún’s giant all-inclusive resorts and beach clubs. It also offers a wide range of adventure and eco-tourism attractions, including cenotes and a lazy river.

Travel + Leisure’s World’s Best Awards 2025 list of the best resorts in Mexico featured both the Conrad Tulum Riviera Maya and La Zebra Tulum.

The town is also home to some of Mexico’s most well-regarded restaurants, with several spots mentioned in the Michelin Guide.

While Tulum came out on top in terms of happiness, Oaxaca was also given a high score for its “food, markets, and its deep Indigenous culture,” ranking in third place.

JustCover’s top 10 Happy Place Destinations are as follows:

Tulum, Mexico Soufrière, Saint Lucia Oaxaca, Mexico Las Vegas Maui, Hawaii New York City Cappadocia, Turkey Rio de Janeiro Chicago Toronto

With reports from Travel + Leisure and USA Today

World.title: Riot breaks out at Tapachula migrant detention center after alleged arson attempt
World.content:
Two migrants were arrested on charges of inciting a riot at an immigration holding center in the southern state of Chiapas on Saturday night. The two men were arrested and transferred to Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the state capital, where they were being processed for immediate deportation.

The incident occurred at the Siglo XXI Migration Station in the border town of Tapachula — the largest immigration detention center in Latin America — where approximately 40 migrants were being processed after being detained in different parts of the country.

The National Migration Institute (INM) said the two men in question — reportedly Venezuelan nationals — began displaying aggressive behavior, prompting a broader disturbance in the station.

The newly arrived migrants began demanding their immediate release, later claiming to be victims of systematic abuse and incommunicado detention.

While agents attempted to calm the tumult, the men are alleged to have attempted to set a mattress on fire.

INM agents, state and municipal security forces and emergency services required more than two hours to quell the uprising, but officials reported that no detainees were injured.

Luis García Villagrán, a human rights activist with the Center for Human Dignity AC, expressed skepticism about the incident, saying the INM often holds migrants incommunicado for periods of up to 10 days and denies them access to legal defense.

“There is a terrible lack of transparency about what is happening at this Immigration Station,” he told the newspaper La Jornada.

The organization said that some 65,000 migrants — many of whom are deported from the U.S. and transferred by land to Tapachula or the INM station in Villahermosa, Tabasco — are stranded in southern Mexico awaiting resolution of their cases. They are processed at these facilities and eventually released, but not permitted to travel outside the area.

The disturbance inside the facility reignited complaints about overcrowding, lack of due process and alleged human rights violations at Siglo XXI which is designed to hold up to 1,500 people.

There have been at least five previous incidents of riots and protests at Siglo XXI, including in April 2019, when migrants rioted, took control of the facilities, and nearly 1,300 migrants escaped.

The attempt to set fire to mattresses was particularly disturbing as it brought to mind the March 23, 2023, fire at a migrant facility in Cd. Juárez that resulted in the death of 40 migrants.

With reports from El Financiero, La Jornada, Proceso, El Economista and El Heraldo de México

World.title: Sheinbaum invites author of ‘The Anxious Generation’ to explain social media’s impacts on kids: Monday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📺 Canal Once occupation ends: Education Minister Mario Delgado said that Canal Once workers peacefully retook the station’s facilities on Sunday, more than two months after IPN students began occupying them, forcing out six protesters; he said the station’s audiovisual archive appears damaged, with material “broken and disorganized on the floor.”

Education Minister Mario Delgado said that Canal Once workers peacefully retook the station’s facilities on Sunday, more than two months after IPN students began occupying them, forcing out six protesters; he said the station’s audiovisual archive appears damaged, with material “broken and disorganized on the floor.” 💰 Sheinbaum alleges paid protest: The president asserted that the protesting students had been paid to occupy Canal Once, saying investigations have not yet determined who made the payments, and called it illogical for a student movement focused on IPN improvements to seize the TV station for so long.

The president asserted that the protesting students had been paid to occupy Canal Once, saying investigations have not yet determined who made the payments, and called it illogical for a student movement focused on IPN improvements to seize the TV station for so long. 📱 Social media debate explained: Sheinbaum said the government opened a public debate on children’s use of social media because studies show excessive use — particularly infinite scrolling and short videos — creates addiction, though she stressed technology also has “extraordinary uses” like global communication and virtual museum visits.

Sheinbaum said the government opened a public debate on children’s use of social media because studies show excessive use — particularly infinite scrolling and short videos — creates addiction, though she stressed technology also has “extraordinary uses” like global communication and virtual museum visits. 🧠 Haidt warns of “digital pacifier”: U.S. psychologist Jonathan Haidt addressed the mañanera, calling children’s social media and touchscreen use a “public health problem” and urging parents not to give kids access to phones until at least age four to six, citing damage to cognitive development.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Monday morning press conference came two weeks after the federal government announced three regional forums to canvass views on children’s use of social media and artificial intelligence tools and platforms ahead of drafting a legislative proposal to regulate these technologies.

At today’s mañanera, Sheinbaum explained why the government initiated a public debate on young people’s use of social media. Two weeks ago, she said that a consultation process with experts, parents, teachers, young people and others should lead to “some scheme of regulation” on the use of social media by minors.

It is not yet known whether the government will seek to ban young people under a certain age from using social media as part of a legislative proposal that could be submitted to Congress later this year. However, Education Minister Mario Delgado, who was at today’s mañanera, said earlier this year that the Mexican government was exploring the possibility of imposing age restrictions.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were the remarks made by both Sheinbaum and Delgado about a lengthy student takeover of the public television station Canal Once.

Student takeover of Canal Once ends

A reporter noted that workers with Canal Once, a public television network owned by the National Polytechnic Institute (IPN), returned to their workplace on Sunday more than two months after a group of IPN students began occupying the TV station’s facilities as part of a protest against alleged financial mismanagement at the university, among other alleged problems.

Protesting students allege that they were violently forced out of Canal Once’s Mexico City facilities on Sunday.

Asked her opinion about the situation, Sheinbaum referred the question to her education minister.

Delgado said that “a group of young people” from IPN decided to occupy the Canal Once facilities on May 20.

“We made many attempts to establish dialogue with them,” he said before highlighting that discussions took place and asserting that none of the students’ demands were related to Canal Once.

Consequently, Delgado said that authorities asked the protesting students to leave Canal Once — which has an extensive audiovisual archive — but they repeatedly refused to do so.

He said that Canal Once workers on Sunday “decided to organize themselves” to “peacefully” retake the television station’s facilities. They achieved their goal, forcing six remaining student protesters out of Canal Once.

“Unfortunately, at first glance, there is damage to the archive,” Delgado said.

“There is material broken and disorganized on the floor,” he said.

“But we’re going to wait to see how serious this damage is. And we said to the young people that we’re going to continue with the roundtable discussions, but it’s not possible for a TV station that belongs to the people of Mexico to remain seized,” Delgado said.

He didn’t say whether the protesting students would face criminal charges for occupying Canal Once and allegedly damaging its archive.

Sheinbaum asserted that the protesting students had been paid to occupy Canal Once.

“On one occasion we presented here about how these students received resources, money,” she said, adding that investigations had not yet determined who made the alleged payments.

“It’s not logical that a student movement that is asking for improvements in the Polytechnic [Institute] occupies Canal Once for so long,” Sheinbaum said.

“… Fortunately, Canal Once never stopped broadcasting,” she said, explaining that the Ministry of Public Education lent equipment and studios to the public television station.

Sheinbaum: Technology has ‘extraordinary uses’ but social media is problematic

After presentations from experts on the impact of screen time and social media on children and adolescents, a reporter asked Sheinbaum her opinion about technology that can assist young people’s learning.

“What we’re seeing here are different studies that show that the excessive use of social media, particularly use linked to infinite scrolling … or [watching] short videos, creates addiction,” the president said.

She went on to say that no one can deny that technology has “extraordinary uses,” citing the ability to communicate with people on the other side of the world and virtually visit “the world’s best museums” as examples.

“The issue is that certain mechanisms of [social media] platforms are creating learning problems, cognitive development problems and addiction,” Sheinbaum said.

“… Mexicans can’t say ‘it’s OK.’ It’s something that we have to review for our daughters and sons, our granddaughters and grandsons,” she said.

“… That’s why we opened the debate,” Sheinbaum said.

Her remarks came after U.S. psychologist Jonathan Haidt — author of the 2024 book “The Anxious Generation: How the Great Rewiring of Childhood Is Causing an Epidemic of Mental Illness” — addressed the mañanera.

Among his remarks, Haidt said that “now we know that it’s terrible to give a young child a touchscreen because they learn to get quick dopamine just by touching, touching, touching.”

“… That means that when they don’t have the phone, they now are very upset,” he said.

“… In the United States, 40% of two-year-olds have their own iPad or iPhone and this is a terrible thing which we now know is damaging their development when they arrive at school. What I’m recommending whenever I’m able to speak to governments around the world is treat this as a public health problem,” Haidt said.

“… This is a public health problem and it is important to educate new mothers, new parents, that they should not use a digital pacifier. They should not give … [their children] access to any phones until they’re at least four, five, six,” he said.

World.title: MND Local: A new art space opens in Guadalajara’s Historic Center, and the latest effort to conserve the Primavera Forest
World.content:
This week, we report on a new proposal to protect the city’s green lung, the Bosque La Primavera (Primavera Forest), from real estate development, and a summer book sale. But first, let’s take a look at an exciting new cultural space in Guadalajara’s Historic Center.

Motor is a new cultural space in Guadalajara’s Historic Center

On Juan Manuel Street in Guadalajara’s center and protected cultural heritage zone, a historical gem dating back to 1850 has recently been restored and reimagined as a new cultural space for artists.

The building has a long and winding history. It initially served as a residence, but was later repurposed as a printing facility, and then a mechanical workshop. Its latest reincarnation is the work of local artist Claudio Limón, whose interest in architecture was sparked by his brother and romantic partner, both of whom are professional architects.

“My brother is passionate about the history of architecture, and he told me a lot about the Historic Center, about what has been lost and the different architectural styles of Guadalajara. Then I married an architect, too, and many of my friends are architects,” Limón recently told Mural.

Motor’s role in historic preservation

Dubbed Motor, the space represents not only a new venue for today’s local artists to create work, but Limón’s desire to contribute to the city’s historic preservation. The building now hosts a production studio, artist workshops (mostly allocated to locals, with one space for international residencies) and a space for rotating exhibitions.

The restoration process of the property where Motor is now located took seven months. The old mechanical workshop was preserved virtually intact and became the conceptual core of the project. The venue’s new name refers not only to the building’s industrial past, but also to a creative energy Limón hopes to trigger within the community.

“I want anyone who comes to an exhibition here to also visit the record store next door, buy books or get to know the neighboring businesses,” Limón explained.

Ultimately, the artist hopes Motor will stand as a counterpoint to the prevailing tendency toward tearing down and building anew, sparking enthusiasm for historic preservation in Guadalajara, where for decades the city has witnessed significant loss of its historical and artistic heritage.

A new proposal is introduced to protect a threatened part of Primavera Forest

Like an incurable chain smoker, Guadalajara has been doing serious damage to its “lungs” in recent years — i.e., developing rather than conserving many of its important green spaces. Now, a local congresswoman representing the Green Party of Mexico (PVEM) seeks to shift the narrative.

Congresswoman Brenda Carrera García presented a proposal earlier this month to protect La Primavera Forest from additional real estate development. Her proposed legislation would block new residential construction on a 60-hectare plot for a project marketed as “Santa Anita Hill” in Tlajomulco de Zúñiga.

The developer has planned to build a new community right in the transition zone of the Primavera Forest, a biosphere reserve with UNESCO status and an area that’s increasingly viewed as critical to safeguarding the Guadalajara metropolitan area’s water supply. The land is home to 20,000 oak trees that are fundamental to recharging the area’s aquifers, absorbing seasonal rainfall and mitigating the city’s chronic air pollution.

An ‘environmental recovery zone’

According to Carrera, “If this construction is authorized, we will lose what nature took cycles to consolidate.”

She also noted that the land has been subject to various administrative anomalies in recent years, including changes in land-use status by municipal authorities following suspicious fires without observance of the required 20-year waiting period — a timeworn ploy by real estate developers to subvert building restrictions in protected areas, in violation of state-level conservation laws.

Instead, Carrera has called on the State Congress to designate the land as an “environmental recovery zone” and regulate its use to protect the public interest. This legislative proposal arrives at a time when thousands of area residents have filed complaints and grievances over ongoing encroachments to the Primavera Forest.

If you’re a voracious reader who finds the FIL (Guadalajara’s annual International Book Fair) a bit overwhelming and expensive, there’s a lower-profile alternative.

Happening now through Aug. 9, Guadalajara’s Historic Center will be transformed into a gathering place for readers looking to expand their book collections without breaking the bank. The event, which brings together Spanish-language publishers, bookstores and distributors, will feature a wide assortment of books for sale at discounts of 40% or more.

This fifth edition of the book sale (in Spanish, “Magno Remate de Libros”) features 100 booths offering a wide selection of books in various genres, including literature, graphic novels, comics and children’s books. During the 10 days of the sale, there will also be more than 50 literary and cultural activities, including presentations, workshops, author talks, performances and more.

If you’ve been on the hunt for discounted books, this is one of the best opportunities of the year to find new titles at affordable prices.

Dates: July 31 until Aug. 9, 2026. Hours TBD. For more information, visit Cultura Guadalajara’s Instagram.

Location: Paseo Fray Antonio Alcalde, across from Plaza de Armas in Guadalajara’s Historic Center.

Cost: Free and open to the public.

MND Writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Mexico partners with Viasat to expand internet access in rural areas
World.content:
Mexico’s Telecommunications Investment Promotion Agency (Promtel) and global communications company Viasat have agreed to establish a framework to foster the development of telecoms infrastructure, expand connectivity and strengthen coverage across the country.

Promtel and Viasat formalized an alliance that will allow both parties, in line with their respective roles, to partner on initiatives to close the digital divide and strengthen Mexico’s connectivity ecosystem.

This will include knowledge transfer, the exchange of technical expertise and resources, the development of specialized content and collaboration on training programs.

The goal is to accelerate broadband deployment in underserved communities while supporting smaller telecommunications operators with infrastructure, technical expertise and digital inclusion initiatives.

“This agreement represents an opportunity to combine strengths and expand connectivity to more regions of Mexico,” said Héctor Rivero, country manager of Viasat México. “At Viasat, we are committed to supporting initiatives that boost infrastructure and generate significant benefits for communities.”

In a statement, Viasat said the joint effort highlights the importance of collaboration between the public and private sectors with the goal of expanding access to telecommunications services in underserved communities, so as to contribute to Mexico’s social and economic development.

According to the national statistics agency INEGI, nearly 24% of Mexico’s population lacks Internet access. Mexico’s Federal Telecommunications Institute has estimated that achieving nationwide internet coverage would require an investment of approximately 30 billion pesos (US $1.73 billion).

Promtel recently began providing support to hundreds of smaller telecommunications providers through financing mechanisms and technical assistance under its National Strategy for Small Operators.

The partnership with Viasat complements these efforts by making satellite capacity available to small operators who then can provide broadband access to communities, primarily rural, where commercial coverage is limited. This helps overcome the lack of fiber or mobile networks which remain impractical due to geography or deployment costs.

The agreement will be valid until 2030, with the possibility of renewal.

Promtel is a decentralized Mexican government agency dedicated to the expansion of nationwide mobile and broadband coverage, especially by fostering rural internet access. It also oversees the deployment of the Red Compartida program (a major wholesale telecommunications project designed to expand mobile internet and phone coverage, lower service costs and boost market competition)

Viasat, Inc. — a provider of high-speed satellite broadband services and secure networking systems covering military and commercial markets — is based in Carlsbad, California.

With reports from El Economista and Mexico Business News

World.title: How had I never heard of Guanajuato? A reflection by MND’s summer intern
World.content:
Traveling is a quintessential part of the study abroad experience.

It is easy for the hordes of American college students who flood Europe every spring. The continent’s complex and wide-reaching network of high-speed rail and abundance of budget airlines make traveling from tourist city to tourist city exceptionally easy. A 20-year-old studying in Rome can reach Athens, Barcelona, Madrid, Milan or Paris in a matter of hours.

I did not go to Europe for my study abroad. I came to San Miguel de Allende for a nine-week journalism internship with Mexico News Daily. I never expected to travel much.

Part of that was knowing that Mexico did not have the best infrastructure for travel. High-speed rail is nonexistent, and highways travel is not recommended at night. The other part was simply not knowing what central Mexico has to offer. If my study abroad experience took me to Rome, I would have made a laundry list of cities I wanted to visit before I even started packing. I could have taken a train down to the Amalfi Coast, seen the ruins of Pompeii or even flown to Egypt.

Central Mexico, meanwhile, is off the beaten path. Few have been. Few want to go.

That’s why I had never heard of San Miguel de Allende until I applied for the internship, let alone Guanajuato city or Querétaro. Nobody that I knew had ever been here. The only place I knew I wanted to visit was Mexico City for the World Cup, which I got to experience after just 10 days in the country. From everything I had heard about Mexico in the United States, the center never seemed like a place that had destinations to visit. Even though I was coming, I felt just as ignorant as the rest of my compatriots.

Mexico is known as a tourist destination for Americans, but they rarely visit the center. Popular resort towns like Cancún, Cabo or Puerto Vallarta routinely take in the swarms of U.S. beach-goers and college kids on spring break. I was shocked when I went to Querétaro a couple of weeks ago — a town that I found beautiful, clean and historic — and saw it nearly untouched by international visitors.

Travelling through Mexico has been easier than I expected. The buses — which are clean, affordable and safe — can take you almost everywhere. Uber is unbelievably affordable and if you are traveling with a local, services like BlaBlaCar can cost less than $20 USD for a trip spanning multiple hours.

Mexico City has become an internationally renowned tourist hotspot. Querétaro has kept its colonial charm while simultaneously transforming into a high-end tech hub. San Miguel is known for its colorful streets, food and many churches.

But last week I went to a city that blew them all out of the water.

That city is Guanajuato. It is a city brimming with color. Where towering mountains force density, which manifests in beautiful winding alleyways. A city where sprawling tunnels are a primary form of transportation and a city with incredible churches, food and bars.

I was only there for about 24 hours, but I fell in love with the city. The hour-long drive from San Miguel weaves through canyons and mountains before reaching Guanajuato city. I was immediately struck by the streets, which felt like stepping into France or Spain. The churches and landmarks were some of the most picturesque that I have seen so far in Mexico.

And the viewpoints. Standing on top of the Pípila, overlooking the city and the rolling hills. Seeing the magnificent churches and the mines in the distance was breathtaking.

Like most of my experiences thus far in Mexico, visiting Guanajuato made me wonder why more Americans do not visit Mexico. I have been to some of the most famous European cities, and Guanajuato, while significantly smaller, was more impressive than many of them.

Guanajuato was not hard to get to. The city was walkable and accessible by ridesharing services.

Yet this beautiful city was unknown to me. Unlike Querétaro, Guanajuato is known for its abundance of Mexican visitors and tourism infrastructure. It is a place where Americans can see something truly unique — a place more colorful than any city in the U.S., with great food and nightlife. But they still don’t go.

Traveling to Mexico is easier than you think. Traveling in Mexico is easier than you think. And Mexico has the cities, the nature and the experiences that warrant the trip. Guanajuato is proof.

Guanajuato, Querétaro, San Miguel and my 24 hours in Mexico City are just the tip of the iceberg. There is pristine coastline to the east and west, Oaxaca to the south, and rainforest to the southeast. I have still seen so little of this beautiful country.

So why do more Americans not come here? Is it for lack of a sense of adventure? A lack of pre-packaged trips? I am still trying to find out.

Jared Tucker is a summer intern at Mexico News Daily in San Miguel de Allende and a rising senior at the University of Washington in Seattle, where he is the sports editor for The Daily UW. He was previously a fellow at TheFulcrum.us, where he covered public participation in American democracy.

World.title: Mexico Well-Read: A review of Reyna Grande’s ‘Migrant Heart’
World.content:
There is a particular unease that arises from hearing stories about crossing a border you have also crossed, but in the opposite direction and under radically better circumstances. I savored Reyna Grande’s new memoir, “Migrant Heart: Essays About Things I Can’t Forget,” in the comfort of my home in San Miguel de Allende, Guanajuato, a gorgeous town famous for its architecture, arts scene, climate and ever-growing expat population. Grande’s life story began only a day’s drive but a world away, in Iguala, Guerrero — a town most of the world now knows, if they know it at all, as the place where 43 students from the Ayotzinapa Teachers’ College disappeared in 2014, an atrocity that still hangs over Mexican public life like an unfinished storm.

The book itself deserves to be met on its own considerable terms, because “Migrant Heart” is not a polemic. It is something much rarer and better: a mid-career writer’s attempt to loosen her grip on the story that made her famous. Grande’s earlier memoirs, “The Distance Between Us” and “A Dream Called Home,” shared the traumas of her childhood and young adulthood, and relayed them so devastatingly that a friend of the author’s once suggested, not entirely as a joke, that the publisher bundle a box of tissues with each copy.

Reyna Grande is the ‘queen of misery’ no more

In this new memoir-in-essays, Grande resists that role. She opens by recounting her experience of being crowned the “queen of misery,” and the whole book can be read as her working out what it might mean to put down that crown without abandoning the truths that earned it.

The 18 essays here range further afield than her previous work, into failing eyesight, gardening, motherhood, menopause and the peculiar vertigo of raising American children who will never fully understand her scars or carry her burdens. She writes about the Ayotzinapa disappearances not as distant news but as a wound in her hometown’s soul. She writes about losing fluency in Spanish as the price of gaining English, and about the complicated inheritance of colorism within Mexican and Mexican American communities — including, in one unsparing passage, her own mother’s hope that her grandchild would have blue eyes.

Grande has said in interviews that she has worried about repeating herself, about her writing calcifying into “immigrant trauma porn,” and in these essays you can feel her actively resisting that fate, reaching instead for the harder, less marketable material of an ordinary life continuing after the extraordinary parts are over. This is a writer who has spent two decades making readers weep; here, she seems more interested in proving she can let herself, as well as her readers, breathe.

In “Migrant Heart,” Grande again affirms that pain can be transformed into power. But she finally permits herself to set some careful boundaries, too, no longer feeling compelled to reexamine every wound for the reader’s benefit.

Not a comfortable read, but one filled with ‘hard truths’

For us expats reading this book in any of the beautiful, sunny Mexican towns that serve as havens for people fleeing not violence and brutal poverty but cold winters, polarized politics and high property taxes, “Migrant Heart” is not entirely comfortable reading, and I don’t think it should be. But it is essential reading precisely because our comfort here was built on a complicated history that these essays insist we look at directly. Living where I live, I could not read this without feeling implicated, gently but unmistakably, in the very economic and political inequities that produced both the author’s and my own radically different migrant experiences.

Grande has written a book about what it costs to leave home when you have no choice; the least those of us who have enjoyed that choice can do is read it all the way through and wrestle with some hard truths along the way.

Ann Marie Jackson is a book editor and the award-winning author of “The Broken Hummingbird.” She lives in San Miguel de Allende and can be reached through her website: annmariejacksonauthor.com.

World.title: How Jorge Campos won over the fans at the 2026 FIFA World Cup
World.content:
You don’t have to be a futbolero to know the national icon that is Jorge “El Inmortal” Campos.

The former Mexican national team goalkeeper, who stood a mere 5-foot-6, dominated throughout the 1990s as a stalwart between the goalposts, supplying acrobatic dives and theatrical saves that have been compiled into countless highlight reels by a zealous fanbase. On the field, he helped popularize the role of an attacking goalie — the rare archetype of a goalkeeper who would leave his own goal to become an offensive weapon against opposing defenses (Campos famously played striker at times, netting over 35 goals in his career).

In fact, Campos developed such a prolific and unprecedented style as an offensive-minded goalie that FIFA was prompted to investigate its own rules about a player who switches positions mid-game.

‘A cult hero for his flamboyant apparel’

From 1988 to 2004, Campos — who grew up near Acapulco, Guerrero — transformed into a larger-than-life force during his prime, playing in Mexico and the United States for teams like UNAM, Atlante, LA Galaxy, Cruz Azul, Chicago Fire, Tigres and Puebla.

But perhaps more than the game itself, Campos became a cult hero for his flamboyant apparel. Bright neon shades and quirky geometric designs highlighted his loud sense of fashion on the pitch and, decades later, he remains one of soccer’s most iconic global personalities. At his zenith, Campos designed his own kit (inspired by Acapulco’s culture) that he wore in the 1994 World Cup. Campos’ creativity inspired other goalkeepers of the decade to follow suit, as a few of his contemporaries would also go on to create their own flamboyant style modeled after his example.

In total, Campos is credited with 130 national appearances for Mexico and over 100 custom uniform designs. In his own words, “I’m not sure if I played that well, but everyone remembers me.” Indeed, they do.

This summer, Campos recaptured the hearts of soccer fans worldwide with his playful personality, generous spirit and the announcement of a new soccer endorsement deal with Nike — a rare feat for a long-retired veteran. Here’s how the immortal Campos further embellished his colorful legacy at the 2026 World Cup.

Nike’s ‘Campos x Jorge’ collection

In his biggest splash, Campos revealed his collaboration with Nike for the “Campos x Jorge” release. Though the exact dates of the drop haven’t been confirmed yet, the sportswear giant teased the clothing line throughout the World Cup. (A few months ago, Campos joined forces with Nike and the Houston rapper Travis Scott, who is a frequent Nike collaborator himself, to release a custom jersey under the BadFriend skate apparel brand, perhaps foreshadowing Campos’ own line.)

The clothing will utilize Campos’ legendary patterns, designs and colors. Best of all, Nike unveiled a Michael Jordan-esque silhouette for the brand, in which the outline of a diving Campos punching a ball away from the goalpost serves as a makeshift “Jumpman” logo.

Images of conceptual sketches have emerged online, generating tons of fan excitement around the clothing line. References to palm trees, Acapulco, beaches, surfing (a hobby that Campos acquired while growing up on Mexico’s Pacific coast) and, of course, soccer are at the forefront.

The collection will honor Campos’ ongoing tradition of converting the soccer field into a fashion runway.

Campos’ role as a cultural ambassador for Mexico

Nowadays, Campos is a versatile diplomat for the game’s universal appeal, a goalkeeper who transcended the sport to become an avatar of Mexico’s vibrancy and warmth beyond the penalty box.

For the 2026 FIFA World Cup, hosted in his native Mexico, Campos was in a uniquely opportune position to represent the sport as an official FIFA World Cup ambassador — along with other soccer notables like David Beckham, Mia Hamm, Ronaldo Nazário and Ronaldinho Gaúcho. Throughout the Cup, Campos was seen inside VIP boxes and attending high-profile events in various host cities, rubbing shoulders with the biggest stars in the sport. He was even given a seat in the presidential box with FIFA President Gianni Infantino.

In addition, Campos served as a World Cup television commentator for Mexico’s Azteca Deportes, providing analysis of in-game action, which he has done for over 20 years since his retirement in the mid-2000s. He is known for being goofy, off the cuff and rather unserious — albeit sincere and endearing — in a way that brings levity to the commentator’s booth.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Jorge Campos Navarrete (@soyjorgecampos1)

His face was seen everywhere, especially in Mexico: on limited-edition children’s juice boxes on Boing!, in Visa s and in television commercials alongside other Mexican celebrities like El Hijo del Santo, Julio César Chávez and Pedro Infante.

‘A meeting of legends’

Beyond the gimmicky commercialism of it all, which admittedly has become an increasingly diluted part of the sporting industry at large in the modern age, Campos helped bring unity across cultures and generations in genuine, organic ways.

Most memorably, Campos brought René “El Loco” Higuita — a famous Colombian goalie from the 1990s known for his daredevil saves and infamous “scorpion kick” — together with Vozinha, who became Cape Verde’s unlikely goalkeeping hero and was considered the fan-favorite goalkeeper of this 2026 tournament. (Vozinha blocked all of Spain’s shot attempts and shut down the eventual World Cup champions with a 0-0 draw in their group stage duel.)

Jorge Campos and the 2026 FIFA World Cup

In a now-viral video, Campos asks Higuita, “Who is the best keeper?” to which Higuita responds, “Jorge Campos.” Campos immediately corrects him with a smile and says, “No, Vozinha,” and calls Vozinha over from across the room, whom Higuita hadn’t yet seen. The trio takes a photo together in a cross-generational meeting of legends. Later, Campos and Vozinha exchanged jerseys, a tradition that represents a sign of mutual respect and admiration between high-caliber players. Campos ends the interaction by telling them all to say “hello to Mexico.”

In Mexico, you can’t mention the 2026 World Cup without mentioning Jorge Campos. And you can’t mention Campos without mentioning Mexico.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

Canada faced a double crisis, racing to dodge looming US duties while roughly 800 wildfires burned and thousands fled their homes.
