The concrete bus shelter design has become so synonymous with Canberra that city merchandise often pays tribute to it. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The shelters have become synonymous with the city, and are emblazoned across Canberra merchandise and artworks.

"The notoriety of them is far beyond anything I think any of us might have expected, but it is just so lovely," Mr Eccles said.

" One of my very favourite things to do is to share it with my son, and he understands who his great-grandfather was and his contribution to bus shelters. "

An early sketch of the design by Canberra architect Clem Cummings. (Supplied: The Cummings family)

Ms Skippington said the addition of the neighbourhood landmarks on the heritage register did not change their use, management or maintenance arrangements.

"We expect that collection to be continued to be maintained [by Transport Canberra] and used as it is, shifted as need be, repaired as need be," she said.

"They've been here for the long haul, and hopefully for a much further future."

World.title: Teacher's advice 35 years ago leads to Commonwealth Games gold
World.content:
It was a moment one teacher at a small public school on the NSW Far South Coast will never forget.

Thirty-five years ago, Paddy "Mr Macca" McAlpin suggested that 11-year-old James Reynolds might like to try his hand at lawn bowls.

Year 4 teacher, Paddy "Mr Macca" McAlpin introduced Reynolds to lawn bowls more than 30 years ago. (ABC South East NSW: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro)

Born with severe scoliosis, the proud owner of a freshly minted Commonwealth Games gold medal had spent much of his childhood in and out of hospital before undergoing surgery to fuse his spine when he was just 10.

"There was nothing he wouldn't give a go, and he just wanted to be like all the other kids and take a few risks and just enjoy himself," Mr McAlpin said.

"[Lawn bowls] suits him perfectly. He's very competitive and he's very clever, so it's a perfect game for him.

"It was something that he could do his whole life and make it as far as he wanted to."

Delgado and Reynolds won gold after defeating New Zealand in the Men's Para Pairs. (Supplied: Bowls Australia, Aidan Davis)

Reynolds and teammate Damien Delgado made it as far as Glasgow, where they claimed gold in para lawn bowls at the Commonwealth Games.

The duo defeated New Zealand 8-1, 7-2 in the gold-medal pairs match, ending an undefeated campaign and securing their second Commonwealth Games medals.

A replay of the final taught some valuable life lessons that might not have otherwise been on the curriculum at Reynolds's old primary school, Pambula Public, where staff and students gathered to watch and cheer during their morning assembly.

Students cheered loudly as they watched a replay of the winning moment. (ABC South East NSW: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro)

"I'm just so proud that he's still going with it, and we just hope every kid can find a story out there and tell it with their own life," Mr McAlpin said.

"We are all so proud of how far James went, starting at Pambula Public School in year 4 and now chasing his dream," year 6 student Jaxon Madex said.

" It means a lot to the school and for Australia, I mean, he's representing our country on the other side of the world, and it must be scary. "

Students created posters to celebrate the win by Reynolds and Delgado. (ABC South East NSW: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro)

Reynolds paid tribute to his family and supporters back home in an interview with Bowls Australia after winning the gold medal.

"It means everything — a lot of sacrifices, a lot of hard work individually and collectively and to get the ultimate outcome — we are so proud of ourselves," he said.

A successful career

Reynolds was just 15 years old when he won the NSW under-18 junior singles title.

He went on to claim bronze for Australia at his first Commonwealth Games in 2002, before representing the nation again in 2014 and winning gold in the men's para pairs with Delgado at the 2023 World Bowls Championships.

This marks Reynolds's third time representing Australia at the Commonwealth Games. (Supplied: Bowls Australia, Aidan Davis)

In June, he was named the 2026 Australian Institute of Sport's International Male Para Bowler of the Year.

Community support

Michael Wilks, a bowls development officer at Club Sapphire in Merimbula, played alongside Reynolds for 15 years, and now mentors junior players with him through the Bowls NSW Junior Committee.

Mr Wilks said there was a real buzz around the region.

"It was pretty hard not to be brought to tears," he said.

" I know what Jimmy's gone through to reach that goal of his. "

Reynolds and Delgado became emotional as they celebrated their win. (Supplied: Bowls Australia, Aidan Davis)

Mr Wilks said the win would be savoured by the entire Far South Coast bowls community.

"He's probably the biggest bowls identity to ever come out of the area," he said.

"It's his association with all the clubs and the whole bowls community that makes it so special."

Reynolds and Delgado will now join Australian Jake Fehlberg as the only para bowlers to win gold at both the Commonwealth Games and the World Bowls Championships.

World.title: Nicci just lost her husband. Now she fears she'll lose her support
World.content:
Nicci Carlson sits in her Canberra apartment working on some needlepoint craft.

Since her husband passed away a few months ago, she's found that art therapy helps with her grief and keeps her mind occupied.

Ms Carlson has multiple autoimmune conditions, including psoriatic arthritis.

She is constantly in pain and is concerned she will soon lose her eyesight.

"I have pain every day," she said.

"All day, every day."

Nicci has found needlepoint to be a good outlet. (ABC News: Georgia Roberts)

Ms Carlson lives with these worries every day, but the burden of the proposed cuts to the NDIS — and potentially her own care — has instilled fear in her and the wider disabled community.

NDIS support is something she has had to fight for, advocating for herself time and time again.

"Fight, fight, fight for everything, it's never been easy," Ms Carlson said.

Nicci's friends all gave her a word to describe her that she could work into a painting as part of her art therapy. (ABC News: Georgia Roberts)

She has been present at rallies against the proposed cuts in the ACT, which she lists as another burden people living with a disability have to face daily: advocating for themselves.

She's exhausted, but she knows this is something she will have to keep fighting for.

"I keep seeing people lately who are angry and saying half the people on the NDIS are fakers," Ms Carlson said.

"Please point them out to me, because how did they get on if they're faking? Because it is incredibly hard to get on the NDIS. Well, it was for me; that's been my experience.

"Everything to do with them has been hard; it's never been easy."

The proposed overhaul

Under the proposed NDIS changes announced in April, recipients would be kicked off or prevented from accessing the now-$50 billion scheme, with many moved on to yet-to-be-built state-run supports.

According to government modelling, more than 240,000 people would exit the NDIS over four years, and an estimated additional 110,000 people who are not yet participants would be diverted from accessing the scheme by 2031.

The changes would save more than $30 billion over the next four years, and address concerns that the NDIS has been growing faster than Medicare, and that it has been exploited by rorters.

Nicci Carlson is worried the NDIS cuts will affect her. (ABC News: Georgia Roberts)

"I had people say to me, 'Well, it won't be you', 'It won't be people like you', — and I thought well, I've heard far too many stories already about people who have had various things removed that you wouldn't think would be removed," Ms Carlson said.

"If they can take a blind person's guide dog away, they can take anything from anybody, any time.

"And if they change the legislation the way they want to, they literally can."

Do you know more? Email Roberts.Georgia@abc.net.au

Social and community participation cut

Ms Carlson is concerned that the proposed legislation grants the NDIS minister sweeping new powers to control funding, restrict participant eligibility, and set pricing.

"I'm worried they are giving way too much power to one person," she said.

Those concerns are shared by Greens Senator Jordan Steele-John, who lives with a disability himself.

Greens Senator Jordan Steele-John (ABC News: David Sciasci)

The senator has been a staunch advocate for the disabled community during the fallout from the proposed cuts, and led the charge on the deal brokered with the federal Labor government to allow a longer inquiry period into the changes.

"This really knocked a number of people to the ground when people were just starting to get up," he said of the proposal.

The cuts to social and community participation alone are expected to account for about a third of the over $30 billion in projected savings over the next four years.

Ms Carlson and Senator Steele-John are worried this will strip NDIS recipients of support workers who assist with everyday tasks like shopping, appointments, and exercise.

"People think that it's [cutting things] like fun, going into the community... and yes it is that too, but it is also [assistance to] go to hydrotherapy, go to a doctor appointment, go to the hospital," Ms Carlson said.

Senator Steele-John fears it will limit choice and autonomy.

"People won't be able to go outside if they need support to do that," he said.

Kelly Brown, chair of the Disability Advisory Council in the ACT. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Council 'concerned' by lack of federal consultation

The ACT government's Disability Advisory Council (DAC), which gives advice to the disability minister of the day, also warned the cuts could bring on unintended consequences.

"We think reform is a good thing; we are just concerned we have had a lack of consultation," the DAC chair, Kelly Brown, said.

Ms Brown welcomed the federal government's decision to extend its inquiry into the cuts.

However, she said further extending the period of consultation would allow the government to work through more of the concerns of the disabled community.

The most contentious parts of the NDIS bill Politicians are presiding over three days of public hearings into a bill paving the way for the biggest ever cuts to the NDIS.

In a statement, ACT Disability Minister Suzanne Orr said she understood the concerns raised by the disability community both in Canberra and across the country about the need for more consultation, planning and safeguards.

"Keeping people with disability at the centre of any reform is critical," Ms Orr said.

"Our priority is that people receive the right supports, and it is important that services outside the NDIS are appropriately funded to meet demand."

A final report from the federal government's extended inquiry into the cuts is set to be handed down on August 14.

World.title: White but ripe, these strawberries are new varieties grown in Australia
World.content:
Sweet, ripe, juicy strawberries are no longer only red, with novel new white and blush varieties now being grown commercially in Australia.

But you may have to wait to try some, as the fruit is still in very short supply.

It has been a race to be the first to get them to market, with years of research, crossbreeding and on-farm trials to reach this point.

Freshly picked Rose Pearl strawberries in the field. (Supplied: TSL Family Farms)

No ordinary strawberries

Growers have been eager to offer consumers colour choices in strawberries, just like we get with other fruit.

White strawberries, which range from cream to blush, originated from a natural genetic mutation, and have lower acidity than their red relatives.

"We all like something new, especially, you know, strawberries are so well loved by kids," Berries Australia CEO Rachel Mackenzie said.

Rachel Mackenzie says consumers want choice. (Supplied: Rachel Mackenzie)

" If you've got something new and exciting to try, that's really exciting for them. "

With a fragrant aroma, the taste differs too. Some varieties are described as sweeter, like candy; others have hints of pineapple, pear, vanilla and guava.

White and red fruit grown by SSS Strawberries in Bundaberg. (Supplied: SSS Strawberries)

Where do they come from?

The fruit slowly making its way to supermarket shelves is being multiplied from varieties imported from Japan and the USA, and plants bred in Australia.

Bundaberg grower Toan Nguyen was intrigued when he saw white strawberries in Japanese stores and wondered why they were not sold here.

Now his family's farm, SSS Strawberries, is growing a few thousand plants with Japanese genetics and has plans to expand.

Gem Nguyen with SSS Strawberries's new white fruit. (Supplied: SSS Strawberries)

"The feedback has been amazing; some say it's actually sweeter than the red ones," Mr Nguyen said.

" We don't have enough to sell at our farm shop; we are sold out by lunchtime. "

But it took time to educate customers.

"They thought it was under-ripe so no-one bought it until we started posting about it and they started tasting it," Mr Nguyen said.

Point of difference

TSL Family Farms at Bellmere, near Brisbane, also cannot keep up with demand for fruit from their 70,000 "Rose Pearl" plants.

"Coles's experience is that there's just none left on the shelves anywhere," co-owner Laura Wells said.

Laura Wells from TSL Family Farms with "Rose Pearl" strawberries. (Supplied: Taste'N'See Strawberries)

" We've only been able to send them through to New South Wales and Victoria currently and only to a few chosen stores. "

Pickers have to learn to tell when the strawberries are ripe. (Supplied: Taste'N'See Strawberries)

The family-owned business secured exclusive rights to the variety, developed in Florida, and Ms Wells was pleased to discover its hardiness in heavy rain.

"We've had next to no crop loss associated with rain events with our white variety, so commercially it's pretty exceptional," she said.

"Rose Pearl" strawberries, grown by TSL Family Farms and Taste'n'See, were developed in Florida. (Supplied: Taste'N'See Strawberries)

Australian strawberry breeding program

Jodi Neal leads the national strawberry breeding program that has developed about half of the strawberry varieties grown commercially in Australia.

She is proud of her team's work breeding fruit for our climatic conditions, growing systems and the Australian consumer's palate.

Jodi Neal leads the Australian strawberry breeding program. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

Growers visited the trial patch at the Queensland Department of Primary Industries' Maroochy research centre, where yet-to-be-named white varieties are growing.

"When the sun hits the fruit, the top of it colours up, kind of like a peach, while the bottom will always stay white," Dr Neal said.

" It tastes incredible and is newly available for our farmers to grow and our consumers to eat. "

Dr Neal said it took seven years to go from cross-pollination to commercial release, with rigorous testing to ensure plants performed for farmers.

Ashbern Farms is trialling Queensland-bred white strawberry varieties. (Supplied: Ashbern Farms)

The focus is on developing hardy, high-yielding, tasty, disease- and bruise-resistant fruit that is easy to pick and pack.

"The best part of my job is seeing the varieties that we've developed here in Australia, grown by our Australian farmers, and being enjoyed by our consumers," Dr Neal said.

"We are trying to make sure that our farmers stay sustainable, that they can stay in business."

Growers in Queensland and Perth are trialling the Australian-bred white strawberries.

Brendon Hoyle at Ashbern Farms in the Glass House Mountains has about 100 of the plants.

Brendon Hoyle with a white Australian-bred strawberry. (Supplied: Ashbern Farms)

"They're looking promising; the flavour is amazing," he said.

"A little bit harder to grow but it's a unique kind of strawberry, and I think that there'd certainly be a market for them."

When are they ripe?

Mr Hoyle said his workers quickly learnt when the white fruit was ripe to pick.

"Once you've seen a few of them, they just need to start turning, just very slightly blush, and then you know they're good to go."

Brendon Hoyle says the strawberries are ready to pick when they start to turn pale pink. (Supplied: Ashbern Farms)

World.title: From suburban dance school to Anastasia the musical
World.content:
Aria Piteo has just landed the biggest role of her young life and will be ready to take one big deep breath before the curtain goes up.

The 10-year-old will make her professional theatre debut in the Anastasia musical during its Adelaide season.



Aria is one of four girls hand-picked to play the role of Little Anastasia and remarkably they all come from the Norwood-based Barbara Jayne Dance Centre.

"I do love it, but I also get really nervous and I'm like, 'You can do it Ari, yes, you can do it,'" Piteo said.

Aria Piteo says she loves performing. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

"I love doing it because I love to express myself and love performing in front of everyone and showing what I can really do," she said.

Audrey Burnett, 11, knows exactly how Piteo feels.

"I definitely think I'll get nervous, but I'll also be like, 'It's okay you got this, you got chosen for a reason,'" she said.

Audrey Burnett says she gets nervous before a big performance. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

The girls had to get through three searching rounds of auditions against dozens of other hopefuls.

"I didn't think I was going to get it because there were so many good people," Daisy Goodall, 10, said.

A tight bond helped the quartet survive each cut.

"They're just like family to me, they're like my bestest friends," Burnett said.

"It's just great to have them and they'll always support me, even if they're nervous, they make me feel calm."

Resilient performers

Barbara Komazec has seen it all while running the Barbara Jayne Dance Centre for 51 years.

She said all the girls selected to perform have singing, dancing and acting skills, but it would take much more if they want to make a living on the stage.

"They've got to have some talent, they've got to have resilience because they get the knocks all the time," Ms Komazec said.

" They've got to be able to get knocked back and then get back up and try again. "

Barbara Komazec says the girls have put a lot of hours into preparing for the show. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

Isla Bahrami is the youngest of the girls at just nine years old.



She said she was stunned when she received the phone call about getting the role.

"I was excited, shocked at the same time," she said.

" I found out in the car with my cousin and he was screaming as well, so basically it was just a screaming car, really. "

Isla Bahrami is the youngest of the girls performing in Anastasia. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

On the eve of show rehearsals, she was looking forward to performing a song with one of the adult cast members.

"I'm singing with a lady called Nancy I'm pretty sure," she said.

'Nancy' is actually Australian theatre icon Nancye Hayes AM, who stars as the Dowager Empress.

Australian theatre icon Nancye Hayes AM will star in the musical. (Supplied: Jeff Busby)

"They will learn so much, they really will," Barbara Komazec said.

"Working with a musical director; when they're doing the singing, working with the choreographer, the director.



"They will learn so much and plus being in the environment with professionals."

But the opportunity hasn't come without years of grind, according to Burnett.

"We work so hard, we do so many lessons a week and it's still so fun, but there's a lot of dedication," she said.

While she was ready to strut her stuff in Anastasia, she said she was a little uneasy about her mum being in the audience.

"My mum gets extremely nervous, she like freaks out and she makes me nervous, so sometimes I'm a little bit, 'Oh, calm down'," Burnett said.

The cast for Anastasia also includes Georgina Hopson and Rhonda Burchmore.

World.title: 'Get this right': Top US Jewish leader's stark warning for Australia
World.content:
The leader of one of the world's most high-profile Jewish organisations says Australia faces a crucial test on how it tackles the rise of antisemitism as the royal commission resumes in Sydney.

On Tuesday, in its seventh hearing block, the commission will analyse the democratic function of protests, hateful conduct that sometimes occurs at protests and how police manage demonstrations.

Anti-Defamation League chief executive Jonathan Greenblatt is on the frontline of fighting antisemitism in the United States and has turned his attention to Australia during a visit this week.

A former White House adviser to Barack Obama, he is among the most senior of Jewish leaders in the US, which is home to about 7.5 million Jewish people.

Jonathan Greenblatt (in the blue blazer) says hateful words can lead to more extreme acts. (ABC News: Gavin Coote)

Lingering consequences of Bondi

On Monday, Mr Greenblatt, accompanied by Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief Alex Ryvchin, paid his respects at the memorial at the site of the Hanukkah massacre.

"It is gut-wrenching. I think the massacre in Bondi is an indelible stain on Australia," Mr Greenblatt told the ABC.

" This is an injury that Australia always will bear. The question is how Australia moves forward from here. "

The royal commission is the only high-level judicial inquiry being held into the rise of antisemitism and Mr Greenblatt says Australia needs to reckon with a concerning record.

A global report published last week by the J7 Large Communities Taskforce Against Antisemitism found the number of antisemitic incidents in Australia has surged by 270 per cent since 2021.

That is the highest increase recorded of any country examined in the study, including the US, UK and Canada.

As the head of the oldest anti-hate organisation in the world, Mr Greenblatt said Australia's long-standing image as a safe place for Jewish people had been "shattered".

"Antisemitism in Australia did not start with the massacre at Bondi," he said.

"In fact, a week before was the one-year anniversary of the firebombing of a synagogue in Melbourne.

"There had been vandalism of people's homes, businesses had been defaced … so you had seen a rash of incidents.

"And indeed, we wondered from afar, where was the Australian government?"

'This is what globalise the intifada looks like'

When the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion resumes hearings on Tuesday, a pro-Palestinian protest outside the Sydney Opera House in October 2023 and a neo-Nazi rally outside NSW Parliament in November last year will be in the frame.

Pro-Palestinian protesters sets off flares at Opera House Flares and fireworks were lit in the crowd and thrown onto the forecourt steps of the Opera House, where rows of police officers were monitoring the situation.

Mr Greenblatt has argued the slogans used at pro-Palestinian rallies have fuelled hateful rhetoric in countries such as Australia.

"It's not anti-Israel. It's pro-hate to harass Jewish people [over] what's happening on the other side of the world," he said.

"I don't believe we would tolerate it if it was directed against any other ethnic group and it is despicable that it happens here."

While visiting the memorial at Bondi Beach, Mr Greenblatt said the attack was an example how rhetoric has led to tragic consequences.

"This is what globalise the intifada looks like," he said.

"The idea that it's just rhetoric — let me tell you, it always just starts with words."

Jonathan Greenblatt says the slogans used at pro-Palestinian rallies have heightened animosity towards Jews. (ABC News: Gavin Coote)

Mr Greenblatt commended the work of the royal commission but said the inquiry would ultimately be judged on its recommendations and the response from governments.

"The world is watching you right now," he said.

"We hope and we pray that Australia will demonstrate how you can be an exemplar for the values that so many of us hold dear.

"So I think my message would be, 'Australia, get this right. We can't afford for you to lose.'"

World.title: Almost $140m in fines written off by Queensland government
World.content:
Almost half a million unpaid fines were written off by the Queensland government's debt collector last financial year, totalling almost $140 million.

That was almost double the number of debts written off two years ago.

There is more than $1.3 billion remaining in outstanding fines being pursued by the State Penalties and Enforcement Registry (SPER), as at June 30.

More than $250 million has been outstanding for more than five years.

The forgiven fines total almost $140 million, with more than $1.3 billion remaining to be paid. (AAP: Joel Carrett )

The figures come amid the rollout of heavy new fines for e-mobility riders flouting laws, and legislation before parliament to drastically increase fines for dangerous drivers.

More than 460,000 debts were written off by SPER last financial year, down from 585,000 in the previous.

'All reasonable action' taken

A SPER spokesperson said the collector makes every effort to track down unpaid fines.

"SPER debts can be written off for a variety of reasons, including where a debtor is deceased, a company is deregistered, or aged debts are simply uneconomical to recover," they said.

"This is consistent with standard industry debt recovery practices.

"Before writing off any debts, SPER undertakes all reasonable action to recover them, which can include data enrichment and verification processes."

Queensland fines to increase Penalties will soon rise for all state government fines in Queensland, with the 3.5 per cent hike applied to infringements including speeding, not wearing a seat belt and using a mobile phone behind the wheel.

Of the written-off fines, almost 90,000 had been outstanding for more than ten years, 213,000 outstanding between five and 10 years, and 151,000 outstanding for three to five years.

Debts owed to victims of crime are not written off.

SPER has the power to reinstate the fine should new information come to light, which will allow it to collect the amount.

The debt collector doesn't publicly disclose the exact guidelines for writing off infringements, to ensure dodgy debtors do not use the information to flout their fines.

There was a total of almost 2.7 million unpaid debts in Queensland as of the end of June.

Almost half of those were outstanding from three months to three years, totalling more than $700 million.

About a million fines were outstanding from three years to more than a decade, with a balance of more than $420 million.

The LNP government has rolled out heftier penalties since coming to power in 2024.

Proposed laws before state parliament will double the penalties for drink and drug drivers and implement harsher consequences for other serious offences.

They include a minimum fine of $1,251 for first-time drug and drunk drivers.

A parliamentary committee examining the proposed laws will report back to the government next week before the legislation returns to parliament for debate.

A British start-up founded by a 25-year-old school dropout has been valued at £2.5 billion ($4.8 billion) as it develops new chips for the AI boom. Olix, led by James Dacombe, an entrepreneur, raised $US312 million ($445 million) from investors as it looks to compete against Nvidia in the market for high-tech chips. UK entrepreneur James Dacombe’s start-up Olix is taking on Nvidia. Getty Images for Flickers' RIIFF The deal values Olix at $US3.3 billion, tripling its valuation since February, when the start-up raised a further $US220 million. Dacombe started Olix two years ago when he was just 23, having launched his first company as a teenager after dropping out of his sixth form college in Harrogate, just two days into starting his A-levels.



He launched his first company, CoMind, a brain-scanning business, at the age of 17 in 2018, and continues to work as its chief executive as well as running Olix. World.content:
Two people have died in the cyclospora outbreak in the US state of Michigan, state health officials have announced, confirming the first deaths in the country related to the microscopic parasite.

The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said on Monday (US time) both people had underlying health conditions that may have been affected by the intestinal illness and dehydration. The department said it would not provide additional information about the deaths.

Cyclospora is a microscopic, spherical parasite that commonly causes watery diarrhoea “with frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Outbreaks tend to occur most often in the late spring and summer.

Federal health officials have identified lettuce from Mexico served at Taco Bell locations in nine states as a source of the widespread outbreak. As of late July, the number of cases linked to the lettuce was 1947, including at least 98 people who had to be hospitalised, according to the CDC.

The agency has said other “brands, restaurants, retailers, or distribution channels” could be tied to the outbreak as the investigation continues.

World.title: ASX set for flat start, Wall Street rallies on falling oil prices; Amazon hits $US3tr valuation, Boeing jumps
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set for flat start, Wall Street rallies on falling oil prices; Amazon hits $US3tr valuation, Boeing jumps Stan Choe Updated August 4, 2026 — 6:24am ,first published 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks rallied the edge of their all-time high after easing oil prices helped calm Wall Street’s worries that inflation could get even worse. The S&P 500 jumped 1.5 per cent and is just 0.1 per cent below its record set earlier this summer. It’s coming off a wild July, where it swung up and down as oil prices shot higher because of the war with Iran and other worries. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 1.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 2.1 per cent. Wall Street has rallied to start the week. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to edge lower, with futures pointing to a loss of 1 point at the open. The ASX jumped 0.5 per cent on Monday after President Donald Trump said over the weekend that he decided to hold off on new strikes against Iran at the urging of allies in the region. US stocks got a lift to kick off their trading week as the price for a barrel of Brent crude sank 5 per cent to $US83.52. Brent’s price careened between $US72 and $US102 last month as worries rose and fell about when the war with Iran would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again to deliver crude to customers worldwide. The latest acquiescence by Trump helped to ease worries about the global flow of crude, and Treasury yields correspondingly fell in the bond market.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury sank to 4.68 per cent from 4.75 per cent late on Friday. It, though, remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran. Related Article Opinion

Home loans The path to first home ownership might be under a flight path Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Higher yields threaten to undercut prices for stocks and other investments, while slowing the economy by making borrowing more expensive for US households and businesses. The average long-term US mortgage rate has already leaped to its highest level in a year. Monday’s ease in oil prices helped airlines and other companies with big fuel bills lead the market. United Airlines flew 5.8 per cent higher, while American Airlines climbed 5 per cent. Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings steamed 6.6 per cent higher. Boeing soared 8 per cent. US regulators certified its new 737 MAX-7 planes, clearing it for commercial service, following years of work to provide pilots with clearer information and warnings, along with other improvements.



Amazon rose as much as 5.8 per cent on Monday to touch an intraday high, becoming only the fifth company to ever cross the $US3 trillion ($4.3 trillion) market-cap threshold. It closed 4.6 per cent higher. Tyson Foods added 2.9 per cent after the meat company reported a slightly stronger profit for the spring than analysts expected. CEO Donnie King said strength is continuing in the company’s chicken business and its prepared foods, which include brands like Jimmy Dean and Hillshire Farm. It joined a lengthening list of big US companies to deliver a bigger profit for the spring than analysts expected. That’s imperative for Wall Street because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate earnings over the long term, and worries were rising that US stock prices may have broadly already shot too high. Companies in the S&P 500 are on track to deliver earnings per share for the spring that are 47 per cent higher than a year before, according to FactSet, with more than half of the companies in the index having already reported. If that ends up being the case, it would be the strongest growth since the spring of 2021, when the economy was roaring out of the COVID pandemic. Also offering encouragement for profits was a report on Monday showing that growth for US manufacturing accelerated to its strongest level since 2022.



Keeping Wall Street unsettled, though, were swings for stocks of companies that make computer chips. They’ve been veering up and down for weeks on worries about whether their surging revenues because of the artificial-intelligence boom are sustainable. If AI ends up producing less profit and productivity than hoped, Big Tech companies could curtail their spending sprees on data centres that have helped chip stocks soar to tremendous heights. It’s still up roughly 190 per cent for the year so far. The manic swings for AI stocks have been most dramatic in South Korea, where the Kospi index is dominated by just two tech titans, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.



Seoul’s Kospi fell 5.1 per cent Monday, coming off Friday’s 17.9 per cent surge that was its best day in history. In neighbouring Japan, Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 fell 0.9 per cent after the United States and Japan confirmed they had moved together to prop up the value of the Japanese yen against the dollar. World.title: Time travel, punk music and a novel written in one sentence: 13 books to read this month
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As we head into the final month of winter, you can find stacks of new books popping up in your local bookshop. Here are 13 that might be up your street. Sophie, Standing There

Meg Mason

Fourth Estate, $34.99, out now

Sorrow and Bliss was such a ginormous hit that it really changed the life of New Zealand-born-and-raised author, Meg Mason. It was her second novel, and her third emerged from the considerable success and fame she found with it. Sophie is a sound technician at writers festivals, who in her solitary life becomes obsessed with a particular writer. But this is more than a study of loneliness. As Mason says in the interview that you can read here, she wanted it to be a fast and easy read that name-checks other writers and employs some surprising techniques. Meg Mason’s third novel is more than a study of loneliness. James Brickwood Blackbirding

Ryan Butta

Simon & Schuster, $36.99, out now

The term “blackbirding” refers to the 60,000 Pacific Islanders brought against their will to Australia to work in Queensland’s sugar fields between 1860 and 1906, and the practice is indicative of Australian historical euphemism to “obscure an action that is morally or emotionally or politically problematic”. Ryan Butta tells the stories based on documentation − it is not his right to tell the stories of the enslaved − and the egregious behaviour of the founder of the trade, Robert Towns, and the murderous James Murray is eye-opening and shocking. Time Travel for Beginners

Jaclyn Moriarty

Ultimo, $34.99, out now

Jaclyn Moriarty had the idea for her third novel for adults, and 17th overall, about 20 years ago. At first, it reminded me of the 2019 French film La Belle Epoque. Single mother Anna hates her job at the Nut Bar but, after getting hit by a car, is offered a job as a time travel agent. Clients revisit significant events with the proviso they can’t change anything; meanwhile, other characters converge in Anna’s life. As Moriarty told Lenny Ann Low, “regret is designed to prevent you making mistakes again … the trouble is, it gets jammed in a loop.” Amy Remeikis decries civility politics in her new book. Screw Nice

Amy Remeikis

Hachette, $34.99, out now

Political analyst Amy Remeikis follows her bestselling On Reckoning with a take-down of what she calls “civility politics [that] lets us stand silent while we see someone with less social power than us being bullied in the classroom, society or workplace”. It’s crammed full of examples from Australia and the US of how politicians and commentators have their say, and the way in which they do so makes for a bracing read. Not surprisingly, Remeikis cites Orwell: “If you turn the other cheek, you will get a harder blow on it than you got on the first one.”



Now, Autonomy

Max Easton

Giramondo, $32.95, out now

If you fancy a trip through Sydney subcultures, Max Easton is your guy. In the third of his novels that navigate these worlds, we’re in 2024 and Helen is out of the share-house at the heart of Paradise Estate and in an apartment with Pat, who has secretly unearthed his memoir of life in the early 2000s. Sunny and Sio join them in a year-long lease on a vacant hotel − they call it “The Quarterly” − in which to stage “events” for their tribes and “save Sydney from itself”. But nothing is as simple as it seems, particularly Helen’s relationship with Maria. Nuclear Archipelago

Elizabeth Tynan

NewSouth, $39.99, out now

The third in Elizabeth Tynan’s award-winning trilogy about Britain’s “nuclear colonialism” in Australia details the tests in the Monte Bello Islands in 1952 and 1956 off the Pilbara coast. The latter was by far the “largest bomb ever exploded in Australia”. As Tynan says, “none of the test sites were properly cleaned up … pristine environments such as the Monte Bello Islands were permanently scarred”. The full story remains untold as the British remain “stubbornly secretive”. Tynan reckons “Australians have a right to know exactly what took place on our soil”. Mine

Adam Ouston

Transit Lounge, $$34.99, out now

Don’t be put off by the fact that Adam Ouston’s second novel is written as one sentence. Angel Down, the winner of this year’s Pulitzer for fiction, is also one sentence, but Daniel Kraus breaks it into paragraphs, each of which begins with the word “and”. Readers should trust authors, and Ouston’s digressive prose soon catches you in its rhythms. His narrator is an 80-year-old poet and environmental activist given to procrastination who wants to write a “hauntology” of Tasmania’s West Coast, but has tumbled into a mineshaft, his fall broken by his backpack. He may be trapped, but his mind isn’t and his consciousness roams far and wide. Adam Ouston has written his new novel in one sentence. The Hurt

Catherine de Saint Phalle

Transit Lounge, $32.99, out now

When she was 18 and struggling to survive in a lycee she despised, Catherine de Saint Phalle met Julien who, a few years older than her, “added voice and texture to Paris” with punk music and his black curls. De Saint Phalle previously wrote a memoir about her parents, Poum and Alexandre, and they feature wonderfully here as well. In writing characterised by vivid imagery − “Eighteen wasn’t very old, but I felt my childhood escaping me on roller skates” − de Saint Phalle relates the story of her relationship with Julien, and how writing it led her out of a later “forest of despair”. Realms of Gold

A.J. Mackinnon

Black Inc., $36.99, out August 4

Most people take the car; some travel by trains or boats or planes, and some, such as Patrick Leigh Fermor, like to walk. But if you’re A.J. “Sandy” Mackinnon, you take a small Mirror dinghy and go as far as you can. He recounted his eccentric journey from Shropshire to the Black Sea in the delicious memoir, The Unlikely Voyage of Jack de Crow; 18 years later, he’s back with an account of another intrepid, slightly bonkers, voyage in a similar dinghy, this time from the port in Romania where the first vessel ended up to Venice. Eye of the Needle

Christopher Raja

Text, $34.99, out August 4

The end of innocence was a key theme of Christopher Raja’s first novel, The Burning Elephant. You could say Eye of the Needle has a similar focus, as one of his two narrators, Kris, a would-be writer in 1990s Melbourne, turns his back on family and slips into the dismal world of heroin addiction, while the other, Kadir, an Afghan cameleer on a scientific expedition venturing into the desert from Beltana in 1882, has his eyes opened about colonialism and its brutal consequences for the Indigenous population. But who is telling Kadir’s story?

World.title: Sydney Opera House’s famous boardwalk to benefit from $120m renovation fund
World.content:
CultureArt & designCity life Sydney Opera House’s famous boardwalk to benefit from $120m renovation fund Linda Morris August 4, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Sydney Opera House will receive a $120 million upgrade over the next four years to renew critical infrastructure, modernise ageing venue technology and replace 150 concrete beams, slabs and piers sitting in a tidal zone beneath the World Heritage masterpiece. In a second act of the Opera House’s major renewal, the Minns government will announce a four-year investment on Tuesday, with most works invisible to the public. Submerged structures beneath the Northern Boardwalk will be replaced. Steven Siewert The announcement was made just four years after the curtain was lifted on a $150 million refurbishment of the Concert Hall, and work will target the building’s smaller western venues and underlying marine structures. The announcement marks a final milestone for outgoing chief executive Louise Herron, who departs this week after 14 years at the helm to take on a Vice Chancellor’s Fellow role at the University of Sydney.



An executive search firm has yet to be appointed, and names thrown up as a possible replacement include Carriageworks’ Fergus Linehan, Sydney Theatre Company’s Anne Dunn and Brenna Hobson, the Opera House’s programming director. The investment was made possible under a new mechanism which quarantines the allocation to the Opera House for use for capital works only. After 14 years Louise Herron is leaving the Sydney Opera House. Steven Siewert “This funding will do wonders for the long-term future of a World Heritage masterpiece,” Herron said. “The area we are referring to is underlying marine structures on the northern side of the Opera House precinct, entirely facing the harbour and subject to the tides and wash of the passing heavy marine traffic. The work is going to tender by the end of the year and work will be staged in the Playhouse and Drama Theatre to minimise disruption.”



Treasurer Daniel Mookhey said the $120 million injection, delivered over four years, would help the Opera House keep pace with modern visitor and performance expectations. Key features of the project include replacing 1970s-era theatre machinery and staging systems in the Playhouse, Studio and Drama Theatre – venues frequently used by companies including Sydney Theatre Company and Bell Shakespeare. The works will introduce automated stage draping, stage risers and acoustic curtains, allowing for faster and more efficient turnarounds between shows as the venue expands its program of contemporary music, talks, comedy, circus and cabaret alongside anchor residents such as the Sydney Symphony Orchestra, Australian Chamber Orchestra and Sydney Philharmonia Choirs. The Drama Theatre relies on manual hand lines – a counter-weight and pulley system – and temporary chain motors. Installing cutting-edge theatre technology will improve safety while enabling greater performance range and complexity. Stage accessibility will also be upgraded, alongside event management and control systems across both indoor and outdoor venues to future-proof precinct-wide communications.



Work begins in 2027, focusing on reinforcing concrete piers and submerged structures of the Northern Boardwalk that have weathered more than 50 years of salt water, ferry wash and heavy foot traffic. Related Article Visual art David Hockney’s immersive display speaks to you ‘over your shoulder’ The upgrades follow recent planning reforms that increased outdoor venue capacity and operational hours, Arts Minister John Graham said, important work for a building that was a “symbol of modern Australia”. The Sydney Opera House welcomes 11 million precinct visitors each year, with 1.4 million audience members attending its 1850 annual performances and more than 8000 people employed across the precinct. The former Coalition government contributed $234 million to the building’s decade-long renewal, its new Centre for Creativity, refurbished function and events centre and Joan Sutherland Theatre upgrades, with the Opera House contributing more than $50 million from its own cash reserves. It was the biggest capital investment in the Opera House since its opening. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: I wish Hill and Stengle well, but the game must learn lessons from their exits
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion I wish Hill and Stengle well, but the game must learn lessons from their exits Mathew Stokes AFL columnist August 4, 2026 — 5:30am

August 4, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The news that Collingwood and Geelong had reached agreements with Bobby Hill and Ty Stengle to depart the club was hardly a surprise. But that didn’t make hearing it any less disappointing as both were extremely talented players who starred on the biggest stages for their clubs. Premierships, All-Australian selection and a Norm Smith medal bear testament to the ability they possessed. Bobby Hill, pictured at training in June, parted ways from Collingwood. Getty Images More importantly they are also people who I care about having enjoyed the interactions I have had with them over the years. Like their teammates and coaches and fans, I only want the best for them in the next chapter of their lives.



But their untimely departures raise questions in my mind about whether we need to reevaluate the way we manage players as they learn what is required to be a professional athlete. Although ultimate responsibility sits with each individual, the game needs to have an honest look at what it can learn from such untimely departures. The first and most important question to consider is why the game seems to allow players to continue to make mistake after mistake without them being held accountable. That’s all players regardless of background, gender or talent. My impression is that the clubs, the AFL and the Players’ Association have become comfortable with a system which allows players too much protection the first time they commit relatively minor indiscretions.



If the offence enters the public arena they might receive a two-match ban. Otherwise the clubs, association and league are more inclined to keep the transgression behind closed doors to work with the player while they keep contributing to the business of winning. That approach sets individuals up for failure because they have the opportunity to move further and further away from meeting the standards required to be a professional athlete. It then becomes more difficult for them to adjust and reset themselves. I am not naive. Such an approach has been part of professional sport for aeons but in the era of unrelenting media coverage, wellbeing and personal issues are too often being used to protect individuals from unwanted scrutiny if they muck up.



Some argue that such a strategy has had successes no-one hears about. Tyson Stengle has left Geelong as a premiership player. Cameron Spencer But we also see the results of that approach when players gradually drift from the club and eventually train spasmodically. It is disappointing for all involved, particularly when you wonder if some tough love early would have set the players on a more realistic course. I suspect it would and if it didn’t it at least shows players what the expectations will be in the real world when skill at football means little and there is no-one to protect you.



Soon after I was charged with possessing cocaine in February 2010 (I eventually accepted a 12-month good behaviour bond) the club told me to go away for three months and work in a real job away from the team. It was hard work with no certainty as to what lay ahead. I learned that the privilege of being an AFL player could be taken from me instantly and I would need to work to win back the respect of the league, club, teammates and supporters. Such hard conversations would also force players to face the prospect that being a professional athlete might not be for them before clubs spend hundreds of thousands of dollars and expect teammates and coaches to speak in riddles about their absence from training or the club. Editor's pick Four Points

AFL 2026 ‘Clarko’ looks exasperated. It’s time for a hard conversation That doesn’t mean those in charge show no empathy for a player’s background or individual circumstances when developing them as a professional athlete. Not at all. Clubs must support people inside their environment.



Understanding players and building good relationships with them is an essential part of any successful club. I am arguing that all players have to meet a certain standard regardless of who they are, their life experiences, or where they come from. If they aren’t met, then the player faces consequences. I would expect clubs, the league and the players’ association to review the decisions which led to Hill and Stengle’s departures from their clubs. A mature conversation needs to be had about what happens if a player is not rocking up to training yet is still being rewarded with an income.



A conversation should also be held about the prospect of applying penalties to players who don’t meet required standards in real time to give them an incentive to lift their game. Such penalties could set them up for a life beyond the AFL rather than rationalising a reason for someone to play the week after a misdemeanour because they are talented. It will also reduce any disincentive a club might have in taking in players from various backgrounds or offering them long-term deals if they know they can deal with situations as they arise how they see fit. People in footy want the best for players but development can only occur when consequences result from behaviour. And the sooner that happens, the better. That’s the real world where the most important lessons are learned.



Mathew Stokes is a Larrakia man who played 200 games with Geelong and Essendon. He played in Geelong’s 2007 and 2011 premiership teams. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Melbourne’s worst-kept secret: Behind the celebrity trappings, Ralph Carr was known simply as ‘The Rug’
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The conviction of veteran artist and sports manager Ralph Carr for rape was one of Melbourne’s worst-kept secrets. What was also well known to many who had crossed paths with the celebrity manager was that Carr was a small man with an enormous ego, prone to bullying and manipulative behaviour. He loved to surround himself with the trappings of success and the famous, but was difficult to work with and chaotic. Ralph Carr outside court in June 2024. Jason South One former staffer went so far as to describe Carr as “revolting” and “a master manipulator”. Carr’s conviction, and the lifting of a near three-year suppression order, has opened the floodgates for many in the music and sporting worlds who have long held a dim view of the man they dubbed “The Rug”. One woman, who worked at Ralph Carr Management in the mid-2010s while in her early 20s, described her tenure there as “an awful and confusing time”, saying she and other staff experienced “outrageous bullying” from him.



“I saw some pretty terrible things,” she told this masthead while asking to speak anonymously to protect her employment. “None of it was nice … his behaviour was revolting.” The former employee said news that Carr, 66, had been found guilty by a jury of one count of sexual assault and two counts of rape would trigger uncomfortable and difficult memories for many women. Tigers champion Dustin Martin (right) with his then-manager, Ralph Carr, after winning the 2017 AFL Players’ Association Most Valuable Player Award. Getty Images “The past 24 hours have been very confronting,” she said. “There is the sexual predator side, but also the toxic work culture. “This is about a pattern of behaviour. There are multiple women with stories about things that have gone on.” Carr continues to strenuously deny he committed any crime, and his lawyer, Dermot Dann, KC, told the County Court on Monday his client planned to appeal against the verdict. Carr’s Instagram account is filled with photos of his famous and wealthy friends and clients.



In one image, the twice-married and twice-divorced father of three is smiling arm-in-arm with country rock star Keith Urban. In others, he poses with supermodel Miranda Kerr, shares a drink with Molly Meldrum, and another with Nine entertainment reporter Richard Wilkins. Then there’s Carr at the Brownlow Medal night with Dustin Martin, the champion Richmond footballer who was his prized celebrity management client. Carr (right) at the unveiling of a statue for Molly Meldrum alongside Michael Gudinski, Meldrum and Jeanne Pratt. Eddie Jim Carr had been the man behind the AFL great when Martin was part of three premiership wins with the Tigers and won the 2017 Brownlow Medal. The pair were more than just manager and client. They were close friends and business associates, having invested together in several, multimillion-dollar commercial properties in Melbourne. However, like Carr’s freedom that relationship is now in tatters. In a statement, Martin said he was “shocked to learn of the outcome of the court proceedings”.



“I had no knowledge whatsoever of the conduct that led to these convictions,” the footy great said. “My thoughts are with those affected. Effective immediately, I have ended my professional relationship with my former manager. As this is a legal matter, I will not be making any further comment.” Related Article Courts Entertainment stalwart Ralph Carr identified as mystery rapist after suppression order lifted While Martin was Carr’s sporting ace in the pack, over the years he also represented a who’s who of stars from across the music industry – including his ex-wife, Tina Arena, former Noiseworks frontman Jon Stevens, Kate Ceberano, Bonnie Anderson, Vanessa Amorosi and Rick Price. He also represented actor Madeleine West, magician Cosentino, Wilkins and singer Mark Vincent who ended up fighting with Carr in the County Court over money. Carr also worked with Priscilla Presley when she visited Australia on a speaking tour, escorting her to Flemington for the Melbourne Cup. Famously, Carr married former Young Talent Time star Tina Arena in 2015. The couple divorced a little over four years later in what was a messy split. Ralph Carr with Tina Arena in 1993. Rodger Cummins



He had been her manager from 1992, with Arena later describing the union in memoirs and interviews as more of a complex business dynamic than a traditional romantic connection. They no longer speak, with Arena reporting that the marriage left her financially devastated and reduced her net worth to zero after years of work. In the AFL, Carr made a splash running his Richmond-based agency, Ralph Carr Management Sport. He was a Carlton Football Club director, serving on the board from December 2006 until October 2008, and remains a fanatical supporter of the Blues. His official player agent accreditation, through the AFL Players Association, was likely to be revoked following his conviction, said a fellow player agent, speaking anonymously to talk freely. Carr enjoyed prominence when it came to hardball, headline-grabbing contract negotiations. One industry source, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said the colourful Carr had brought a “Hollywood” vibe to the managerial role, befitting his background in the entertainment industry. He was also dubbed “The Rug” in some circles, because of the distinct black toupee which he still sported in court. Loading

World.title: ‘Impenetrable border’: Farage claims Australian plan can stop the boats to Britain
World.content:
WorldEuropeImmigration ‘Impenetrable border’: Farage claims Australian plan can stop the boats to Britain David Crowe August 4, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: British warships would turn back asylum seekers in the English Channel under plans unveiled by Reform UK leader Nigel Farage to embrace Australia’s tough border policy to stop the boats. Farage vowed to launch the largest military operation of its kind to deter thousands of asylum seekers from boarding inflatable boats on French beaches to seek new lives in Britain, citing the Australian approach as a template. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage in London on Monday. Getty Images The plan came at a time of heightened argument about border policies after more than 50,000 people rushed from Morocco into the Spanish territory of Ceuta, leading to at least 72 deaths. But the Reform plan sparked immediate objections from UK critics who said it would provoke France by using Royal Marines to force asylum seekers back to the beaches where they started.



Farage insisted the French would accept Britain’s right to protect its borders if he became prime minister at the next election, declaring the British public wanted tougher measures even if that meant diplomatic and military tensions. “The country will get behind the message that we have a Royal Navy, it’s there to protect this country from invasion, and that now is what it should be used for,” he said. Related Article Analysis

Immigration How the storming of Ceuta shifts Europe to the right Reform issued a border policy document that devoted several pages to the Australian regime imposed when Tony Abbott led the Liberal Party into government in 2013, including turning back boats. The Reform plan explicitly cited the command structure for Operation Sovereign Borders under the Labor government in Australia, with Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke overseeing multiple agencies to deter arrivals.



While the next UK national elections are not due for another three years, Farage appears likely to shape British debate on border control given Reform UK has a strong position in the opinion polls. The Labour government has revived its fortunes by installing former Manchester mayor Andy Burnham as prime minister, with a YouGov survey last week showing Labour had lifted its support to 22 per cent, matching Reform for the first time in 16 months. Burnham sought to assure voters on Sunday that he could manage tough borders, visiting operations in Dover where border control officials take asylum seekers after intercepting the small inflatable boats in the channel. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham (second from left) stands by a recovered small boat, which was used by migrants crossing the English Channel. Getty Images “The public don’t like the idea that the border looks like it’s not controlled. We need to bring back that control. But, also, we need to offer support for people who genuinely need it,” the prime minister said.



Farage, however, demanded tougher measures in a plan he called Operation Fortress, replicating the formal Australian policy that anyone who arrived by boat would not be settled in the country. Reform said the policy would make Britain’s border impenetrable. Related Article Immigration Spain plans new border barrier in Ceuta as death toll revealed The Reform plan set out Australian measures such as turning back boats where it is safe to do so, setting up a single command, using military vessels to stop boats and issuing temporary protection visas that do not offer permanent protection or allow family reunion. “Under Operation Sovereign Borders, boats were turned around and people were left to complete the final leg of the return journey alone and unescorted,” the Reform policy said.



“Under Operation Fortress, everyone will be rescued and safely returned to their point of departure. What the Australian precedent proved, however, is that the certainty of interception and the guarantee of return is the most successful deterrent possible.” Conservative Party home affairs spokesman Chris Philp dismissed the Reform plan on the grounds it was not credible. “They can’t answer the question [about] how they would disembark immigrants back in France if the French don’t agree,” he said. Migrants try to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. AP Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood defended an existing deal with France to discourage asylum seekers by sending some back across the channel, although she acknowledged this was “trickier” than the approach being taken in Spain in the border crisis at Ceuta.



Mahmood and her department said the National Crime Agency had doubled the number of officers who were tackling people smugglers, saying there were now 800 on this task. As well, almost 1000 law enforcement, intelligence and military officers were on the French coast to stop small boats. “More than 1900 traffickers and gang leaders who helped to facilitate Channel crossings have been arrested in the last year alone, 74 per cent more than the previous year,” the Home Office said in a statement. Related Article Immigration ‘I don’t know why they let us through’: How 50,000 people surged into a Spanish exclave Spain mobilised its armed forces to send thousands of asylum seekers back to Morocco after they swam and walked across a rocky coastline to reach the enclave of Ceuta. In its latest estimate, the Spanish government said about 69,500 migrants had returned to Morocco over four days, up from its earlier estimate that 50,000 had arrived.



Officials said that 72 had died on the Spanish side of the border, while 11 died on the Moroccan side. Spanish newspaper El País said many asylum seekers remained in Ceuta and this included 862 minors, a number that has quadrupled in the past two weeks. World.title: High school dropout’s company valued at $4.8 billion
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesEntrepreneur High school dropout’s company valued at $4.8 billion Louis Goss August 4, 2026 — 7:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A British start-up founded by a 25-year-old school dropout has been valued at £2.5 billion ($4.8 billion) as it develops new chips for the AI boom. Olix, led by James Dacombe, an entrepreneur, raised $US312 million ($445 million) from investors as it looks to compete against Nvidia in the market for high-tech chips. UK entrepreneur James Dacombe’s start-up Olix is taking on Nvidia. Getty Images for Flickers' RIIFF The deal values Olix at $US3.3 billion, tripling its valuation since February, when the start-up raised a further $US220 million. Dacombe started Olix two years ago when he was just 23, having launched his first company as a teenager after dropping out of his sixth form college in Harrogate, just two days into starting his A-levels.



He launched his first company, CoMind, a brain-scanning business, at the age of 17 in 2018, and continues to work as its chief executive as well as running Olix. Related Article AI The mysterious ‘baby-faced’ Chinese billionaire who sent markets into a panic Dacombe was made a fellow of billionaire Peter Thiel’s charitable foundation in 2022, which provides grants to young entrepreneurs who drop out of college to launch startups. His new start-up is working to develop faster microchips to lower the costs of AI and now employs more than 140 staff across London, Bristol, Canada and the US. The start-up says its chip designs, which rely on beams of light to move data instead of copper such as a traditional semiconductor, can help “unlock a step change in AI performance and cost”.



Investors in Olix’s latest funding round included Cambridge semiconductor giant Arm, Reed Hastings, the Netflix founder and Hudson River Trading, the US trading firm. It also secured backing from the Government’s £500 million Sovereign AI Fund, set up under Labour to invest in promising technology companies in an effort to keep them in the UK. Dacombe was made a fellow of billionaire Peter Thiel’s charitable foundation in 2022, which provides grants to young entrepreneurs who drop out of college to launch startups. AP A series of new British start-ups has raised hundreds of millions of pounds this year as venture investors seek to capitalise on booming demand for AI chips. Fractile, a Bristol start-up, raised $US220 million in May this year in a fundraising round led by Mr Thiel’s Founders Fund, which was an early investor in tech giants, including SpaceX, Palantir and Facebook.

Two people have died in the cyclospora outbreak in the US state of Michigan, state health officials have announced, confirming the first deaths in the country related to the microscopic parasite.

The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said on Monday (US time) both people had underlying health conditions that may have been affected by the intestinal illness and dehydration. The department said it would not provide additional information about the deaths.

Cyclospora is a microscopic, spherical parasite that commonly causes watery diarrhoea “with frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Outbreaks tend to occur most often in the late spring and summer.

Federal health officials have identified lettuce from Mexico served at Taco Bell locations in nine states as a source of the widespread outbreak. As of late July, the number of cases linked to the lettuce was 1947, including at least 98 people who had to be hospitalised, according to the CDC.

The agency has said other “brands, restaurants, retailers, or distribution channels” could be tied to the outbreak as the investigation continues.

World.title: ASX set for flat start, Wall Street rallies on falling oil prices; Amazon hits $US3tr valuation, Boeing jumps
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set for flat start, Wall Street rallies on falling oil prices; Amazon hits $US3tr valuation, Boeing jumps Stan Choe Updated August 4, 2026 — 6:24am ,first published 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks rallied the edge of their all-time high after easing oil prices helped calm Wall Street’s worries that inflation could get even worse. The S&P 500 jumped 1.5 per cent and is just 0.1 per cent below its record set earlier this summer. It’s coming off a wild July, where it swung up and down as oil prices shot higher because of the war with Iran and other worries. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 1.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 2.1 per cent. Wall Street has rallied to start the week. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to edge lower, with futures pointing to a loss of 1 point at the open. The ASX jumped 0.5 per cent on Monday after President Donald Trump said over the weekend that he decided to hold off on new strikes against Iran at the urging of allies in the region. US stocks got a lift to kick off their trading week as the price for a barrel of Brent crude sank 5 per cent to $US83.52. Brent’s price careened between $US72 and $US102 last month as worries rose and fell about when the war with Iran would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again to deliver crude to customers worldwide. The latest acquiescence by Trump helped to ease worries about the global flow of crude, and Treasury yields correspondingly fell in the bond market.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury sank to 4.68 per cent from 4.75 per cent late on Friday. It, though, remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran. Related Article Opinion

Home loans The path to first home ownership might be under a flight path Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Higher yields threaten to undercut prices for stocks and other investments, while slowing the economy by making borrowing more expensive for US households and businesses. The average long-term US mortgage rate has already leaped to its highest level in a year. Monday’s ease in oil prices helped airlines and other companies with big fuel bills lead the market. United Airlines flew 5.8 per cent higher, while American Airlines climbed 5 per cent. Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings steamed 6.6 per cent higher. Boeing soared 8 per cent. US regulators certified its new 737 MAX-7 planes, clearing it for commercial service, following years of work to provide pilots with clearer information and warnings, along with other improvements.



Amazon rose as much as 5.8 per cent on Monday to touch an intraday high, becoming only the fifth company to ever cross the $US3 trillion ($4.3 trillion) market-cap threshold. It closed 4.6 per cent higher. Tyson Foods added 2.9 per cent after the meat company reported a slightly stronger profit for the spring than analysts expected. CEO Donnie King said strength is continuing in the company’s chicken business and its prepared foods, which include brands like Jimmy Dean and Hillshire Farm. It joined a lengthening list of big US companies to deliver a bigger profit for the spring than analysts expected. That’s imperative for Wall Street because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate earnings over the long term, and worries were rising that US stock prices may have broadly already shot too high. Companies in the S&P 500 are on track to deliver earnings per share for the spring that are 47 per cent higher than a year before, according to FactSet, with more than half of the companies in the index having already reported. If that ends up being the case, it would be the strongest growth since the spring of 2021, when the economy was roaring out of the COVID pandemic. Also offering encouragement for profits was a report on Monday showing that growth for US manufacturing accelerated to its strongest level since 2022.



Keeping Wall Street unsettled, though, were swings for stocks of companies that make computer chips. They’ve been veering up and down for weeks on worries about whether their surging revenues because of the artificial-intelligence boom are sustainable. If AI ends up producing less profit and productivity than hoped, Big Tech companies could curtail their spending sprees on data centres that have helped chip stocks soar to tremendous heights. Trump's America Fool’s gold: Trump is set to break his promise to America Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Micron Technology went from a drop of 6.4 per cent to close 0.7 per cent higher. It’s still up roughly 190 per cent for the year so far. The manic swings for AI stocks have been most dramatic in South Korea, where the Kospi index is dominated by just two tech titans, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.



Seoul’s Kospi fell 5.1 per cent Monday, coming off Friday’s 17.9 per cent surge that was its best day in history. In neighbouring Japan, Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 fell 0.9 per cent after the United States and Japan confirmed they had moved together to prop up the value of the Japanese yen against the dollar.
