World.title: Time travel, punk music and a novel written in one sentence: 13 books to read this month
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As we head into the final month of winter, you can find stacks of new books popping up in your local bookshop. Here are 13 that might be up your street. Sophie, Standing There

Meg Mason

Fourth Estate, $34.99, out now

Sorrow and Bliss was such a ginormous hit that it really changed the life of New Zealand-born-and-raised author, Meg Mason. It was her second novel, and her third emerged from the considerable success and fame she found with it. Sophie is a sound technician at writers festivals, who in her solitary life becomes obsessed with a particular writer. But this is more than a study of loneliness. As Mason says in the interview that you can read here, she wanted it to be a fast and easy read that name-checks other writers and employs some surprising techniques. Meg Mason’s third novel is more than a study of loneliness. James Brickwood Blackbirding

Ryan Butta

Simon & Schuster, $36.99, out now

The term “blackbirding” refers to the 60,000 Pacific Islanders brought against their will to Australia to work in Queensland’s sugar fields between 1860 and 1906, and the practice is indicative of Australian historical euphemism to “obscure an action that is morally or emotionally or politically problematic”. Ryan Butta tells the stories based on documentation − it is not his right to tell the stories of the enslaved − and the egregious behaviour of the founder of the trade, Robert Towns, and the murderous James Murray is eye-opening and shocking. Time Travel for Beginners

Jaclyn Moriarty

Ultimo, $34.99, out now

Jaclyn Moriarty had the idea for her third novel for adults, and 17th overall, about 20 years ago. At first, it reminded me of the 2019 French film La Belle Epoque. Single mother Anna hates her job at the Nut Bar but, after getting hit by a car, is offered a job as a time travel agent. Clients revisit significant events with the proviso they can’t change anything; meanwhile, other characters converge in Anna’s life. As Moriarty told Lenny Ann Low, “regret is designed to prevent you making mistakes again … the trouble is, it gets jammed in a loop.” Amy Remeikis decries civility politics in her new book. Screw Nice

Amy Remeikis

Hachette, $34.99, out now

Political analyst Amy Remeikis follows her bestselling On Reckoning with a take-down of what she calls “civility politics [that] lets us stand silent while we see someone with less social power than us being bullied in the classroom, society or workplace”. It’s crammed full of examples from Australia and the US of how politicians and commentators have their say, and the way in which they do so makes for a bracing read. Not surprisingly, Remeikis cites Orwell: “If you turn the other cheek, you will get a harder blow on it than you got on the first one.”



Now, Autonomy

Max Easton

Giramondo, $32.95, out now

If you fancy a trip through Sydney subcultures, Max Easton is your guy. In the third of his novels that navigate these worlds, we’re in 2024 and Helen is out of the share-house at the heart of Paradise Estate and in an apartment with Pat, who has secretly unearthed his memoir of life in the early 2000s. Sunny and Sio join them in a year-long lease on a vacant hotel − they call it “The Quarterly” − in which to stage “events” for their tribes and “save Sydney from itself”. But nothing is as simple as it seems, particularly Helen’s relationship with Maria. Nuclear Archipelago

Elizabeth Tynan

NewSouth, $39.99, out now

The third in Elizabeth Tynan’s award-winning trilogy about Britain’s “nuclear colonialism” in Australia details the tests in the Monte Bello Islands in 1952 and 1956 off the Pilbara coast. The latter was by far the “largest bomb ever exploded in Australia”. As Tynan says, “none of the test sites were properly cleaned up … pristine environments such as the Monte Bello Islands were permanently scarred”. The full story remains untold as the British remain “stubbornly secretive”. Tynan reckons “Australians have a right to know exactly what took place on our soil”. Mine

Adam Ouston

Transit Lounge, $$34.99, out now

Don’t be put off by the fact that Adam Ouston’s second novel is written as one sentence. Angel Down, the winner of this year’s Pulitzer for fiction, is also one sentence, but Daniel Kraus breaks it into paragraphs, each of which begins with the word “and”. Readers should trust authors, and Ouston’s digressive prose soon catches you in its rhythms. His narrator is an 80-year-old poet and environmental activist given to procrastination who wants to write a “hauntology” of Tasmania’s West Coast, but has tumbled into a mineshaft, his fall broken by his backpack. He may be trapped, but his mind isn’t and his consciousness roams far and wide. Adam Ouston has written his new novel in one sentence. The Hurt

Catherine de Saint Phalle

Transit Lounge, $32.99, out now

When she was 18 and struggling to survive in a lycee she despised, Catherine de Saint Phalle met Julien who, a few years older than her, “added voice and texture to Paris” with punk music and his black curls. De Saint Phalle previously wrote a memoir about her parents, Poum and Alexandre, and they feature wonderfully here as well. In writing characterised by vivid imagery − “Eighteen wasn’t very old, but I felt my childhood escaping me on roller skates” − de Saint Phalle relates the story of her relationship with Julien, and how writing it led her out of a later “forest of despair”. Realms of Gold

A.J. Mackinnon

Black Inc., $36.99, out August 4

Most people take the car; some travel by trains or boats or planes, and some, such as Patrick Leigh Fermor, like to walk. But if you’re A.J. “Sandy” Mackinnon, you take a small Mirror dinghy and go as far as you can. He recounted his eccentric journey from Shropshire to the Black Sea in the delicious memoir, The Unlikely Voyage of Jack de Crow; 18 years later, he’s back with an account of another intrepid, slightly bonkers, voyage in a similar dinghy, this time from the port in Romania where the first vessel ended up to Venice. Eye of the Needle

Christopher Raja

Text, $34.99, out August 4

The end of innocence was a key theme of Christopher Raja’s first novel, The Burning Elephant. You could say Eye of the Needle has a similar focus, as one of his two narrators, Kris, a would-be writer in 1990s Melbourne, turns his back on family and slips into the dismal world of heroin addiction, while the other, Kadir, an Afghan cameleer on a scientific expedition venturing into the desert from Beltana in 1882, has his eyes opened about colonialism and its brutal consequences for the Indigenous population. But who is telling Kadir’s story?

World.title: Sydney Opera House’s famous boardwalk to benefit from $120m renovation fund
World.content:
CultureArt & designCity life Sydney Opera House’s famous boardwalk to benefit from $120m renovation fund Linda Morris August 4, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Sydney Opera House will receive a $120 million upgrade over the next four years to renew critical infrastructure, modernise ageing venue technology and replace 150 concrete beams, slabs and piers sitting in a tidal zone beneath the World Heritage masterpiece. In a second act of the Opera House’s major renewal, the Minns government will announce a four-year investment on Tuesday, with most works invisible to the public. Submerged structures beneath the Northern Boardwalk will be replaced. Steven Siewert The announcement was made just four years after the curtain was lifted on a $150 million refurbishment of the Concert Hall, and work will target the building’s smaller western venues and underlying marine structures. The announcement marks a final milestone for outgoing chief executive Louise Herron, who departs this week after 14 years at the helm to take on a Vice Chancellor’s Fellow role at the University of Sydney.



An executive search firm has yet to be appointed, and names thrown up as a possible replacement include Carriageworks’ Fergus Linehan, Sydney Theatre Company’s Anne Dunn and Brenna Hobson, the Opera House’s programming director. The investment was made possible under a new mechanism which quarantines the allocation to the Opera House for use for capital works only. After 14 years Louise Herron is leaving the Sydney Opera House. Steven Siewert “This funding will do wonders for the long-term future of a World Heritage masterpiece,” Herron said. “The area we are referring to is underlying marine structures on the northern side of the Opera House precinct, entirely facing the harbour and subject to the tides and wash of the passing heavy marine traffic. The work is going to tender by the end of the year and work will be staged in the Playhouse and Drama Theatre to minimise disruption.”



Treasurer Daniel Mookhey said the $120 million injection, delivered over four years, would help the Opera House keep pace with modern visitor and performance expectations. Key features of the project include replacing 1970s-era theatre machinery and staging systems in the Playhouse, Studio and Drama Theatre – venues frequently used by companies including Sydney Theatre Company and Bell Shakespeare. The works will introduce automated stage draping, stage risers and acoustic curtains, allowing for faster and more efficient turnarounds between shows as the venue expands its program of contemporary music, talks, comedy, circus and cabaret alongside anchor residents such as the Sydney Symphony Orchestra, Australian Chamber Orchestra and Sydney Philharmonia Choirs. The Drama Theatre relies on manual hand lines – a counter-weight and pulley system – and temporary chain motors. Installing cutting-edge theatre technology will improve safety while enabling greater performance range and complexity. Stage accessibility will also be upgraded, alongside event management and control systems across both indoor and outdoor venues to future-proof precinct-wide communications.



Work begins in 2027, focusing on reinforcing concrete piers and submerged structures of the Northern Boardwalk that have weathered more than 50 years of salt water, ferry wash and heavy foot traffic. Related Article Visual art David Hockney’s immersive display speaks to you ‘over your shoulder’ The upgrades follow recent planning reforms that increased outdoor venue capacity and operational hours, Arts Minister John Graham said, important work for a building that was a “symbol of modern Australia”. The Sydney Opera House welcomes 11 million precinct visitors each year, with 1.4 million audience members attending its 1850 annual performances and more than 8000 people employed across the precinct. The former Coalition government contributed $234 million to the building’s decade-long renewal, its new Centre for Creativity, refurbished function and events centre and Joan Sutherland Theatre upgrades, with the Opera House contributing more than $50 million from its own cash reserves. It was the biggest capital investment in the Opera House since its opening. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: I wish Hill and Stengle well, but the game must learn lessons from their exits
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion I wish Hill and Stengle well, but the game must learn lessons from their exits Mathew Stokes AFL columnist August 4, 2026 — 5:30am

August 4, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The news that Collingwood and Geelong had reached agreements with Bobby Hill and Ty Stengle to depart the club was hardly a surprise. But that didn’t make hearing it any less disappointing as both were extremely talented players who starred on the biggest stages for their clubs. Premierships, All-Australian selection and a Norm Smith medal bear testament to the ability they possessed. Bobby Hill, pictured at training in June, parted ways from Collingwood. Getty Images More importantly they are also people who I care about having enjoyed the interactions I have had with them over the years. Like their teammates and coaches and fans, I only want the best for them in the next chapter of their lives.



But their untimely departures raise questions in my mind about whether we need to reevaluate the way we manage players as they learn what is required to be a professional athlete. Although ultimate responsibility sits with each individual, the game needs to have an honest look at what it can learn from such untimely departures. The first and most important question to consider is why the game seems to allow players to continue to make mistake after mistake without them being held accountable. That’s all players regardless of background, gender or talent. My impression is that the clubs, the AFL and the Players’ Association have become comfortable with a system which allows players too much protection the first time they commit relatively minor indiscretions.



If the offence enters the public arena they might receive a two-match ban. Otherwise the clubs, association and league are more inclined to keep the transgression behind closed doors to work with the player while they keep contributing to the business of winning. That approach sets individuals up for failure because they have the opportunity to move further and further away from meeting the standards required to be a professional athlete. It then becomes more difficult for them to adjust and reset themselves. I am not naive. Such an approach has been part of professional sport for aeons but in the era of unrelenting media coverage, wellbeing and personal issues are too often being used to protect individuals from unwanted scrutiny if they muck up.



Some argue that such a strategy has had successes no-one hears about. Tyson Stengle has left Geelong as a premiership player. Cameron Spencer But we also see the results of that approach when players gradually drift from the club and eventually train spasmodically. It is disappointing for all involved, particularly when you wonder if some tough love early would have set the players on a more realistic course. I suspect it would and if it didn’t it at least shows players what the expectations will be in the real world when skill at football means little and there is no-one to protect you.



Soon after I was charged with possessing cocaine in February 2010 (I eventually accepted a 12-month good behaviour bond) the club told me to go away for three months and work in a real job away from the team. It was hard work with no certainty as to what lay ahead. I learned that the privilege of being an AFL player could be taken from me instantly and I would need to work to win back the respect of the league, club, teammates and supporters. Such hard conversations would also force players to face the prospect that being a professional athlete might not be for them before clubs spend hundreds of thousands of dollars and expect teammates and coaches to speak in riddles about their absence from training or the club. Editor's pick Four Points

AFL 2026 ‘Clarko’ looks exasperated. It’s time for a hard conversation That doesn’t mean those in charge show no empathy for a player’s background or individual circumstances when developing them as a professional athlete. Not at all. Clubs must support people inside their environment.



Understanding players and building good relationships with them is an essential part of any successful club. I am arguing that all players have to meet a certain standard regardless of who they are, their life experiences, or where they come from. If they aren’t met, then the player faces consequences. I would expect clubs, the league and the players’ association to review the decisions which led to Hill and Stengle’s departures from their clubs. A mature conversation needs to be had about what happens if a player is not rocking up to training yet is still being rewarded with an income.



A conversation should also be held about the prospect of applying penalties to players who don’t meet required standards in real time to give them an incentive to lift their game. Such penalties could set them up for a life beyond the AFL rather than rationalising a reason for someone to play the week after a misdemeanour because they are talented. It will also reduce any disincentive a club might have in taking in players from various backgrounds or offering them long-term deals if they know they can deal with situations as they arise how they see fit. People in footy want the best for players but development can only occur when consequences result from behaviour. And the sooner that happens, the better. That’s the real world where the most important lessons are learned.



Mathew Stokes is a Larrakia man who played 200 games with Geelong and Essendon. He played in Geelong’s 2007 and 2011 premiership teams. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Melbourne’s worst-kept secret: Behind the celebrity trappings, Ralph Carr was known simply as ‘The Rug’
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The conviction of veteran artist and sports manager Ralph Carr for rape was one of Melbourne’s worst-kept secrets. What was also well known to many who had crossed paths with the celebrity manager was that Carr was a small man with an enormous ego, prone to bullying and manipulative behaviour. He loved to surround himself with the trappings of success and the famous, but was difficult to work with and chaotic. Ralph Carr outside court in June 2024. Jason South One former staffer went so far as to describe Carr as “revolting” and “a master manipulator”. Carr’s conviction, and the lifting of a near three-year suppression order, has opened the floodgates for many in the music and sporting worlds who have long held a dim view of the man they dubbed “The Rug”. One woman, who worked at Ralph Carr Management in the mid-2010s while in her early 20s, described her tenure there as “an awful and confusing time”, saying she and other staff experienced “outrageous bullying” from him.



“I saw some pretty terrible things,” she told this masthead while asking to speak anonymously to protect her employment. “None of it was nice … his behaviour was revolting.” The former employee said news that Carr, 66, had been found guilty by a jury of one count of sexual assault and two counts of rape would trigger uncomfortable and difficult memories for many women. Tigers champion Dustin Martin (right) with his then-manager, Ralph Carr, after winning the 2017 AFL Players’ Association Most Valuable Player Award. Getty Images “The past 24 hours have been very confronting,” she said. “There is the sexual predator side, but also the toxic work culture. “This is about a pattern of behaviour. There are multiple women with stories about things that have gone on.” Carr continues to strenuously deny he committed any crime, and his lawyer, Dermot Dann, KC, told the County Court on Monday his client planned to appeal against the verdict. Carr’s Instagram account is filled with photos of his famous and wealthy friends and clients.



In one image, the twice-married and twice-divorced father of three is smiling arm-in-arm with country rock star Keith Urban. In others, he poses with supermodel Miranda Kerr, shares a drink with Molly Meldrum, and another with Nine entertainment reporter Richard Wilkins. Then there’s Carr at the Brownlow Medal night with Dustin Martin, the champion Richmond footballer who was his prized celebrity management client. Carr (right) at the unveiling of a statue for Molly Meldrum alongside Michael Gudinski, Meldrum and Jeanne Pratt. Eddie Jim Carr had been the man behind the AFL great when Martin was part of three premiership wins with the Tigers and won the 2017 Brownlow Medal. The pair were more than just manager and client. They were close friends and business associates, having invested together in several, multimillion-dollar commercial properties in Melbourne. However, like Carr’s freedom that relationship is now in tatters. In a statement, Martin said he was “shocked to learn of the outcome of the court proceedings”.



“I had no knowledge whatsoever of the conduct that led to these convictions,” the footy great said. “My thoughts are with those affected. Effective immediately, I have ended my professional relationship with my former manager. As this is a legal matter, I will not be making any further comment.” Related Article Courts Entertainment stalwart Ralph Carr identified as mystery rapist after suppression order lifted While Martin was Carr’s sporting ace in the pack, over the years he also represented a who’s who of stars from across the music industry – including his ex-wife, Tina Arena, former Noiseworks frontman Jon Stevens, Kate Ceberano, Bonnie Anderson, Vanessa Amorosi and Rick Price. He also represented actor Madeleine West, magician Cosentino, Wilkins and singer Mark Vincent who ended up fighting with Carr in the County Court over money. Carr also worked with Priscilla Presley when she visited Australia on a speaking tour, escorting her to Flemington for the Melbourne Cup. Famously, Carr married former Young Talent Time star Tina Arena in 2015. The couple divorced a little over four years later in what was a messy split. Ralph Carr with Tina Arena in 1993. Rodger Cummins



He had been her manager from 1992, with Arena later describing the union in memoirs and interviews as more of a complex business dynamic than a traditional romantic connection. They no longer speak, with Arena reporting that the marriage left her financially devastated and reduced her net worth to zero after years of work. In the AFL, Carr made a splash running his Richmond-based agency, Ralph Carr Management Sport. He was a Carlton Football Club director, serving on the board from December 2006 until October 2008, and remains a fanatical supporter of the Blues. His official player agent accreditation, through the AFL Players Association, was likely to be revoked following his conviction, said a fellow player agent, speaking anonymously to talk freely. Carr enjoyed prominence when it came to hardball, headline-grabbing contract negotiations. One industry source, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said the colourful Carr had brought a “Hollywood” vibe to the managerial role, befitting his background in the entertainment industry. He was also dubbed “The Rug” in some circles, because of the distinct black toupee which he still sported in court. Loading

World.title: ‘Impenetrable border’: Farage claims Australian plan can stop the boats to Britain
World.content:
WorldEuropeImmigration ‘Impenetrable border’: Farage claims Australian plan can stop the boats to Britain David Crowe August 4, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: British warships would turn back asylum seekers in the English Channel under plans unveiled by Reform UK leader Nigel Farage to embrace Australia’s tough border policy to stop the boats. Farage vowed to launch the largest military operation of its kind to deter thousands of asylum seekers from boarding inflatable boats on French beaches to seek new lives in Britain, citing the Australian approach as a template. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage in London on Monday. Getty Images The plan came at a time of heightened argument about border policies after more than 50,000 people rushed from Morocco into the Spanish territory of Ceuta, leading to at least 72 deaths. But the Reform plan sparked immediate objections from UK critics who said it would provoke France by using Royal Marines to force asylum seekers back to the beaches where they started.



Farage insisted the French would accept Britain’s right to protect its borders if he became prime minister at the next election, declaring the British public wanted tougher measures even if that meant diplomatic and military tensions. “The country will get behind the message that we have a Royal Navy, it’s there to protect this country from invasion, and that now is what it should be used for,” he said. Related Article Analysis

Immigration How the storming of Ceuta shifts Europe to the right Reform issued a border policy document that devoted several pages to the Australian regime imposed when Tony Abbott led the Liberal Party into government in 2013, including turning back boats. The Reform plan explicitly cited the command structure for Operation Sovereign Borders under the Labor government in Australia, with Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke overseeing multiple agencies to deter arrivals.



While the next UK national elections are not due for another three years, Farage appears likely to shape British debate on border control given Reform UK has a strong position in the opinion polls. The Labour government has revived its fortunes by installing former Manchester mayor Andy Burnham as prime minister, with a YouGov survey last week showing Labour had lifted its support to 22 per cent, matching Reform for the first time in 16 months. Burnham sought to assure voters on Sunday that he could manage tough borders, visiting operations in Dover where border control officials take asylum seekers after intercepting the small inflatable boats in the channel. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham (second from left) stands by a recovered small boat, which was used by migrants crossing the English Channel. Getty Images “The public don’t like the idea that the border looks like it’s not controlled. We need to bring back that control. But, also, we need to offer support for people who genuinely need it,” the prime minister said.



Farage, however, demanded tougher measures in a plan he called Operation Fortress, replicating the formal Australian policy that anyone who arrived by boat would not be settled in the country. Reform said the policy would make Britain’s border impenetrable. Related Article Immigration Spain plans new border barrier in Ceuta as death toll revealed The Reform plan set out Australian measures such as turning back boats where it is safe to do so, setting up a single command, using military vessels to stop boats and issuing temporary protection visas that do not offer permanent protection or allow family reunion. “Under Operation Sovereign Borders, boats were turned around and people were left to complete the final leg of the return journey alone and unescorted,” the Reform policy said.



“Under Operation Fortress, everyone will be rescued and safely returned to their point of departure. What the Australian precedent proved, however, is that the certainty of interception and the guarantee of return is the most successful deterrent possible.” Conservative Party home affairs spokesman Chris Philp dismissed the Reform plan on the grounds it was not credible. “They can’t answer the question [about] how they would disembark immigrants back in France if the French don’t agree,” he said. Migrants try to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. AP Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood defended an existing deal with France to discourage asylum seekers by sending some back across the channel, although she acknowledged this was “trickier” than the approach being taken in Spain in the border crisis at Ceuta.



Mahmood and her department said the National Crime Agency had doubled the number of officers who were tackling people smugglers, saying there were now 800 on this task. As well, almost 1000 law enforcement, intelligence and military officers were on the French coast to stop small boats. “More than 1900 traffickers and gang leaders who helped to facilitate Channel crossings have been arrested in the last year alone, 74 per cent more than the previous year,” the Home Office said in a statement. Related Article Immigration ‘I don’t know why they let us through’: How 50,000 people surged into a Spanish exclave Spain mobilised its armed forces to send thousands of asylum seekers back to Morocco after they swam and walked across a rocky coastline to reach the enclave of Ceuta. In its latest estimate, the Spanish government said about 69,500 migrants had returned to Morocco over four days, up from its earlier estimate that 50,000 had arrived.



Officials said that 72 had died on the Spanish side of the border, while 11 died on the Moroccan side. Spanish newspaper El País said many asylum seekers remained in Ceuta and this included 862 minors, a number that has quadrupled in the past two weeks. World.title: Labour leader Chris Hipkins rules out working with Winston Peters as foreign affairs minister
World.content:
Weekly interview with opposition leader, Chris Hipkins Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Labour leader Chris Hipkins has ruled out working with New Zealand First's Winston Peters at the next election.

New Zealand First's leader responded to heckling in the House on Wednesday last week by attacking the Greens' Lawrence Xu-nan, telling him to go back to his "own country".

Hipkins said Winston Peters' position as foreign affairs minister was completely untenable.

"He's making international headlines for all the wrong reasons. He can't continue in that job, he can't credibly represent New Zealand on the world stage."

Hipkins said he ruled out working with Winston Peters and New Zealand First before the last election and he had not regretted it.

"Behaviour like we've seen with Winston Peters and Shane Jones as well with his racist comments towards Indians in recent months is not compatible with the sort of government I want to lead."

Quilae Wong rules out working with Peters as Foreign Minister Midday Report Download MP3 5m

Asked if he would rule out having Winston Peters as a foreign affairs minister if he led the next government, Hipkins said he could not be foreign affairs minister in any government.

"He cannot represent New Zealand credibly on the world stage when he's making outwardly racist comments."

Asked whether he could work with New Zealand First, Hipkins said "we couldn't work with them at the last election, nothing really has changed that makes this more likely at the coming election."

Peters has already ruled out forming a government with Labour at the next election.

Speaking at a post-Cabinet media conference on Monday afternoon, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said he had spoken to Peters about the comments, but refused to outline what exactly was discussed, nor would he say whether he expressed disappointment in his foreign minister.

Earlier on Monday, Luxon told Morning Report that Peters' comments were racist but that he had not yet spoken to Peters directly.

At the media conference Luxon would not say if he would have Peters as foreign minister again if he won the election, saying that was all "hypothetical", nor would he be drawn on questions about the risk to coalition stability if Luxon were to discipline or try fire Peters.

Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong has also said her party would not support a government that had Peters as foreign minister.

"As we've always said, we will sit down and try to find common ground, and that remains the case with New Zealand First," she said.

World.title: Wild deer costing Hawke's Bay farmers tens of thousands of dollars - study
World.content:
Study reveals cost of wild deer damage Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A new study of wild deer populations in Hawke's Bay has found the problem is costing farmers tens of thousands of dollars.

The research, by primary sector economist Peter MacIntyre, reveals extensive pasture and crop losses from deer, as well as damage to native plantings and bush.

He said wild deer may be causing far greater economic damage to farms than many landowners realise.

"There is good evidence from drone and helicopter thermal imaging that many landowners could have five to six times more deer than they think.

"Once deer numbers grow from 50 to 100 and more, the economic damage gets significant, more so if they are getting 100 percent of their feed from your property," said MacIntyre.

Porangahau farmer Sam Stoddart is all too familiar with the problem, with 8000 hectares of bush on his farm boundary.

"There'd be at an estimate... 800 plus deer right on our boundary, so a young kale crop will get pulled.. plucked out before it's had time to establish," said Stoddart.

He said if those 800 deer grazed on his land they'd eat about the same amount as 1200 sheep, which could be making him $145,000 a year.

Instead, with hundreds of wild deer creeping onto his land, the farmer has paddocks he can't put into higher value crops, winter grass that's being chewed up and native plants that are disappearing.

He said wild deer populations have ballooned over the past 10 years or so.

"The numbers have just exploded. They were released as a bit of game for hunters but were never really controlled I don't think by DOC [Department of Conservation] or anything... now it's got to stage where we need some sort of government intervention," said Stoddart.

Wild deer in the Central Hawke's Bay village of Pōrangahau. Supplied

He's one of 14 landowners that rural economist Peter MacIntyre talked to for his research into the wild deer problem in Hawke's Bay.

"It was a rather depressing story. People had lost a lot of natives, people were losing forage crops," said MacIntyre.

"It was a pretty sobering story from everybody."

The research was organised by Marie Taylor from Plant Hawke's Bay and funded by the Hawke's Bay Regional Council, the Joan Fernie Charitable Trust and the Pan Pac Environmental Trust.

During the study, one landowner who thought he had 50 deer on his property found nearly 300 with thermal imaging - and Taylor said this highlighted how huge the wild deer problem had become.

"Numbers have increased really exponentially. They are a real limiting factor for all things on farm including plantings, they're also really totalling our biodversity because they graze species by species, they take most palatable things out of the landscape first.

"Even though the canopy of the forest looks great, we are losing everything underneath," she said.

The study showed when 100 deer got half of their annual feed requirements from productive pasture, farmers lost more than $10,000 per year.

MacIntyre said over 10 years, using an 8.4 percent discount rate, that was more than $100,000 in lost value.

"If farmers are losing forage or won't plant forage because of the likely damage, you can more than double the losses above."

Wild deer on the run in New Zealand Department of Conservation

'I want to see people working together'

MacIntyre said new deer fences cost in the vicinity of $40,000 per kilometre and sustained shooting programmes were costly and required ongoing effort. He calculated that electric fencing added to existing fences, would be less, at around $8000 per kilometre.

However, he said when you took into account the losses from deer grazing, it becomes more economically viable to fence.

"If you try to ringfence your farm it's going to cost you quite a lot... If you gang up with your neighbours and ringfence off the problem area then it's going to be a lot more cost effective for each farmer," he said.

Taylor agreed.

"We need to work as catchment goups and put up deer fencing where we can defend the fence. I want to see people working together like they did with possum control areas - that was hugely successful in Hawke's Bay," said Taylor.

But she said to achieve that, what is really needed is more funding for conservation and pest control.

"There has been an uncontrolled invasion of feral deer into farmed land from the ranges in Hawke's Bay with no coordinated control programmes and a consequent destruction of years of careful biodiversity planning, planting and management as well as economic loss to farmers.

"Unless DOC does its job properly this situation will only get worse with deer numbers increasing and environmental damage becoming even more significant and economic costs to farmers becoming unsustainable," she said.

Wild deer can be found in both the North and South Islands of New Zealand on public conservation land and private property. Supplied

The Department of Convservation's wild animals manager, Mike Perry, told RNZ that DOC actively managed deer in areas where they had the greatest impact on biodiversity, with around 200,000 hectares of deer management undertaken nationwide.

"We acknowledge that wild animal numbers are increasing. National monitoring shows ungulates (wild deer, goats, pigs, chamois and tahr) are present at approximately 83 percent of monitored sites on public conservation land, up from 63 percent in 2013.

"In response, DOC has significantly increased control efforts across the country in recent years through additional funding provided in Budget 2022, alongside more than $10 million received through the International Visitor Levy," said Perry.

DOC said deer management is carried out at several sites across Hawke's Bay and surrounding areas, such as in the Ruahine Forest Part.

However, Perry said in Hawke's Bay wild goats posed a greater ecological threat than deer in many conservation areas.

"DOC undertakes goat control across a range of sites in the region and is carrying out extensive work in the northeastern Ruahine Range with the goal of making that part of the park wild goat free."

He said managing wild animals is a shared responsibility that extended beyond public conservation land.

World.title: Who's feeling job market recovery? And where has downturn hit hardest?
World.content:
What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

It has been a tough few years to be a jobseeker. Data this week is expected to show the unemployment rate still hovering around the highest level it's been in a decade.

But fortunes have varied depending on where you are in the country, and the type of work you do.

The job market peak was reached in October 2023, when there were 2.395 million filled jobs nationwide. The trough was in October last year, when that had dropped to 2.337m.

Provisional estimates are that the number is now about 2.35m filled jobs.

Westpac chief economist on fuel prices and unemployment Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said from the peak of the market to the bottom, there were just under 60,000 jobs lost but since then, 17,575 have been recovered, leaving the country still 40,924 jobs short compared to the busiest time in the labour market.

Here are some of the winners and losers of the labour market both since the peak, and over the past five years.

Sectors

Since the job market peaked in October 2023, the biggest drop in jobs in percentage terms has been felt in the information media and telecommunications sector, down 11.2 percent or 3761 jobs.

Over five years, smoothing out the post-Covid high, job numbers in that sector are still down 5.6 percent.

Construction has also had a sharp fall from the peak, having lost 8.4 percent of its jobs, or 17,249, but the number is flat compared to 2021.

Some sectors have continued to grow since the peak, such as arts and recreation services, which is up 6.1 percent from 2023 and 16.2 percent over five years. Of this sector, the largest proportion of jobs is in sports and physical recreation, such as people working in gyms. Their numbers have lifted from 22,700 in 2023 to 24,400 last year. There has also been significant growth in businesses. Personal health and fitness training business numbers increased 112.5 percent between 2019 and 2025.

Who's feeling job market recovery? Morning Report Download MP3 2m

Healthcare and social assistance jobs have also increased since the job market peak, up 5.4 percent since 2023 and 12.7 percent from five years ago.

Education and training is up 4.4 percent from the peak and 6.6 percent over five years.

Eaqub said, on a per population basis, there had not yet been any real recovery. Data would show there were more hours being worked, he said, but the recovery in jobs so far had only kept pace with population growth. "It's not a high-quality recovery yet."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub. RNZ

Construction's increase was the largest in number terms, followed by manufacturing down 11,822.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said the strongest parts of the labour market were those that were tied to underlying population growth.

"It's the expansion of certain elements of public service-related industries as well, particularly in health, education… those sectors have grown a lot because the population has grown in the last five years. They've continued to grow, albeit at a slower rate since 2023, because that was when the population growth peaked… there's quite a few industries that are a lot more government or public sector dominated, and they just tend to not be really influenced by the cycle so much."

In contrast, sectors such as construction were much more closely tied to the fortunes of the wider economy.

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen said the October 2023 peak was exaggerated by the election, with a burst of short-term filled jobs in public administration. "Excluding that boost, jobs activity likely peaked around March 2024."

"The large increases in healthcare, public administration, and education and training reflect a growing population and of course one of the largest health-related events in memory.

"Further hiring in education is also likely due to retraining of people throughout the pandemic, and then as the unemployment rate increased, with more people looking at training options to re- or up-skill."

He said construction had gone through a significant period of change.

"At one point, residential construction intentions were the highest in half a century, fuelled by rocketing house prices and low interest rates, and the sector scaled up to meet that high demand. But when interest rates rose and house prices and activity dropped, construction activity pulled back too, having upped capacity to meet peak needs that just didn't, and were never going to, persist."

He said both admin and information media and telecoms jobs had been holding up for a while until the downturn became more pronounced.

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

By age

Young people have experienced the biggest impact of the downturn.

There are now 61,009 fewer jobs held by people aged under 30 than there were at the peak, and 43,726 fewer than five years ago.

The number of people over 55 working has increased 9.7 percent over five years and the number aged 30 to 54 has increased 9.1 percent.

"It's definitely the younger people who had quite a big increase, particularly the 15 to 19-year-olds had a big increase in jobs or employment during that really tight labour market period, when there was a hiring frenzy during the Covid years, those numbers were unusually high.

"The cost of living particularly for necessities skyrocketed so a lot of young people, kids at school, started to work and that's kind of fallen off and hasn't really recovered."

Ministry of Social Development data shows the biggest increase in main benefit recipient numbers has been in the 25 to 39 age group where there are now 20 percent more people receiving a benefit than there were in June 2021.

Eckhold said it was a "no hire, no fire" market.

"We haven't necessarily seen enormous amounts of layoffs in aggregate across the economy, but it has become quite hard to find a job. And that's particularly impacted the younger age group, because they've got less skills and experience, so it's always just a bit harder."

Region

Canterbury has had some of the strongest job growth. Its job numbers are up 1.4 percent compared to the peak and 8.9 percent over five years.

Auckland is down 2.7 percent form the peak and 5.1 percent up over five years.

Wellington is down 3.8 percent from the peak and 0.3 percent up over five years.

Gisborne has been hard hit, down 4.2 percent from the peak and 1.5 percent over five years.

Wellington and Auckland have had the largest percentage increase in benefit recipients between June 2021 and June 2026, in percentage terms.

Eckhold said he expected to see a small increase in the unemployment rate this week and his current forecast was for that to be the peak.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold. Supplied / LinkedIn

"I will say though, we'll be doing a whole new set of forecasts this month. When we put in place our previous forecasts, it was in the context of a better outlook, because it looked like energy prices were quite a lot lower. It looked like we're going to have a period of more stability, and that seems to have tended not to be the case now that we've got a little bit further on. So, it may be optimistic to expect that the unemployment rate will be peaking now. Perhaps we might have to wait a bit longer for that."

He said the job market would be the last thing to pick up.

"GDP has actually been picking up now for three or four quarters or so. It looks like we had an interruption to growth in Q2, but three quarters before that we'd had some decent growth. But there's always a lag between when you actually see growth occur and then when hiring really picks up.

"Probably at the start of the year, we would have expected that hiring growth to really be starting to hit its straps now, in the second half of the year. But I think the Iran war has really just pushed that back."

World.title: No need for Luxon to apologise over Rotorua business meeting comments, mayor says
World.content:
Rotorua Business Chamber responds to PM’s apology Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The Rotorua mayor says the prime minister's comments to a business audience last week were him being honest, and she doesn't think he needed to apologise.

"I don't think it's a time for our leaders in New Zealand to be soft. We need to know the truth. We need to be honest, and we need to set a pathway forward," Nationa party-aligned Tania Tapsell said.

Meanwhile, the Rotorua Business Chamber is welcoming the apology from Christopher Luxon, but hoped there's "genuine reflection behind it".

Luxon had told the audience at a Rotorua Business Chamber event on Friday that some businesses had a "parent-child mentality" and too often looked to the government for help.

His office later released a transcript.

Craig McCulloch on PM’s apology to business owners Morning Report Download MP3 5m

On Monday, he apologised, saying he was sorry his comments "did not properly acknowledge the challenges that many small business owners are facing".

"I didn't want to cause any offence. That's not what I intended to do."

President of the Rotorua Business Chamber Paul Ingram welcomed the apology, but hoped there was "genuine reflection behind it".

Ingram told RNZ small and medium businesses were the backbone of the New Zealand economy, and it was important that the sector was taken seriously by "every government".

Rotorua Business Chamber president Paul Ingram. Supplied / Rotorua Business Chamber

"Because collectively we have the ability to enable the growth and success that we're collectively looking for.

"I don't think we're looking for a handout. We're looking for understanding," Ingram added.

The reflection he wanted Luxon to consider was that there was an understanding of what these business owners were going through.

He acknowledged some of the comments last week may have been "unintended", or as "sharp and as pointed as they were", and he understood the prime minister came from a business background.

But he hoped there'd be a consideration that whatever was going on in the economy translated into what was real for New Zealand businesses.

"For mum and dad businesses that have got a mortgage, the house is on the line."

In welcoming the apology, Ingram said he would look forward to seeing what actions the government would take now to support small businesses going forward.

Overall Ingram said other parts of the discussion he "totally" agreed with, it was just the "whole parent-child narrative that came out that didn't really land very well".

The Rotorua mayor told RNZ the business community really appreciated having the prime minister in town.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Tapsell was the National Party candidate for the East Coast electorate in 2020.

She acknowledged it was "tough times, and that was the context in which the question was answered".

She said Luxon didn't need to apologise because "he had a room full of people that was taking on his advice".

Tapsell, who wasn't at the event herself, was told that the feeling in the room afterwards was "definitely that they appreciated his thoughts on it".

"We need to get real in New Zealand," Tapsell said. "Sometimes it is us that actually needs to solve our own problems, and I feel like that's what he's doing not only in those comments but also actually in Parliament.

"So good on him."

Tapsell said Luxon was being honest, and that was "the best thing we can ask from people".

"At least he's not running us around in a circle, not answering the question, and honestly, that was appreciated and valued on the day in the room."

She said it was "very lovely" that he did apologise, and reflected Luxon's honesty and integrity, "he's being honest as he was in the room".

"It's a pretty big thing for a politician to apologise. This doesn't happen very often."

Tapsell said from the business perspective, he was answering a question in the context of difficult times.

"Yes, things are bad, but don't rely on government handouts - I can understand that as a mayor from a council as well.

World.title: At least 10 police staff face criminal charges after anti-corruption investigation
World.content:
A police staff member accused of kidnapping and sexual offending is among at least 10 staff facing criminal charges following investigations by the police's anti-corruption unit, RNZ can reveal.

Other staff are before the courts charged with firearms trafficking-related offending, drug supply, and another staffer is charged with assault, blackmail, threats and damage.

As of May, there were about 40 staff under investigation by the unit.

The National Integrity Unit (NIU) was established in 2020, with then Police Commissioner Mike Bush saying it had been created to "bolster Police's capability in protecting against the risk of corruption and, where appropriate, investigating corruption within New Zealand Police".

In May, RNZ requested under the Official Information Act the total number of cases investigated by the NIU since it was established, as well as the total number of active cases.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

The information - which was initially due back in June - was provided to RNZ on Friday.

In the response, director of integrity and conduct Detective Superintendent Kylie Schaare said the NIU received information from a wide variety of sources, much of it often incomplete or unverified.

"Each piece of information is recorded as a "matter" and undergoes preliminary assessment. A matter may be progressed to a criminal investigation where it can be corroborated or expanded or, it may be closed as having no substance or insufficient merit."

From January 2020 to May 2026, 117 "matters" had progressed to investigations, with no further action taken by the NIU.

"This generally reflects cases where there is no evidence of criminal offending or there is insufficient evidence for a prosecution.

"However, this does not preclude action being taken by other Police work groups, such as employment investigations or preventative interventions at a district level."

During the same time period, 22 prosecutions have commenced following NIU investigations.

Of those, 12 are no longer before the courts. This includes one staffer being convicted for cocaine supply, corrupt use of official information, and computer access offending. Three staff have been convicted for accessing a computer system for a dishonest purpose.

There were 10 staff before the courts as of May following NIU investigations.

This includes a staffer facing "multiple serious offences" including firearms, violence, kidnapping and sexual offending. One staff member is charged with firearms trafficking-related offending, while another is charged with assault, blackmail, threats and damage.

Other charges faced by other staff include Passport Act offences, drug supply and obtaining by deception.

There were 39 active NIU investigations under way as of 11 May.

RNZ asked Police for further information on the cases before the courts.

A spokesperson replied: "As the matter is before the court, we are unable to provide any further information or comment in relation to the active criminal proceedings."

Sexual misconduct allegations

RNZ earlier requested under the Official Information Act the total number of police staff under investigation, both criminal and employment as well as how long they had been under investigation for.

Figures released reveal that as of 18 June there were 271 open investigations involving 325 police employees. 109 are listed as an employment process only, the rest involve both employment and criminal matters.

Seven of the investigations had been open for more than 1000 days, including two staff who had been under investigation for 1542 days. Nearly 30 investigations were older than 500 days.

Allegations included perjury, manual use of force, such as striking, kicking or restraining, conflict of interest, drugs/alcohol and disgraceful behaviour.

There were 33 staff under investigation for sexual misconduct. Six of those had been going on for more than 500 days.

In response to questions about the figures, NZ Police acting chief operating officer Leigh MacDonald said allegations of sexual misconduct were taken seriously, regardless of who was involved.

"The message is clear - nobody is above the law or the standards expected of police employees.

"Every member of police's more than 16,000 staff is expected to act with integrity and professionalism and will be held to account where misconduct is established."

Police did not believe the figures indicated a widespread issue across the organisation, MacDonald said.

World.title: Pacific women MPs share the push for more representation in parliaments
World.content:
Last week, 29 women parliamentarians from 14 Pacific jurisdictions traded their own legislatures for New Zealand's Parliament in wintry Wellington.

The women changing Pacific politics Pacific Waves Download MP3 4m

They were in the capital to take part in the Tuākana, Tēina, Whenua, Talanoa Wānanga, a three-day programme focused on leadership development, networking and sharing ideas, with the overall theme of encouraging more women to take on leadership roles in parliaments and governments across the Pacific.

The gathering comes as Pacific nations continue to grapple with the barriers preventing more women from entering politics. Ignoring New Zealand and Australia, women make up just 7.7 percent of MPs across Oceania, compared with a global average of 27.6 percent.

Those barriers are varied, and can be cultural, with men traditionally dominating governance roles in many Pacific societies.

The barriers can be economic, with women often balancing family responsibilities alongside the demands of public office.

For some, the way women are treated in political spaces can itself be a deterrent.

Among those attending was Lenora Qereqeretabua, assistant minister and deputy speaker of Fiji's parliament.

Qereqeretabua said the model of special temporary measures had consistently proven effective in bypassing these barriers and increasing the number of women in politics.

"It starts with the political parties having that (special members) in their constitutions first, to make sure that they have adequate women, or a certain percentage of women, as candidates in every election, whether it's local government, or national government elections," Qereqeretabua said.

Although women remain underrepresented in Fiji's parliament, the parliamentarian says those who are in politics and other leadership roles are making a significant impact in boardroom, departmental and governance roles.

One example is Fiji's fisheries and forests minister, Alitia Bainivalu, the first woman to hold the portfolio.

Bainivalu said that since being in the job, she had overseen a high number of enrolments by women into the fishing and forestry industries.

Ruta Baabo Manate, meanwhile, one of just four women MPs in Kiribati's parliament, said her country's geography creates an additional challenge for women seeking elected office.

With the government centred in the capital, Tarawa, people living on the country's many outer islands can face significant barriers to participating in politics.

Ruta Baabo Manate Louis Collins

"The female representation of parliamentarians now in the parliament that we have is mainly women that have lived on the capital, on Tarawa, but are from these respective different islands, and so me, I've lived my whole life on Tarawa as well," Manate said.

"It's really complex that we're scattered, but it's also a blessing."

World.title: Solomon Islands government confirms response to rescue trapped NZ climbers
World.content:
The Solomon Islands government is working on "response actions" to rescue two New Zealanders who are stranded on the country's highest mountain.

Keane Isaksson, 25, and Luca Zylstra, 19, were on a climbing expedition to the remote volcanic mountain, Mount Popomanaseu, on the main island of Guadalcanal.

Mt Popomanaseu is the highest peak in the Solomon Islands, standing at an elevation of 2335 metres or 7661 feet.

The pair have been stranded in a remote ravine for five days due to bad weather, which has prevented them from continuing their descent, according to media reports overnight.

"The government is aware of the situation and authorities are currently working on response actions," the Solomon Islands Prime Minister's press secretary said in response to questions from RNZ Pacific.

The Royal Solomon Islands Police Force said it would be releasing a statement on the situation.

New Zealand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade told the ABC in a statement it was providing consular assistance to the families of two New Zealanders in the Solomon Islands.

World.title: 'Lot of nonsense': Dearden clears air on Cowboys future
World.content:
North Queensland co-captain Tom Dearden has cleared the air about his future and given the club a boost as he targets returning from injury to inspire a finals run.

At the end of the 2023 season Dearden, 26, signed a five-year contract extension through to the end of 2029.

But multiple reports in recent weeks linked him to an early exit for personal reasons due to his pregnant partner, Millie Over, living in Sydney.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

Dearden fronted the media to refute the reports due to the impact they were having on his personal life.

"There's been a fair bit of speculation getting around at the moment. There's been a lot of suggestions that I wanted to move or leave the club," Dearden said.

"That's not the case at all. I don't feel like I should have to get up here and explain myself against speculation.

"It's just been a whole lot of nonsense. I've got my private life with a partner who's pregnant and I'd like for that all to be kept private.

"I'm committed to the Cowboys until the end of 2029 and I think it's a bit silly that you have to get up here and speak to a bit of nonsense that's going around."

Dearden made it clear that he was "not recommitting".

"I've always been committed to the Cowboys and none of that has ever changed, so it's a bit disappointing that my partner and family have had to deal with a lot of questions," he said.

Maroons dealt massive blow Queensland selectors have been forced to cope with the news one of their best playmakers will miss up to eight weeks with his ankle injury.

"It's had an impact on the personal life. I've got a pregnant partner and I think when there's speculation getting around like that, people are reading that and it gives them questions to ask and you always have to answer to people."

Dearden has played just once since suffering a syndesmosis and ankle fracture in round 10.

The injury ruled him out of the State of Origin series and he returned against the Dolphins in round 20 only to tear a muscle in his shin on the other leg.

Dearden played through the match but during the following week discovered the issue.

"It's been a frustrating year having to sit out because I love representing the Cowboys," Dearden said.

"It's a bit of a weird injury but it's tracking pretty well and hopefully I've only got a few more weeks [on the sidelines]."

Dearden and the club have targeted the round 26 home clash with Wests Tigers in Townsville as his return date, after the Cowboys' round 25 bye.

North Queensland is in ninth position and plays Gold Coast away on Thursday night before an away clash with Parramatta without its influential half.

AAP

World.title: Former Sea Eagle, ABC radio personality John Gibbs diagnosed with cancer
World.content:
Former Manly-Warringah Sea Eagles halfback and ABC Sport rugby league commentator John Gibbs has been diagnosed with cancer.

Gibbs, 70, has been part of the ABC Sport team since 2016 and has been a popular personality among listeners.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

He was on the ABC Sport call with Andrew Moore and Matthew Elliott on Sunday afternoon when the Parramatta Eels defeated Wests Tigers.

"Gibbsy", who played 81 first grade games for the Sea Eagles and represented New South Wales and Australia, announced his diagnosis on Monday, and that he would be stepping away from broadcasting to focus on his health.

Moore, ABC Sport's lead rugby league caller, said his friend Gibbs wanted listeners to know he was prepared for his upcoming treatment on NRL MONDAY.

"John Gibbs called me this afternoon to confirm something he had been fearing for a while. He's been diagnosed with cancer — Hodgkin's lymphoma," Moore said.

"He knows he's in for a fight, but he wants you to know he's up for it.

"We are family and, as I discovered a year ago, the wave of support from the ABC team, it's significant, it's powerful, it's amazing and it helps.

"Like so many of you, he's ready to kick cancer to the kerb and beat the mongrel."

The former international has been a constant on Sydney radio since the 1980s as a commentator, presenter, and host for 2UE, 2GB and ABC Sport.

World.title: Young Tiger banned as gut-punch crackdown continues
World.content:
Richmond defender Luke Trainor has received a one-match ban for striking as the AFL's crackdown on gut punches continues.

Trainor will miss the Tigers' trip to face Adelaide at Adelaide Oval on Saturday after punching West Coast forward Jack Williams in the stomach as the two were jostling in the goal square at the MCG on Sunday.

Williams dropped to the turf while Trainor jogged off.

Coach Adem Yze had hoped Trainor would only be fined for the second-quarter incident in the 11-point win over the Eagles.

But the match review officer took a dim view of the incident, assessing it as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact, which draws a one-match ban.

It leaves Richmond short of a tall defender against Adelaide's powerful forward line headlined by Riley Thilthorpe.

AAP

World.title: Wallabies to battle heat, typhoon in Japanese Test
World.content:
The Wallabies are not concerned Japan's searing heat and lingering typhoon will play a part in their preparation or Test match as they look to face old foes in Les Kiss's debut as coach.

Australia will take on Japan in the first of two Tests on Saturday night at Hanazono Rugby Stadium in Osaka, although conditions are not expected to be easy to play in.

Temperatures are tipped to stay in the high 20s to mid-30s degrees Celsius all week as the country grapples with a heatwave.

To make matters worse, Typhoon Dolphin is bringing wind gusts of up to 216kph and heavy rainfall ahead of hitting the Southern Japanese Ryukyu Islands on Friday, about 1,500 kilometres south of Osaka.

Wallabies thrash Italy as Schmidt era ends in triumph The Wallabies record a convincing 57-10 victory over Italy in Perth, as Joe Schmidt's coaching tenure finishes on a winning note.

But Queensland hooker Josh Nasser is treating the conditions as just another day in Australia.

"Obviously it's pretty warm over here, but I grew up in Brissy. We get some pretty hot summers as well. So humidity's up, temperatures up, but it's no different to some of the conditions we get back home," he told reporters on Monday.

"In the wet, the ball gets slippery, things tighten up a little bit. But I think we've got a big focus on just still trying to express ourselves.

"We play a fixture in Fiji each year, which we get pretty extreme conditions for.

"We're really not hyper-focused on it. We're just accepting that it will be hot, and then sticking to our processes."

Wallabies assistant coach Scott McLeod also warned of another typhoon that could affect Australia's clash.

"Is that Eddie Jones?" he joked when a journalist asked about Typhoon Dolphin.

Jones, who led Australia to a dismal Rugby World Cup showing in 2023 before resigning, will coach his second game against the green and gold with the Brave Blossoms.

Former Wallabies coach Eddie Jones will face Australia for the second time as Japan's coach. (AAP: Darren Pateman)

Nasser expects his presence to add extra spice to the fixture, especially as the master agitator took over the Japanese side just six weeks after resigning and was forced to deny that he had been in talks with Brave Blossoms officials during the World Cup.

Jones will not be the only Australian on the opposition, with former Queensland lock Harry Hockings along with Ben Gunter, Jack Cornelsen, Dylan Riley, Michael Stolberg and Tiennan Costley all options to play.

The Wallabies have been humbled by Australians featuring for different national teams in the past, most notably Canberra-born Mack Hansen when he scored a stunning first-half hat-trick to help Ireland win 46-19 last November.

"They'll be fired up to prove a point against us, I'm sure. [There's] nothing too strange about seeing them there, but it'll be a good battle," Nasser said.

"A couple of them are my good mates. Harry Hockings is one of my best mates.

"[I haven't spoken to him] on the rugby front, but I'm sure I'll catch up with him for a beer after the game."

The reunions will all culminate in Kiss's first match in charge of the national team since Joe Schmidt departed following the Wallabies' rousing 57-10 victory over Italy on July 18.

AAP

World.title: NRLW star in hot water for dangerous lifting tackle
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos NRLW star Ali Brigginshaw is facing the prospect of a lengthy stint on the sidelines after being referred straight to the judiciary for a lifting tackle during last weekend's Magic Round.

The Broncos remained unbeaten and on top of the ladder with a commanding 34-4 victory over the Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs, but the win was soured by Brigginshaw's first-half tackle on Bulldogs halfback Tayla Preston.

Brigginshaw was sent to the sin bin after her tackle on Preston, where the Bulldogs player was swung around and lifted before being driven into the ground head-first.

Preston avoided serious injury, and Brigginshaw was handed a grade three dangerous throw charge.

The 36-year-old, who is playing her final season of NRLW before retirement, has never missed a Broncos game since the competition's inception in 2018.

She will argue her case at the judiciary on Tuesday, where she could face a significant ban.

Sydney Roosters forward Aliyah Nasio was the last NRLW player to be referred directly to the judiciary following a brawl at the conclusion of last year's grand final, where she struck Brisbane's Julia Robinson.

Nasio was banned for four matches after being hit with a grade three striking charge.

Brisbane, reigning NRLW premiers, faces Canberra this week, followed by a grand final rematch with the Roosters, then a derby against the Gold Coast Titans.

World.title: Canberra secures new NBL role amid expansion team hopes
World.content:
Canberra is one step closer to hosting an NBL team for the first time in more than two decades, the league's parent company chief executive has said.

The NBL's in-season competition, the Ignite Cup, will undergo a shake-up with the tournament's finals set to move from the Gold Coast to Canberra's AIS Arena.

It is the latest competition development in the nation's capital as speculation grows that the league is looking to expand into Canberra along with Darwin, the Gold Coast and a second Sydney team.

Ingles comes 'home' in coup NBL signing The legendary Boomers and NBA star will return to Australia's NBL for the first time since 2009, signing with Melbourne United for two years.

Competition executives have said they want to grow the current 10-team league, but new clubs will have to have the capacity to host at least 8,000 spectators.

With the ACT government announcing it will build the Canberra Convention and Entertainment precinct, hope remains the city can secure an NBL team for the first time since the Canberra Cannons were last involved in 2003.

The Cannons won three NBL titles before relocating to Newcastle, while the Sydney Kings now play some regular season matches at AIS Arena.

Admitting he would have loved to announce a Cannons rebirth on Monday, NBL Group CEO David Stevenson still gave every indication the league was eyeing the capital.

"We've got strong confidence that we can work together with Basketball ACT, with everyone involved in the sport to make sure that hopefully once the venue gets approved, that we can build a great team," he said.

"What we're building is a really strong business case, and it's not just about what happens at the game; it's the economic contribution that's really important for us."

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr added that a minimum of 7,500 seats were planned for the Canberra Convention and Entertainment precinct.

"A key element of the business case is having a basketball team play there, or more than one basketball team, actually. But it's not just a basketball stadium, it's got to accommodate other uses as well," Barr said.

"The AIS Arena is a fantastic venue, but it sort of maxes out at about 5,000 people.

"It was very clear in talking both to live music promoters, to the major sporting organisations … that we were missing out because 5,000 was too small."

But before expansion, the nation's capital will have to settle for the midweek Ignite Cup, an NBL competition involving 20 games held on Wednesday nights.

The four most successful teams will compete for a share in $550,000 when they progress to the semifinals in Canberra on February 19 before the decider on February 21.

The NBL's MVP Awards are also moving from Melbourne for the first time in more than a decade and will be hosted at the Great Hall in Canberra's Parliament House.

AAP

World.title: McIlroy headlines summer of golf with DeChambeau targeted
World.content:
The return of grand slam winner Rory McIlroy and the first Australian PGA Championship in Sydney this century highlights a 19-event summer of golf starting this month.

With the global professional golf scene in a state of flux, the Australasian Tour has secured a record partnership and announced a jam-packed schedule with major championship and European Tour spots once again up for grabs.

McIlroy back gracing Melbourne fairways, this time at iconic Kingston Heath from December 3–6, and the PGA Championship at The Lakes possibly featuring big-hitting fan favourite Bryson DeChambeau, are the two hottest tickets.

McIlroy completes one of his missions Rory McIlroy's appearance at the Australian Open in Melbourne has gone a long way to restoring the prestige of the tournament.

Record crowds followed the Northern Irishman at last year's Australian Open at Royal Melbourne before McIlroy successfully defended his US Masters title at Augusta National in April.

Officials revealed they were also targeting two-time US Open winner DeChambeau for the PGA, which was last held in Sydney back in 1998.

The new season begins in the now traditional style with the PNG Open at Royal Port Moresby Golf Club on August 27–30 before visiting all mainland states in Australia, as well as New Zealand's north and south islands, across the 19-tournament schedule.

The centenary Queensland PGA Championship will take place on the Kurrai course at Nudgee Golf Club in Brisbane from November 19–22.

Boasting a past champions list that includes Australian greats Greg Norman, David Graham and Peter Senior, the event will be played immediately before the Australian PGA Championship.

Co-sanctioned by the European Tour, the Australian PGA Championship also marks the start of the Race to Dubai, the tour's season-long rankings competition.

The PGA Tour of Australasia will also feature two new tournament venues in 2026–27.

Secret Harbour Golf Links, south of Perth, will host the WA Open for the first time, while Peninsula Kingswood Country Golf Club becomes the new home of Players Series Victoria as a forerunner to hosting next year's Australian Open.

There is a switch of order for the three-leg New Zealand swing in February that proved to be a huge success in 2026.

The New Zealand Open will now be the finale, following the Japan-Australasia Championship that returns for its second year at Royal Auckland & Grange Golf Club.

PGA Tour of Australasia schedule

PNG Open, Royal Port Moresby Golf Club, August 27–30

WA PGA Championship, Kalgoorlie Golf Course, October 8–11

WA Open, Secret Harbour Golf Links, October 15–18

Players Series SA, Willunga Golf Course, October 22–25

NSW Open, The Vintage Golf Club, November 12–15

Queensland PGA Championship, Nudgee Golf Club, November 19–22

Australian PGA Championship, The Lakes Golf Club, November 26–29

Australian Open, Kingston Heath Golf Club, December 3–6

Vic PGA Championship, Moonah Links Resort, December 10–13

Players Series Perth, Royal Fremantle Golf Club, January 7–10

Players Series Victoria, Peninsula Kingswood Country Golf Club, Jan 14–17

Vic Open, 13th Beach Golf Links, January 21–24

Players Series Murray River, Cobram Barooga Golf Club, January 28–31

Players Series Sydney, Castle Hill Country Club, February 4–7

NZ PGA Championship, Paraparaumu Beach Golf Club, February 11–14

Japan-Australasia Championship, Royal Auckland & Grange Golf Club, February 18–21

New Zealand Open, Millbrook Resort, February 25–28

The National Tournament, The National Golf Club, March 18–21

AAP

World.title: Quick hits: Delta stuns with Aussie classic, 76yo claims history-making gold
World.content:
Delta Goodrem belts out an Aussie classic, a 76-year-old makes Commonwealth Games history and a cycling star is proud to have not thrown up on the podium.

Here are the quick hits from day nine of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Delta makes it a hat-trick with Aussie classic

Delta Goodrem produced a breathtaking performance in the closing ceremony. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

It was a closing ceremony featuring some serious Australian star power, with Delta Goodrem headlining proceedings.

It was the third time, after Melbourne 2006 and Gold Coast 2018, that Goodrem had performed at a Commonwealth Games, and the Australian icon was in fine form at the Hydro indoor arena in Glasgow.

Goodrem was revealed to the crowd in dramatic fashion, lit by a spotlight and sitting at a grand piano, belting out her classic Born To Try, before rising from her seat and welcoming the athletes into the venue with an inspired medley of her hits.

And the performance reached a real crescendo when she welcomed Scottish pop star Cammy Barnes to the stage for a rendition of the most classic of Aussie classics, John Farnham's You're the Voice.

Goosebumps in Glasgow.

2. 76-year-old creates Games history

Louise Hoskins made history on the final day of competition. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Louise Hoskins, 76, made history on the final day of competition in Glasgow, becoming the oldest medal winner in Commonwealth Games history.

She, along with partner Serena Bonnell, won gold in the women's Para bowls, defeating New Zealand in a classic.

It was Bonnell who provided the winning moment for the Aussies, conjuring a sublime shot late in the second set to secure the win.

The oldest competitor in Glasgow, Hoskins was struggling to wrap her head around the enormity of the achievement.

"It is incredible. I'm still pinching myself," she said.

"I never thought I'd ever get [a gold medal] at my age. Get out there and have a go, and never give up."

Asked how she planned to celebrate, Hoskins noted Bonnell still owed her a few drinks.

What will it be then?

"Whatever Serena's going to give me," Hoskins laughed.

3. Cycling star proud not to spew on podium

Leigh Hoffman looked far from comfortable on the podium. (Getty Images: Rob Casey/SNS Group)

Australian Leigh Hoffman won four medals in a packed track cycling program, including a gold on the final day of competition.

He was the second-last rider in the men's 1,000m time trial, so had a truncated warm-down before climbing onto the podium to receive his gold medal.

And he looked far from comfortable on the top step.

"You don't feel human," he says.

"You're just so cooked, my legs are still burning right now, I think it's been a solid hour. There's no pain like it for sprint and endurance – 1 kilometre all-out sprint, 58 seconds of pure pain. I'm still feeling it.

"I made sure to eat about four hours out so my stomach was pretty empty. I'm proud I didn't spew."

This is the sprint and keirin specialist's first 1km time trial in six years, but he says he has no plans to keep riding them at world titles, although he may go again in Amdavad in four years' time.

4. Aussie chef de mission gets ink

Loading...

Australia's chef de mission Petria Thomas loves the Friendly Games — and understandably so.

She was a nine-time Commonwealth gold medallist during her decorated swimming career and has just overseen a Games in which Australia claimed 70 golds, 41 more than the next best nation, England.

On the final day of competition, Thomas was seen out in Glasgow getting herself a permanent testament to the event for which she has so much affection.

She said the Games have a special place in her heart, and now a special place on her body.

"I've thought about it for a long time and the Commonwealth Games has been such a big part of my life, as big a part as the Olympics. So I thought why not get the Commonwealth Sport mark as well, and I'll wear it very proudly," Thomas said.
